description: An archival service and a captain's log of the news: the desk's analysis, stamped objective, and the world's reporting filed beneath it, stamped subjective. Founded 2026.

items.title: Inflation Runs Hot at 0.4 Percent, Hegseth Calls the Charges a Farce, and Abu Dhabi\u2019s First Day Ends Without a Breakthrough
items.content_html:
The Midday File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Inflation Runs Hot at 0.4 Percent, Hegseth Calls the Charges a Farce, and Abu Dhabi’s First Day Ends Without a Breakthrough

The news at midday: the morning’s one scheduled number came in a tenth hotter than the morning expected it, on both measures; the morning’s one scheduled witness answered his accusers for twenty-five minutes and the vote on him moved up a day; the market that rose on Monday gave back part of the rise at the open and then steadied on a filing; and the two tables the week opened—Abu Dhabi and Paris—produced a duration, a seating plan and no agreement by noon.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Tuesday, November 10, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 28, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today, and from Edition No. 27, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today. Where the midday figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open, and the earlier editions stand unrevised, as a log stands.

The Midday in Brief

Midday corrected the morning on the number, on the vote, and on the speaker, and it left every negotiation and every count exactly where the night left them. The Bureau of Labor Statistics put October’s consumer prices up 0.4 percent on the month and core prices up 0.3 percent, in the Reuters account filed below; the overnight edition carried a consensus of 0.3 and 0.2, and the correction is a tenth on each measure, stated in the section below. At the Pentagon, Secretary Hegseth held his first press conference since May and called Representative Massie’s eight articles a farce, a stunt and sabotage, in the Washington account filed below; Mr. Massie answered that the House votes today, on a procedural motion first, with votes expected at 1730—not Wednesday, as the midnight file had it. In New York the three main indexes opened lower, the ten-year yield stood near 4.99 percent, and Brent crude traded below ninety dollars for the first time since August, before the Anthropic filing, printed below, steadied the technology shares by mid-morning. In Abu Dhabi the first day of the three-way talks ended after nearly four hours and resumes Wednesday, with no breakthrough announced. In Jerusalem the opposition named its candidate for speaker, Matan Kahana of Yashar, and the 26th Knesset opened in the afternoon with Speaker Ohana taking the oath and the chair. Neither Senate race was called by noon, and no new figure for either was published in the morning.

The Correction at Noon: The Number Came In a Tenth Hot on Both Measures

The day’s first official statement was a number, and the number corrects the consensus this paper printed at 0400. The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, after rising 0.6 percent in September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said in its release; core prices, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as they did in September and in August—a third straight month at that rate, in the bureau’s figures as carried and the release account filed below. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 0.3 percent on the headline and 0.2 percent on the core. The overnight edition carried that consensus; the print is a tenth above it on both measures, and the desk files the correction at the head of the edition, where corrections belong. Inside the index: energy rose 0.7 percent, against 5.2 percent in September, with gasoline up 1.0 percent against 9.1 percent; food rose 0.5 percent, with food at home up 0.4 percent; shelter rose 0.3 percent and accounted for more than 30 percent of the monthly increase; real average hourly earnings were unchanged on the month. No annual rate was published, for the reason the overnight edition gave: the bureau collected no October 2025 data during last year’s lapse in appropriations, so there is no October-to-October comparison to print. September’s annual rate, 3.7 percent, remains a September figure. The next report, covering November, is scheduled for December 10—one day after the Federal Reserve meeting this report now feeds.

The print met, exactly, the test a governor of the Federal Reserve had set for it four and a half hours before it landed. Governor Christopher Waller, speaking in London in remarks published at 0900 GMT, said he was leaning toward supporting a 25-basis-point increase at the December 8–9 meeting even if October improved on September, and that if core prices rose around 0.3 percent or higher, a 50-basis-point increase should be considered, because hiking only 25 would put the Fed’s credibility at risk, in the London account and the remarks account filed below. Core printed 0.3 percent. The governor’s condition is therefore met on his own stated terms; the committee’s decision is not his alone and has not been taken. The market’s pricing moved in the same direction before and after the release: traders priced an almost 99 percent chance of a December increase in one account filed below, fully priced two quarter-point increases by March in another, and had priced better than 80 percent for December before the print. The accounts differ on the instrument and the hour; they agree on the direction, and the desk prints the agreement and the differing figures in the Cocked Hat.

Washington at Noon: Twenty-Five Minutes at the Pentagon, a Vote at 1730

Secretary Hegseth answered the articles the way the articles were filed—in public, by name, and without conceding any of them. In his first Pentagon press conference since May—six months in the Associated Press count, 180 days in the count this paper has carried—the secretary said no Secretary of War or Secretary of Defense has ever been impeached in 250 years for carrying out lawful military operations, that the effort is about policy disagreements and not high crimes, and that his accuser is a rogue lawmaker, in the Associated Press account filed below. The other accounts carry the same sentences in his sharper words: a farce and a stunt, in the Reuters account; “This is not patriotism. This is sabotage,” in the briefing account; and, on the troops, that anyone coming for the warriors would have to come through him, in the Pentagon account filed below. On the record he defends, he cited Operation Epic Fury’s more than 13,000 targets struck and the destruction of Iran’s navy and of more than 80 percent of its nuclear industrial base; those are the secretary’s figures, printed as his. The conference lasted roughly 25 minutes and took a handful of questions. The articles themselves are unchanged since Monday: three charging the Iran campaign under the War Powers Resolution, and the rest covering the school strike at Minab, the vessel strikes, Venezuela, Yemen, and the alleged retaliation against Senator Kelly. They are allegations in a charging document, found by no court.

The second correction of the day is the House’s clock. The midnight edition carried House leaders as having until Wednesday to table, refer or vote. On Tuesday morning Representative Massie posted that the House votes today: the first vote is on a procedural motion to kill the resolution, such as a motion to refer it to committee, and if that effort is overcome the House proceeds to debate and a vote on the articles, in the schedule account and the Reuters account filed below. The daily schedule Mr. Massie shared puts the House in at 1000 for morning hour and at noon for legislative business, with the first and last votes expected at 1730. At noon the procedural motion stands listed and unvoted. A simple majority impeaches in the House; conviction and removal would require two-thirds of the Senate, where Republicans hold 53 seats in the accounts filed below. Whatever Tuesday evening decides, the accounts agree the effort returns in January if it fails now, when the new Congress is sworn in on January 3.

The Markets’ Reading at Noon: A Hotter Print, a Lower Open, and Oil Below Ninety

Wall Street’s reading of the morning was given at the open, and it was a partial retraction of Monday, not a reversal of it. The Dow fell 226.5 points, or 0.43 percent, at the open to 52,163.21; the S&P 500 fell 36.8 points, or 0.49 percent, to 7,513.09; and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 205.7 points, or 0.81 percent, to 25,047.448, in the Reuters snapshot filed below. A second snapshot at 0948 ran a touch lower on all three—the Dow down 0.47 percent, the S&P 500 down 0.58 percent, the Nasdaq down 0.70 percent—with the ten-year Treasury yield at 4.988 percent, up from Monday’s close of 4.862 percent, in the early-session account filed below. Nvidia fell 2.6 percent in one opening account and 1.6 percent in a pre-open account; the chip shares that led Monday’s rise gave back part of it. Europe, which had risen into the number—the FTSE 100 up 0.5 percent at London’s midday, the CAC 40 up 1.2 percent and the DAX up 1.3 percent, in the London midday account filed below—pared its gains after it. Oil completed the morning’s sentence: Brent fell more than 3 percent and traded below ninety dollars a barrel for the first time since late August, at $89.88 in one account, with West Texas Intermediate down more than 2 percent to below $85, in the global markets account filed below. The same barrel that settled at $92.57 on Monday has now fallen through two round numbers in two days, on the same cause the accounts have named throughout: a president holding off further strikes on Iran.

By mid-morning the fall had steadied, and the steadying had a name. Both Nasdaq indexes erased their opening losses and traded into positive territory as attention shifted to Anthropic’s planned listing, before backing off to stand near unchanged, in the rebound account filed below. The filing behind the move is the morning’s second large document. Anthropic, in an updated prospectus filed Tuesday, will offer 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78 a share, raising $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion, at a valuation of up to $1.404 trillion on a fully diluted basis, in the filing account filed below; the Reuters accounts put the non-diluted value at about $1 trillion to $1.02 trillion, the difference being the treatment of options and restricted stock, in the Reuters account and the exclusive account filed below. A separate $26 billion private placement with cornerstone investors including Google, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices stands beside the offering. The terms filed Tuesday are lower than the terms briefly circulated to bankers on Monday night and retracted—about 867 million shares at up to $80—and lower than the $2 trillion discussed earlier in the year, against a May private valuation of $965 billion. Run-rate revenue stood at $81 billion at the end of October. Trading is expected on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT near November 19. On the morning the print argued for dearer money, the largest test of the AI boom priced itself anyway, at a lower price than it first asked.

Abu Dhabi at Noon: Four Hours, a Framework Proposed, and the Land Left for Wednesday

The talks the overnight edition filed as open are, at noon, adjourned for the day, and the day produced a duration and a method and no result. The first day concluded after nearly four hours, the RIA Novosti account said, and the talks are expected to resume Wednesday, according to the press office of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, in the Associated Press account filed below. The day’s order is on the record: it began with a meeting of the Ukrainian team, the American envoys and representatives of the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission, and then moved to the trilateral format with Russia. Mr. Kushner, opening, said the United States wanted to draw lessons from previous efforts and develop a new structure, and Washington is pressing a new European security framework, in the framework account filed below. One account citing an American official puts day one on policing a future ceasefire, with territory waiting until day two, and reports the same official saying both sides had privately shown some flexibility over a possible swap of territory, in the running-order account filed below. That flexibility rests on one unnamed official’s briefing and is printed as such. The stated positions have not moved in public, and no breakthrough has been announced by any delegation. The desk files four hours, a framework proposed, and the land question carried to Wednesday.

Paris at Noon: The Second Day, Ukraine’s Minister in the Room, No Statement in the File

The G7’s two days in Paris ran out at midday with the argument it opened with, now spoken by the guest as well as the hosts. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, joined Tuesday’s session on Ukraine—air defence, economic pressure, Black Sea navigation—having said before departing, “No one has the right to decide our fate behind our backs,” in the Paris account filed below. Germany’s sentence stands: Europe belongs at this table, and no fundamental change to Europe’s security architecture is necessary, right or appropriate—an answer, in substance, to the framework Mr. Kushner proposed in Abu Dhabi the same morning. France’s stands: Europeans will participate in the Abu Dhabi discussions. The Kremlin’s stands against both: the negotiations remain trilateral. The Abu Dhabi lists at noon agree with the Kremlin on the main table and with France on the rooms around it. The second session took up instability in the Middle East, with the European ministers warning against renewed American strikes on Iran and arguing for restoring normal shipping through Hormuz, in the ministers account filed below. Canada announced fresh sanctions on Russia on Monday. France had indicated the meeting might produce no joint statement; at noon none is in the file, and the desk files its absence as an absence, not as a rupture.

Jerusalem at Noon: A Candidate Named, an Oath Taken, and the Chair Held for Now

Jerusalem supplied the day’s third correction: the unnamed speaker of the overnight file has a name. The opposition bloc on Tuesday chose former minister Matan Kahana of Mr. Eisenkot’s Yashar party as its candidate for speaker, to replace Amir Ohana of Likud, in the candidate account filed below. The naming settles the question the mandate carried from Sunday—who, if the chair changes hands—and leaves the other two open: at least 61 members must sign or vote for a replacement, Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc stands at 48, and Mr. Ohana has said he will not hold the vote on inauguration day but will schedule it within the following week on a valid request. The ceremony itself ran on its printed schedule: a plaza ceremony at 1520 Jerusalem time and the plenary at 1600, which is 0900 in Washington. In the opening broadcast account, President Herzog addressed the session, called on lawmakers to debate with respect, and invited Speaker Ohana to take the oath before handing him the chair; Mr. Ohana pledged, Psalm 122 was recited, and the roll-call pledges of the 120 members proceeded under his chairmanship, with one warning issued to a member over an interruption, in the opening account filed below. The account itself cautions that the broadcast segments reviewed do not establish that all 120 oaths were completed, and the desk prints the caution with the fact. Mr. Ohana’s assumption of the chair for the opening is a step in the ceremony, not the outcome of the speaker question; Mr. Netanyahu remains prime minister, and the mandate runs to December 6. One figure in the file disagrees with itself: the overnight edition carried 47 first-time members, and Tuesday’s candidate account carries 46. The desk prints both in the Cocked Hat and settles neither.

Iran at Noon: No New Sentence, and a Barrel Below Ninety as the Market’s Translation

Neither capital added a sentence to the Iran file in the morning, and the file at noon is the standing one, with one price changed underneath it. The president’s position stands as Monday’s: fresh strikes held off for now after appeals from Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait; the naval blockade and Operation Iron Gate kept in place; forces locked and loaded if the position changes, in the Reuters account and the pause account filed below. Tehran’s two registers stand: negotiate with dignity, from its president; imaginary talks and the seven conditions, from its security council secretary. Secretary Rubio’s sentence stands against both: no progress, and the demands not realistic. One unconfirmed report in the morning file says, on unnamed sources, that the United States is prepared to let Iran keep enriching uranium at 3.67 percent and that Tehran is willing to accept that limit; neither government has confirmed it, and the desk files it as one unconfirmed report, not as a term. The movement in the file is financial, not verbal: Brent’s fall below ninety dollars is the market’s translation of the pause. What the two capitals agree on remains what they agreed on at midnight: the blockade exists. It is imposed in one account and demanded lifted in the other, and it stood all morning.

Kraków at Noon: The Autopsies’ Second Day, and No Findings Published

Kraków’s file at noon is an instrument running, not a result. The autopsies of the nine victims, begun Monday, were expected to take about two days, which puts their completion at about today; no findings from them had been published by noon, and the desk does not fill the space where findings will go. The standing facts are Monday’s: the suspect died at about 0430 on Monday after at least three operations; the case against the dead man will in time be closed while the investigation around him—whether he acted alone or was inspired, the phones, computers and 11 firearms under analysis—continues; and the prosecutors’ limit stands, that they have no findings that would let them state responsibly that he was inspired by any particular ideology. The interior ministry’s review of gun licensing, announced after police data showed more than 50,000 new licences issued in 2025, is the file’s one new policy instrument; both the gunman and his father held permits. The city’s own mourning runs through tomorrow, November 11. The wounded stand at 15 in hospital in the governor’s count, against 17 in the prosecutors’ earlier count; the disagreement is carried in the Cocked Hat, as it has been since Monday.

The Count at Noon: Both Deadlines Fall Today, and No New Figure by Noon

For a sixth day neither Senate race was called, and the morning published no new figure for either race; Tuesday’s part in both files is deadlines, not numbers, until the counts run. Alaska’s next scheduled count falls today, carrying early votes cast October 30 to November 2, absentee and questioned ballots, on a race standing in the last state posting at Mary Peltola 102,962 to Dan Sullivan 102,325—a margin of 637 first-choice votes, with no candidate near 50 percent and the ranked-choice tabulation set for November 18. A running results account updated Tuesday carries the same race in rounder figures as of November 9—Ms. Peltola at 48.6 percent to Mr. Sullivan’s 47.5 percent, more than 220,000 ballots counted and about 78.5 percent of ballots in, in the running account filed below; the percentages and the raw posting are two printings of one standing count, not two counts. Mississippi’s deadlines fall today: mail ballots postmarked by Election Day must arrive and affidavit voters must cure their identification, on a race standing at Scott Colom 467,930 to Cindy Hyde-Smith 465,356, a margin of 2,574 on about 97 percent counted in the Associated Press estimate; the same running account carries Mississippi in percentages as 49.1 to 48.8 with 99 percent counted, a figure the desk cannot reconcile with the 97 percent estimate and prints as a disagreement in the Cocked Hat, in the delay account filed below. Counties certify by November 13, and Mississippi has no automatic recount provision. Alaska’s count, when it posts, will move in the state’s afternoon, which is Washington’s evening; the midday file therefore closes the count where the night left it, with both of its named days arrived and neither of its numbers yet moved. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide. Colorado’s 4th District stands uncalled with them.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On the December increase, almost 99 percent in one pricing account, fully priced by March in another, and better than 80 percent before the print in a third—three instruments, one direction. On Anthropic, $1.404 trillion fully diluted against about $1.02 trillion not diluted: a difference of definition, printed as one. On the open, the Reuters snapshot and the 0948 snapshot differing by tenths on all three indexes, as snapshots an hour apart will. On Abu Dhabi’s flexibility, one unnamed official’s briefing against every delegation’s public silence. On the enrichment report, one unconfirmed account against no confirmation from either capital. On Jerusalem’s new members, 47 in the overnight file and 46 in Tuesday’s candidate account. On Mississippi’s completeness, about 97 percent in the wire estimate and 99 percent in the running account, irreconcilable at noon. On Kraków’s wounded, 15 in the governor’s hospital count against 17 in the prosecutors’ earlier count. Against the triangle, the midday’s single-valued facts are these: prices rose 0.4 percent and core prices 0.3 percent in October, a tenth hot on both measures against the consensus, with no annual rate in existence; Governor Waller’s stated condition for considering a half-point increase was met by the core print; Secretary Hegseth spoke for about 25 minutes and conceded nothing; the House’s first vote on his articles is set for Tuesday evening; Brent traded below ninety dollars; Anthropic filed at $70 to $78; Abu Dhabi’s first day ran nearly four hours and produced no announced breakthrough; Matan Kahana is the opposition’s candidate for speaker and Amir Ohana holds the chair; and no Senate race was called. The log proceeds to the evening.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 35 items.

Subjective
Reuters, via SRN News — a hot October inflation report rattles markets

United States consumer prices increased more than expected in October, leaving the Federal Reserve on course to raise interest rates next month. The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent last month after advancing 0.6 percent in September; economists polled by Reuters had forecast 0.3 percent. Core prices rose 0.3 percent, against a forecast of 0.2 percent. The bureau did not publish year-over-year readings because last year’s shutdown prevented collection of October 2025 data; annual inflation was 3.7 percent in September. Governor Waller, the account notes, had said the central bank ought to raise borrowing costs in December even if inflation cooled.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine — consumer inflation slows to 0.4 percent in October as energy pressures ease

The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers increased 0.4 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in October after rising 0.6 percent in September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Core inflation was unchanged at 0.3 percent, the same rate as September and August. Energy prices increased 0.7 percent, sharply slower than September’s 5.2 percent rise; food prices rose 0.5 percent after remaining unchanged in September. No annual rate was published, because comparable October 2025 data were unavailable following the lapse in appropriations.

Subjective
USA Today — inflation slowed in October, but annual data is missing after the shutdown

Consumer prices climbed 0.4 percent in October, down from 0.6 percent in September and higher than forecasters expected; the Cleveland Fed’s nowcast had projected 0.24 percent. Core inflation rose 0.3 percent. The report is the last look at consumer prices the Federal Reserve will get before its December meeting, and one economist quoted says it most likely seals a rate increase to close the year. The account carries the gasoline figures: regular gasoline up 34 percent and diesel up 64 percent since February 28, on AAA data, with the national average at $3.98 on November 10.

Subjective
SHRM — inflation continued to rise in October

The consumer price index increased 0.4 percent in October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on November 10, higher than the 0.3 percent economists expected. Shelter rose 0.3 percent and accounted for more than 30 percent of the monthly increase; food increased 0.5 percent, with food at home up 0.4 percent and food away from home up 0.5 percent; energy increased 0.7 percent after jumping 5.2 percent in September. Real average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October.

Subjective
Zacks — pre-markets drop on warmer CPI numbers

Pre-market futures swung lower ahead of the opening bell on October consumer prices of plus 0.4 percent on the month, 20 basis points below September’s 0.6 percent and 10 above consensus; core came in at plus 0.3 percent, also 10 hotter than expected. Bond yields climbed with the numbers: 4.936 percent on the ten-year, 4.627 percent on the two-year and 5.292 percent on the thirty-year, in the account’s prints. The small-business optimism index for October ticked down to 97.8.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine, carrying Reuters — Governor Waller plans to support at least a quarter-point rate hike in December

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday he would support raising short-term borrowing costs next month even if the data showed inflation cooled, and would consider an upsized half-point increase if the picture worsened. If core consumer prices rise 0.3 percent or more from September, a 50-basis-point hike should be considered at the December meeting, he said, adding that hiking only 25 would put the Fed’s credibility at risk. Markets, the account says, had priced in about an 85 percent chance of a December increase to a 4.00 to 4.25 percent range.

Subjective
American Banker — Governor Waller calls for raising interest rates 25 basis points, at least

Governor Waller, in prepared remarks delivered in London on Tuesday morning, said he anticipates supporting a rate increase at the December meeting even if the consumer price print improves, and that if October’s monthly reading comes in at or above September’s level a 50-basis-point increase should be considered. The account’s key insight is that one of the Board’s leading monetary experts is committed to a December increase and could support a half-point move. He cited concern at the breadth of price increases, including core goods and core market-based services excluding housing.

Subjective
Associated Press, via Military.com — Secretary Hegseth says the impeachment push is about policy disagreements, not high crimes

WASHINGTON (AP): Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth dug in for a fight on Tuesday against his potential impeachment, telling reporters a rogue lawmaker is targeting him over policy disagreements and not the high crimes the founders intended. In the 250 years of the republic, no Secretary of War or Secretary of Defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations, he said. The briefing was his first from the Pentagon in six months. Representative Massie, who lost his primary to a president-backed opponent, filed the resolution on Monday; it focuses largely on the Iran war and includes Yemen and Venezuela.

Subjective
USA Today — Secretary Hegseth defends himself against impeachment: it is a farce

Facing a looming impeachment vote, the Pentagon chief dug in at a news conference on November 10. “What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle,” he said. “It’s a farce and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it.” The news conference lasted roughly 25 minutes and ended after he took a handful of questions, mostly from reporters representing conservative media outlets, in the account’s description. The House was planning to vote on whether to move forward later on November 10.

Subjective
Reuters — the Pentagon chief calls moves to impeach him a farce that will fail

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday called moves to impeach him over abuse of power in the Iran war a farce that would fail. He made the comment at a news conference a day after Representative Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against him, in his first Pentagon news conference since May. In a post on X, Mr. Massie said the House would hold a first vote on Tuesday on a procedural motion to kill the resolution, and that if that effort is overcome, the House will proceed to a real debate and a vote on the articles.

Subjective
New York Post — Secretary Hegseth rips the impeachment effort in his first press conference since May

The secretary went on a fiery tirade on Tuesday against Representative Massie over his bid to impeach him, accusing the rogue legislator of sabotage: “This is not patriotism. This is sabotage.” He insisted he has done nothing worthy of being just the third cabinet official in history to be impeached. The articles announced Monday include three charges over the war in Iran, one on the operation to capture Venezuela’s leader, one on attacks against the Houthis in Yemen, one on ignoring laws aimed at minimizing civilian casualties, one for extrajudicial killings on alleged drug boats, and one for free-speech violations against Senator Kelly.

Subjective
Defense News — Secretary Hegseth denounces the farce impeachment in his first briefing since May

The secretary vehemently defended himself on Tuesday against impending impeachment proceedings, listing military successes in his first Pentagon press briefing in over six months. The conference lasted fewer than 25 minutes and he answered few questions. The articles, he said, are partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize the military. He painted himself as a champion for the troops, saying that if they want to come for the warriors, they will have to come through him. He praised Operation Epic Fury, claiming Iran’s navy and more than 80 percent of its nuclear industrial base were destroyed. Speaker Johnson will decide if lawmakers vote on each article individually or all eight as a whole, the account says.

Subjective
Military.com — Secretary Hegseth claims an Iran victory in the press conference as the war and impeachment fight continue

The secretary defended the administration’s military campaigns on Tuesday morning, declaring the president had kicked their teeth in in Iran and promising that anyone pursuing American service members would have to come through him. He celebrated Operation Epic Fury as a historic victory, citing more than 13,000 targets struck, extensive damage to Iran’s military infrastructure and destruction of much of its nuclear industrial capacity. The account notes the resolution seeks to impeach him as a civilian cabinet secretary and does not charge service members, and that the allegations concern his responsibility, including three articles alleging violations of the War Powers Resolution.

Subjective
ANI, via APNA MA TV — “Today the House will vote,” Representative Massie says

Representative Thomas Massie said on Tuesday the House of Representatives would vote on his impeachment resolution against Secretary Hegseth, with an initial procedural vote expected to determine whether it proceeds to debate and a vote on the articles. The first vote would concern a procedural motion aimed at blocking the resolution, including a possible motion to refer it to committee. The daily legislative schedule for Tuesday, November 10 listed the procedural motion among the day’s business; the House was due at 10 a.m. for morning hour and at noon for legislative business, with the first and last votes expected at 5:30 p.m.

Subjective
Reuters, via DevDiscourse — a defiant Secretary Hegseth blasts the impeachment effort ahead of the House vote

The secretary on Tuesday blasted efforts to impeach him as a farce that would embolden adversaries, as the House scheduled a procedural vote for late Tuesday that will test support for the impeachment. Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass even with the president’s Republicans still controlling the House until the new Congress takes over on January 3. Conviction appears unlikely in the Senate, the account says, where a two-thirds majority is required and Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats.

Subjective
Associated Press, via WNCW — Russia and Ukraine hold nearly four hours of United States-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi

ABU DHABI: three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the Emirates, the first such meeting since February, in a two-day session focused on security guarantees. The first day of talks concluded after nearly four hours, RIA Novosti said; they are expected to resume Wednesday, according to the press office of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service. Mr. Umerov said the day began with a meeting between the Ukrainian team, the American envoys and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission, before the trilateral format.

Subjective
National Daily — the United States pushes a new European security framework as the talks begin in Abu Dhabi

United States-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine began in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, with Washington pushing for a new European security framework aimed at ending the war and preventing future conflicts. Opening the negotiations, Mr. Kushner said the United States wanted to develop a new framework by examining previous diplomatic arrangements and identifying what had worked and failed. Ukraine’s delegation, led by Mr. Umerov, began the day with discussions involving American representatives and European officials before moving into the trilateral format with Russia. The talks take place amid continued military operations, with both countries reporting overnight drone and missile attacks.

Subjective
Il Politico — Abu Dhabi peace talks: security guarantees before territory

The round runs Tuesday and Wednesday, November 10 and 11, the first since February, when talks in Geneva broke up without a deal on land. Day one is about policing a future ceasefire and the shape of security once the guns fall silent; territory waits until day two, according to Bloomberg citing an American official. The same official told Reuters both sides had privately shown some flexibility over a possible swap of territory, and that any deal on land would come at the very end, once everything else is settled. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov insisted the talks are trilateral, full stop.

Subjective
Grenada Chronicle — “Europe belongs at this table,” Germany tells the United States before the Ukraine talks

European foreign ministers told Secretary Rubio that Europe must have a say in any deal to end the war, on Monday in Paris at the G7 meeting. “It is certainly neither necessary, nor right, nor appropriate to make a fundamental change” to Europe’s security architecture, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said after talks with Mr. Rubio; “Europe belongs at this table. There can be no solution without Europe, only with Europe.” The two-day Paris meeting ends Tuesday and overlaps the Abu Dhabi talks. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, is set to join a session on Ukraine on Tuesday; “No one has the right to decide our fate behind our backs,” he said before departing. Iran is expected to feature prominently in Tuesday’s discussions.

Subjective
Europe Says — G7 ministers press Secretary Rubio on Iran and Ukraine at the Paris talks

PARIS: G7 top diplomats began a two-day meeting in Paris on Monday, with European foreign ministers set to press Secretary Rubio to ensure any settlement in the war with Russia is fair to Ukraine and to steer clear of any new escalation with Iran. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Europeans would be represented at the Abu Dhabi talks, with France also participating. European ministers warned against renewed American military strikes and advocated instead for the restoration of normal commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. On the sidelines, Canada announced fresh sanctions on Russia on Monday.

Subjective
Reuters, via DevDiscourse — Wall Street opens lower after October’s hot inflation print

Wall Street’s main indexes opened lower on Tuesday after hotter-than-expected inflation data for October threatened to pause a two-day rebound in technology shares and revive the selling pressure of last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 226.5 points, or 0.43 percent, at the open to 52,163.21. The S&P 500 fell 36.8 points, or 0.49 percent, to 7,513.09, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 205.7 points, or 0.81 percent, to 25,047.448.

Subjective
JBizNews — stocks open lower after the October inflation report as bond yields jump

Stocks opened lower on Tuesday as Treasury yields rose after the October inflation report, cutting into Monday’s rally. The Dow was down 0.47 percent at 52,144.30 in a quote stamped 9:48 a.m. Eastern; the S&P 500 was down 0.58 percent at 7,506.25 and the Nasdaq Composite down 0.70 percent at 25,076.221 at the same stamp. The ten-year Treasury yield stood at 4.988 percent, up from the previous close of 4.862 percent. These are early-session snapshots, not closing prices, the account notes. Chip shares were mixed as the market pulled back.

Subjective
Reuters, via DevDiscourse — stocks cut gains, the dollar and yields rise as the CPI cements December rate-hike bets

United States stocks were set for a lower open and European shares pared gains after a hotter-than-anticipated inflation reading bolstered the case for a December increase. Traders are now fully pricing two 25-basis-point increases by March, with the first expected in December, on data compiled by LSEG; the two-year yield rose 14 basis points to 4.69 percent. Brent crude futures fell over 3.2 percent, dipping below the ninety-dollar mark for the first time since late August. Earnings due this week from technology companies including CoreWeave will be another test for markets, the account says.

Subjective
InvestingLive — stocks rebounding despite the higher-than-expected CPI

United States stocks opened on the defensive after the stronger-than-expected report pushed Treasury yields higher, but the tone changed as attention shifted to reports about Anthropic’s planned listing. The Nasdaq Composite was down as much as 294.83 points before trading up as much as 33.69 points, a swing of more than 328 points; the Nasdaq 100 swung more than 449 points from its low to its high. At the account’s writing the Nasdaq Composite was down 0.03 percent and the Nasdaq 100 up 0.07 percent, both off their rebound highs, with the unchanged line back in play. Nvidia remained under pressure.

Subjective
London Stock Exchange — London market midday: the FTSE 100 rises ahead of United States inflation data

Stock prices in London were higher at midday on Tuesday as investors awaited the American inflation figures, while oil majors weighed on the FTSE 100 amid growing hopes of a diplomatic resolution between Washington and Tehran. The FTSE 100 was up 50.82 points, or 0.5 percent, at 10,833.69; the CAC 40 in Paris was up 1.2 percent and the DAX 40 in Frankfurt up 1.3 percent. Shell fell 1.8 percent and BP 1.6 percent. Brent was trading at $91.15 a barrel at midday in London, lower than $94.27 late Monday. New York was called mixed, with the Dow set to open up 0.3 percent and the Nasdaq down 0.2 percent, in the account’s earlier call.

Subjective
TechCrunch — Anthropic sets an IPO price range of $70 to $78 to reach an implied valuation of $1.404 trillion

Anthropic said in an updated filing on Tuesday it would offer a total of 825 million Class A shares at an estimated range of $70 to $78 a share, a sale expected to raise $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion. At the top of the range the company could be worth $1.404 trillion on a fully diluted basis, up from $965 billion in a May fundraise and below the $2 trillion reportedly targeted a couple of months ago. Net proceeds are estimated between $84.6 billion and $93.7 billion in the account’s figures. Run-rate revenue reached $81 billion by the end of October, about $10 billion more than at the end of September. Trading is intended on the Nasdaq near November 19, under the symbol ANT.

Subjective
Reuters, via SRN News — Anthropic eyes a $1.4 trillion valuation in a test of Wall Street’s AI fervor

Anthropic’s listing is set to give the company a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, slightly lower than some investors’ expectations amid a cooling in appetite for AI, setting up a test of Wall Street’s faith in the boom. The company and some investors aim to raise up to $64.4 billion by selling 825 million shares at up to $78. A separate $26 billion will be raised via a private placement with cornerstone investors such as Google, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices. On a non-diluted basis the market value would be about $1 trillion. Details of the deal were briefly circulated to banks late on Monday before being retracted; the preliminary terms showed about 867 million shares at up to $80, for as much as $69.3 billion.

Subjective
Reuters, via Duke FM — Anthropic sets a $1 trillion IPO valuation target in a test of AI fervor

Anthropic is targeting a valuation of up to $1.02 trillion in its listing, its filing showed on Tuesday, well short of the previously discussed amount in the latest sign of cooling investor appetite for AI. The company and some investors aim to raise up to $64.4 billion by selling 825 million shares in a band of $70 to $78. It will also raise $26 billion via a separate private placement with cornerstone investors including Google, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley lead the syndicate of banks underwriting the offering, the account says.

Subjective
The Insight International — the opposition picks Matan Kahana to replace Mr. Ohana as Knesset speaker

JERUSALEM, November 10, 2026: the opposition bloc on Tuesday chose former minister Matan Kahana as its candidate for Knesset speaker, in a bid to take control of parliament from the prime minister’s allies while it tries to form a government. Mr. Kahana, of Mr. Eisenkot’s Yashar party, would replace Amir Ohana of Likud; the speaker controls the Knesset’s agenda, including which bills come to a vote and how committees are run. The announcement came hours before the 26th Knesset was due to be sworn in on Tuesday afternoon. Forty-six of its 120 members are serving for the first time, in this account. At least 61 lawmakers must sign a request or vote to replace the speaker; Mr. Ohana will not hold the vote on inauguration day but will schedule it within the following week on a valid request.

Subjective
JBizNews — President Herzog opens the 26th Knesset session; Mr. Ohana takes the oath and assumes the chair

President Isaac Herzog addressed the opening session of the 26th Knesset on Tuesday, called on lawmakers to debate with respect, and then invited Speaker Amir Ohana to take the parliamentary oath before handing him the chair. In the official broadcast account, Mr. Ohana pledged loyalty to the State of Israel and faithful fulfillment of his mission, and the president transferred management of the session to him. A recital of Psalm 122 followed, and a later segment showed the roll-call pledges under way, with the chair warning a member during an interruption that the next disruption would lead to removal. The account notes these were opening-session steps, not a coalition agreement or a vote to replace the speaker, and that the segments reviewed do not establish that all 120 members had completed their oaths.

Subjective
JBizNews — the 26th Knesset to be sworn in, with the prime minister and president in attendance

The 26th Knesset convenes for its inaugural session and swearing-in ceremony on Tuesday, with President Herzog, Speaker Ohana and Prime Minister Netanyahu in attendance. Lawmakers arrive from 8:00 a.m.; the official ceremony begins at 3:20 p.m. in the plaza, the president arriving with a motorcycle escort and mounted horsemen; the plenary session begins at 4:00 p.m., the secretary-general announcing the president, three trumpet fanfares, the president opening with three strikes of the gavel and an address, then inviting Mr. Ohana to take the oath and preside. The secretary will then call the names of all 120 lawmakers one by one to declare their pledge.

Subjective
USA Today — the Mississippi and Alaska Senate races remain uncalled; the results

The running results file, updated on November 10 to reflect the latest results. In Mississippi, on the account’s tally as of November 9, Mr. Colom leads Ms. Hyde-Smith 49.1 percent to 48.8 percent with 99 percent of votes counted. In Alaska, on the tally as of November 9, Ms. Peltola leads Mr. Sullivan with 48.6 percent of the votes to 47.5 percent, with about 78.5 percent of ballots counted; more than 220,000 ballots have been counted, with 401 of the state’s 403 precincts reporting. The ranked-choice tally in Alaska would not start until November 18 under state law, the account notes.

Subjective
political.org — why the Mississippi and Alaska Senate races remain uncalled days after Election Day

Nearly a week after the November 3 midterms, the Senate contests in Mississippi and Alaska are the only two in the country that remain uncalled. In Mississippi, Mr. Colom led by 43 votes early on November 4 and was ahead by about 2,500 votes with 97 percent counted as of November 7; the deadline for counting ballots is Tuesday, November 10, and certification is Friday, November 13. In Alaska, Ms. Peltola leads by 637 votes with roughly a quarter of ballots outstanding; the ranked-choice tabulation is not expected until after the November 18 deadline for late absentee ballots. Mississippi has no automatic recount provision; Alaska’s contest carries a Justice Department lawsuit, rejected by a federal judge, and a public-records suit from the Peltola campaign, the account notes.

Subjective
The Business Standard, carrying Reuters — the president says he will hold off on fresh Iran strikes for now

President Trump said on Monday he plans to hold off on new military strikes against Iran for the time being, after appeals from countries in the region including Qatar’s prime minister, and plans to keep up a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz for now. Iran’s proposal involves an end to the blockade of its ports, the lifting of some sanctions and a halt to bombing in return for Tehran stopping its own blockade of the strait, with talks on its nuclear programme to follow; the United States has repeatedly rejected that plan, with Secretary Rubio describing Tehran’s conditions in terms the account quotes. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman defended the plan on Monday as the most reasonable offer on the table. Attacks on tankers in the Gulf and the strait ramped up sharply in October and have continued at the highest rate since the war began, the account notes.

Subjective
AnewZ — the president pauses Iran strikes and keeps the Hormuz blockade

President Trump said on Monday he would hold off on new military strikes against Iran for now, after appeals from Gulf countries, but would keep the naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz in place. “The United States of America is fully locked and loaded with the best equipment ever made, and we don’t think there’s going to be any reason to use it,” he told reporters. He named Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait among those wanting Washington to avoid new attacks. Iran gave the meeting a cool reception: Mr. Rezaei said the United States should stop manufacturing fake news about imaginary talks. Iranian media said the United States struck Qeshm island late on Sunday night, in the account’s final item.
items.summary: The midday file for Tuesday, November 10, 2026: October consumer prices rose 0.4 percent on the month and core prices 0.3 percent for a third straight month, both a tenth above the consensus the overnight edition carried, with no annual rate published because the 2025 shutdown left no October 2025 index; Governor Waller’s stated test for considering a half-point December increase—core at 0.3 percent or higher—was met by the print. Secretary Hegseth, in his first Pentagon press conference since May, called the eight impeachment articles a farce, a stunt and sabotage, and the House takes its first procedural vote Tuesday evening, two days earlier than the midnight file expected. Wall Street opened lower, Brent broke below ninety dollars for the first time since August, and the Anthropic filing steadied technology by mid-morning. In Abu Dhabi the first day ended after nearly four hours with no breakthrough announced; in Paris the G7 closed its second day with Ukraine’s foreign minister in the room and no joint statement in the file; in Jerusalem the opposition named Matan Kahana for speaker as the 26th Knesset opened and Speaker Ohana took the oath and the chair. Neither Senate race was called and no new count figure was published by noon. Collected at 1200.

items.title: Starship Flight 15: The First Attempt to Catch Both Stages of the World’s Largest Rocket
items.content_html:
Technology Report

A Launch Briefing—The Vehicle, the Flight Record, Friday’s Plan, the Two Catches, the Starlink Payload, the Economics, the Moon and Mars, the Field, the License, and the Risks

Objective

Starship Flight 15: The First Attempt to Catch Both Stages of the World’s Largest Rocket — Technology Report

SpaceX is targeting Friday, November 13, 2026, for the fifteenth flight of Starship, the tallest, heaviest, and most powerful rocket ever flown, and the flight is a target and not a settled event: the Federal Aviation Administration license modification that would permit its central maneuver had not been issued as of Tuesday, November 10. The plan, as SpaceX published it on November 7, is to launch from Orbital Launch Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas, in a 75-minute window opening at 5:45 p.m. EST, catch the Super Heavy booster in the launch tower’s arms at 6 minutes 35 seconds after liftoff, deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites, keep the ship in orbit for about 22 hours and roughly 14 revolutions, and then attempt the first catch of an orbital upper stage in history at the same tower, an attempt gated on health conditions the FAA has approved in advance and that the ship’s own commander, Elon Musk, prices at 50 to 60 percent. The ship does not launch into orbit: it ascends on a suborbital trajectory ending in a cleared patch of the Indian Ocean, enters orbit only if it is healthy at 26 minutes, and is offered three scheduled ocean disposals across the day before it commits to the Texas corridor. This briefing files the vehicle and the one size record it has not taken—its demonstrated payload to orbit is about 44 tons, against a planned figure of more than 100 that has not been flown; the fourteen-flight record that leads to Friday, including the first orbital flight on September 28, 2026, and the booster engine-relight failures of Flights 12 and 13 that are the program’s live technical problem; the catch mechanics and the reason the vehicle carries no landing legs; the payload and what 26 third-generation Starlinks mean; the economics, in which every figure is labeled with its claimant, from an estimated $100 million per test flight today to the company’s stated target of $100 to $200 per kilogram; the Moon and Mars architecture that stands behind the flight; the competitive field in November 2026, in which the list of organizations that have recovered an orbital upper stage is empty; the licensing record; and the risks, ranked by the record rather than by drama.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0959 ET, Tuesday, November 10, 2026.

The File in Brief

The flight is a target, and the paper that decides it was still unsigned on Tuesday morning. SpaceX published its Flight 15 mission page on November 7, 2026: the fifteenth flight of Starship is “preparing to launch as soon as Friday, November 13, pending regulatory approval,” from Orbital Launch Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas, in a 75-minute window opening at 4:45 p.m. Central time—5:45 p.m. EST, 22:45 UTC—with backup airspace coverage running November 14 through 19. The Federal Aviation Administration license modification the flight requires is not a routine one: it must authorize, for the first time, the return of the upper stage to the launch site for a tower catch, on a reentry path that crosses northern Mexico and southern Texas and overflies populated areas. Reporting from November 5 through November 10 records no issuance, and SpaceX’s own page still carried the word “pending” at collection time; the license for Flight 14 was issued two days before that flight, so a Thursday or Friday issuance would match the program’s pattern, and nothing in this briefing treats Friday as settled. What follows is the record of the machine, the fourteen flights behind it, the plan as published, and the risks as the record ranks them—filed on Tuesday, four days before the window, and standing unrevised whatever Friday brings.

The vehicle is the largest rocket ever flown by three of the four measures that matter, and the fourth measure is the one the headlines usually get wrong. Starship in its Block 3 form stands 124.4 meters—408 feet—taller than Saturn V’s 110.6; it lifts off at a mass of about 5,300 to 5,533 tons, against Saturn V’s roughly 2,970; and its liftoff thrust, printed as a range because two rating conventions produce two figures, runs from 80.8 to 90.6 meganewtons, more than twice Saturn V’s 34.5 by either reading. It is the tallest, heaviest, and most powerful rocket ever flown. Payload is the measure it has not taken: the figure of more than 100 tons to low Earth orbit is SpaceX’s design target for the fully reusable configuration, a planned figure that has not been demonstrated, while the largest mass the system has actually placed in orbit is about 44 tons of Starlink satellites on Flight 14—below the roughly 118 to 140 tons Saturn V delivered in expendable service. This briefing prints the 100-ton figure only as a target, and the 44-ton figure as the record, every time the subject arises.

Friday’s plan is two catches at one tower, twenty-two hours apart, around a payload deployment and the longest mission the program has attempted. The Super Heavy booster, after separation and a boostback burn, is to be caught by Pad 2’s tower arms at T+6 minutes 35 seconds—the first booster catch attempt since Flight 8 on March 6, 2025, the first of a Block 3 booster, and the first catch of any kind at Pad 2. The ship is to deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites of the Group 31-2 batch between T+35 minutes and T+1 hour 18 minutes, coast through roughly 14 orbits over about 21 hours, deorbit on a single Raptor engine at T+21 hours 36 minutes, reenter over the Pacific, glide across northern Mexico and southern Texas, and be caught by the same tower’s arms at T+22 hours 32 minutes 34 seconds—on Saturday afternoon, Texas time, if Friday’s window opens on schedule. No upper stage of any orbital rocket has ever been caught, or recovered this way, by anyone. A successful double catch would be, in SpaceX’s own framing, “the first full recovery of an orbital launch system.”

The plan is built as a ladder of revocable commitments, and the ladder, not the catch, is its real architecture. The ship does not launch toward orbit. It ascends on a passively safe suborbital trajectory aimed at a cleared area of the Indian Ocean, and only a ship judged healthy performs the orbital insertion burn at T+26 minutes 10 seconds; a sick ship simply comes home the old way. Across the long coast, three scheduled checks—at about T+1 hour 28 minutes over a disposal option near Hawaii, at T+7 hours 16 minutes near Chile, at T+20 hours 42 minutes near Hawaii again—offer controlled ocean disposals before the ship commits. Three of the satellites it deploys carry cameras to photograph its heat shield in orbit, and that imagery feeds the final decision: SpaceX’s published language is that flight controllers “will only permit Starship to return to Starbase if the vehicle’s status meets our internally developed, and FAA-approved, conditions for a return to launch site and catch.” Only after the deorbit burn is the ship committed to the land corridor, and even in entry the profile retains a burn-up option over the ocean and a contingency water landing in the Gulf. Elon Musk’s stated estimate for the ship catch itself, repeated since September, is “at least 50 or 60 percent”—printed here as his estimate, because that is what it is.

The fourteen-flight record behind Friday is better on the ship’s side than on the booster’s, and its live problem has a name: engine relights. The program’s totals stand at 14 flights, nine successes and five failures on the record’s own accounting; three booster catches in four attempts, all at Pad 1 in 2024 and early 2025; one booster reflight; no ship catch attempted. Flight 14, on September 28, 2026, was the first orbital flight: the ship reached about 275 kilometers despite losing one of its three vacuum engines early, deployed all 26 of its Starlink V3 satellites, and then, on a conservative health judgment, cut a planned six-orbit coast to under two orbits and splashed down in the Pacific about three hours after launch. The last three ships have all completed reentry and controlled water landings. The boosters have run the other way: on Flight 12, in May, only 20 of 33 engines relit for boostback and the booster struck the Gulf at high speed; on Flight 13, in July, the landing burn lit 10 of 13 engines and lost five more before a hard impact. Every Block 3 flight so far has had at least one engine anomaly, and Friday asks a Block 3 booster to complete the landing sequence not into the forgiving Gulf but into the arms of the only tower currently flying the type.

The economics are a ladder of labeled claims, and this briefing prints the ladder rather than any rung of it as fact. A Starship flight today, on outside reporting’s estimate, costs roughly $100 million, nothing recovered, which at Flight 14’s 44 tons is over $2,000 per kilogram—worse than Falcon 9 on the same arithmetic. Analyst models of early operations, assuming booster reuse works and ship recovery is validated, produce $15 to $30 million per flight and roughly $100 to $200 per kilogram at full payload; a skeptical school holds at $500 to $1,000 per kilogram through mid-decade on refurbishment and cadence grounds; SpaceX’s stated long-term design target is $100 to $200 per kilogram; and the founder’s floated aspirations, about $10 million per flight and in the limit about $10 per kilogram, are printed in this file as aspirations, the 2019 version of which—about $2 million a flight—operations have not borne out. SpaceX publishes no Starship price and no rate card. The physics under the argument is not disputed: a recovered stack spends propellant and inspection where an expended one spends 39 Raptor engines, two airframes, and a heat shield—and the ship, whose recovery Friday tests for the first time, is where the recurring manufacturing cost concentrates.

Behind the flight stands everything else the machine is for, and all of it waits on the same two undemonstrated capabilities: routine full recovery and orbital refueling. Artemis, restructured in February 2026 after Artemis II’s crewed lunar flyby in April, now plans a crewed Earth-orbit test in mid-2027 and the first crewed landing since Apollo 17 on Artemis IV in 2028, on a lander—SpaceX’s or Blue Origin’s—whose readiness is to decide the assignment; Starship’s lander contract is $2.89 billion, and its architecture requires a propellant depot filled by tanker flights whose published count per landing runs from about 6 to about 22 with no official figure fixed, ahead of a ship-to-ship cryogenic transfer demonstration NASA charts for the first quarter of 2027 that no one has ever performed. Friday’s 22-hour coast is itself part of that preparation: the longest a Starship has stayed in orbit is about three hours, and the boil-off data from a full day aloft does not yet exist. The competitive field, meanwhile, is a study in partial arrival: four organizations have recovered an orbital-class booster—SpaceX, Blue Origin, and, in 2026, China’s CASC and LandSpace—two have reflown one, and the list of those that have recovered an orbital upper stage is empty, while the closest Western rival sits grounded with a wrecked pad and the second sits grounded on a booster nozzle failure, leaving Western heavy lift, this quarter, effectively one company’s.

1. The Vehicle: Tallest, Heaviest, Most Powerful—and the One Measure It Has Not Taken

Starship is a two-stage, fully reusable super heavy-lift launch system, built of stainless steel, burning subcooled liquid methane and liquid oxygen in Raptor engines. The first stage, Super Heavy, is 72.3 meters tall and 9 meters in diameter in Block 3 trim, with 33 Raptor 3 sea-level engines—20 fixed in an outer ring, 13 gimbaling in the center for steering—three enlarged grid fins for aerodynamic control during descent, and no landing legs. The second stage, called Starship or simply the ship, is both upper stage and spacecraft: about 52.1 meters tall on the same 9-meter diameter, six Raptor 3 engines of which three are vacuum-optimized with large bells, a payload bay sized for stacked flat-packed satellites or cargo, four aerodynamic flaps that steer a belly-first descent, and a windward heat shield of about 18,000 hexagonal silica ceramic tiles over an ablative backup layer, built to survive reentry heating of roughly 1,400 degrees Celsius and to be reflown with minimal maintenance. The stages separate by hot staging: the ship lights its engines while still attached and pushes itself away, at about T+2 minutes 21 seconds on Friday’s timeline. The vehicle page SpaceX maintains is clipped below.

Block 3, the version flying Friday, is the third and largest iteration, and its enabling change is the engine. The stack stands 124.4 meters—408.1 feet—on stretched propellant tanks in both stages; propellant capacity across the generations has run from about 4,600 tons in Block 1 to about 4,900 in Block 2 and more again in Block 3. The Raptor 3 produces about 280 tonnes-force of sea-level thrust per engine against the Raptor 2’s 230, at a chamber pressure of about 350 bar, with its plumbing and sensors integrated into the engine body so it needs no separate heat shield of its own. Block 3 also redesigns the booster’s methane feed architecture, replaces its single quick disconnect with two separated connection points, enlarges the grid fins to three, and—on trade reporting, printed at that grade—doubles those fins as the tower’s catch points. The booster’s forward dome now takes the hot-staging blast directly, shielded by a non-structural steel layer and tank pressure, where earlier designs jettisoned a vented interstage.

The biggest-rocket question, which the commission put to the desk directly, has a precise answer, and it is measure by measure. Height: Starship Block 3 at 124.4 meters is the tallest rocket ever flown, ahead of Saturn V at 110.6 meters and NASA’s Space Launch System at about 98. Liftoff mass: about 5,300 to 5,533 tons, against Saturn V’s roughly 2,970—the heaviest object ever flown to space, a distinction a Starship ship already held on Flight 2 in November 2023. Thrust: the Block 3 stack prints two ways, 80.8 meganewtons in block-specific references and about 90.6 computed from 33 Raptor 3s at their published per-engine rating; the gap is a rating-convention gap—installed average against per-engine maximum—not a dispute about the hardware, and either figure is more than twice Saturn V’s 34.5. Payload to orbit is the fourth measure and the exception: Saturn V delivered roughly 118 to 140 tons to low Earth orbit in expendable service, and Starship’s largest demonstrated delivery is about 44 tons. The sentence “Starship can lift roughly 100 tons, far more than any other operational rocket,” in circulation this week, is therefore filed in this briefing at the grade it earns: the 100-ton figure is the reusable configuration’s design target for a vehicle on its fifteenth test flight, not a demonstrated capability, and the honest sentence is that Starship is the largest and most powerful rocket ever flown by height, mass, and thrust, while its payload record, as distinct from its payload target, does not yet exceed Saturn V’s.

The propellant choice is a Mars decision taken on the ground in Texas. Methane and oxygen—methalox—can in principle be manufactured on Mars from water ice and atmospheric carbon dioxide by the Sabatier reaction, which the entire Mars architecture depends on, and methane burns cleaner than kerosene in reusable engines, reducing the coking that complicates reflight. Both reasons are SpaceX’s stated rationale, and both are printed here as rationale; the Sabatier plant that would make Mars propellant exists in no flown form, and the engines’ cleanliness across repeated flights is a record still being written, flight by flight, in section 2.

2. The Flight Record: Fourteen Flights, Five Failures, One Orbital Debut

The record grades each flight against its stated test objectives, and on that accounting the program stands at nine successes and five failures in fourteen flights. The desk prints the accounting with its rule attached, because the rule is generous to the program—a flight that loses a vehicle after meeting its objectives is not a failure on it—and because the flight-by-flight facts below let a reader apply a stricter grade. Three booster catches in four attempts, one booster reflight, zero ship catches attempted, one orbital flight: those are the totals Friday’s plan is written against.

Flights 1 to 4 built the profile the rest of the program stands on. Flight 1, on April 20, 2023, lost several engines and its thrust vector control and was destroyed by its flight termination system about four minutes in, having torn up a launch mount that had no water deluge system; the regulatory process that followed imposed 63 corrective actions. Flight 2, on November 18, 2023, fired all 33 engines for the full first-stage duration, performed the first hot-staging separation, and lost both stages—the booster in its boostback flip, the ship to a fire and automated destruction after it had passed the Kármán line as the heaviest object ever to reach space. Flight 3, on March 14, 2024, reached its target trajectory, ran an internal propellant-transfer demonstration and a dispenser-door test, and lost both stages on return. Flight 4, on June 6, 2024, was the first fully successful profile of the early campaign: the booster splashed down under control in the Gulf on a “virtual tower,” rehearsing the catch, and the ship survived reentry with severe forward-flap burn-through and splashed down in the Indian Ocean within its target region.

Flight 5 made the catch, and Flights 6 to 8 completed the booster half of the recovery record that has stood, untested, for twenty months. On October 13, 2024, Booster 12 flew back to Pad 1 and was caught in midair by the tower’s chopstick arms on SpaceX’s first attempt, while its ship made a controlled reentry and a precise Indian Ocean splashdown. Flight 6, on November 19, 2024, aborted its catch on automated health checks of tower hardware damaged at liftoff—the precedent for every gate in Friday’s plan—diverted to a soft Gulf splashdown, and flew the program’s first in-space Raptor relight. Flight 7, on January 16, 2025, caught Booster 14 cleanly and lost Ship 33 to a propellant leak, its debris raining over the Caribbean. Flight 8, on March 6, 2025, caught Booster 15—the third and, as of this briefing, most recent catch, achieved despite two boostback relight failures—and lost Ship 34 to engine shutdowns on ascent. No catch of any kind has been attempted in the twenty months since Flight 8.

Flights 9 to 11 are the program’s failure year and its recovery of form, in that order. Flight 9, on May 27, 2025, flew Booster 14 a second time—the first reflight of a Super Heavy, with 29 previously flown engines—and lost it at the start of its landing burn; the ship’s payload door failed, a fuel leak cost it attitude control, and it broke up over the Indian Ocean, the Block 2 ship’s third consecutive failure, after which the program paused for three months. Flight 10, on August 26, 2025, deployed eight Starlink simulators, relit a Raptor in space, and splashed the ship down within three meters of its Indian Ocean target despite substantial engine-section damage, while its booster splashed in the Gulf after simulating an engine-out landing. Flight 11, on October 13, 2025, the last Block 2 flight and the last from Pad 1 before its retrofit, brought both stages to controlled splashdowns and its ship through reentry largely undamaged despite tiles deliberately removed—Block 2 ending with its objectives substantially recovered.

The three Block 3 flights of 2026 state Friday’s problem and Friday’s promise in the same hand. Flight 12, on May 22, 2026, the Block 3 debut and Pad 2’s first launch, lost Booster 19 when only 20 of its 33 engines relit for boostback and only one relit in the landing sequence; its ship lost a vacuum Raptor, reached cutoff on engine-out capability, deployed 20 simulators and two modified functional Starlink V3 satellites, and completed a nominal reentry and landing flip. Flight 13, on July 24, 2026, watched Booster 20’s landing burn light 10 of 13 engines and lose five more before a hard Gulf impact, while Ship 40 made the first deployment of production Starlink V3 satellites—20, on a suborbital arc, burned up as planned after testing—then flew a banking maneuver mimicking a Starbase return, splashed down, tipped over, stayed afloat, and was returned to Starbase by boat in October, the first ship to come back to its launch site, albeit by barge. Flight 14, on September 28, 2026, was the orbital debut: Booster 21 to a controlled Gulf splashdown, Ship 41 to orbit at about 275 kilometers on two of its three vacuum engines, all 26 Starlink V3s of Group 31-1 deployed—about 44 tons, the first operational payload Starship has delivered to orbit—and then the coast cut short on a conservative health call and a Pacific splashdown about three hours after launch. The pattern the record shows is printed in the File in Brief and repeated here because Friday turns on it: the ships have completed their side of the profile three flights running, the boosters’ engine relights have failed in sequence, and the company’s demonstrated instinct, once in orbit, is to shorten the mission and protect the vehicle. The program’s launch list, from which this section’s accounting is drawn and against which it was checked, is clipped below.

3. Friday’s Plan: A Ladder of Revocable Commitments

The mission, as SpaceX published it on November 7, flies Booster 22 and Ship 42, the fourth Block 3 pair, under the designation Starlink Group 31-2. The booster’s serial is carried at the grade of reporting—SpaceX’s page names Ship 42, announced October 28, and does not name the booster—while the ship’s is documented. Booster 22 static-fired at Pad 2 on October 25; Ship 42 static-fired at the Massey’s test site on October 26 to 27; Ship 42 had already been through catch rehearsals on September 11 to 12, when Pad 2’s arms lifted and held it in a simulated post-catch position and mated it against the ship quick-disconnect arm while suspended. As of Tuesday the booster stood rolled to Pad 2 and seated on the launch mount, with the ship still to be stacked, flight termination charges to be installed, and the satellites to be loaded. The flight director’s poll for propellant load comes at T−50 minutes on Friday; the webcast begins about 30 minutes before liftoff. SpaceX’s Flight 15 mission page, the source of the timeline that follows, is clipped below.

The ascent and the first catch occupy the flight’s first nine minutes. Liftoff at the window’s opening or after; maximum dynamic pressure at T+58 seconds; booster main engine cutoff at T+2 minutes 19 seconds; hot staging at T+2:21; the boostback burn from T+2:26 to T+3:02; the booster’s landing burn from T+6:10; and the tower catch at T+6:35, the landing burn’s shutdown and the arms’ closure in the same second on the published timeline. The ship’s engines cut off at T+8:09, at which point the ship is on its passively safe suborbital trajectory toward the Indian Ocean and the mission’s first real decision arrives: the orbital insertion burn, T+26:10 to T+26:30, flown only if the ship is healthy. A ship that fails that judgment is not lost; it is simply on the trajectory it was launched on, and it comes down in cleared water as ships have done eight times.

The long middle of the mission is a working coast, not a wait. Between T+35 minutes 1 second and T+1 hour 17 minutes 40 seconds, the ship deploys its 26 Starlink V3 satellites—three of them carrying the camera suites that will image its heat shield—and then settles into the roughly 21-hour coast at about 275 kilometers that SpaceX’s plan describes as roughly 14 orbits. The coast is the program’s first long-duration operating period: propellant boil-off and tank pressure management, battery and thermal cycling through about 14 day-night passes, avionics endurance, and the state of a vehicle that must, at the end of it, light a single engine precisely. Every prior Starship orbital endurance is measured against Flight 14’s three hours; the data the coast produces on boil-off is identified in the technical reporting as a primary objective in itself, because the propellant-transfer architecture of section 7 needs ships to loiter for days to weeks and no one has the numbers yet.

The return is gated three times before it is committed, and the gates are timed to geography. At T+1 hour 27 minutes 46 seconds, an early-return check over a disposal option near Hawaii; at T+7 hours 15 minutes 35 seconds, a mid-mission check over an option near Chile; at T+20 hours 41 minutes 55 seconds, a final check near Hawaii again. At any of them, a ship whose health, heat-shield imagery, propellant state, or destination weather argues against the catch can be deorbited into remote ocean instead. Past the final check, the catch decision itself is taken under SpaceX’s published conditions, quoted in the File in Brief: return proceeds only if the vehicle’s status meets the company’s internally developed, FAA-approved conditions, with controllers confirming that the systems critical for reentry maneuvers, the final landing burn, and the tower approach are healthy. The deorbit burn—a single Raptor, on SpaceX’s November 7 update—runs ten seconds, T+21:35:57 to T+21:36:07, and after it the ship is committed to the corridor.

The corridor is the first of its kind in the program: a reentry over land, ending at a tower the ship left the previous evening. Entry interface at T+22:10:46, over the Pacific; then a gliding descent across northern Mexico and southern Texas, steering around populated areas, passing north of South Padre Island, crossing the Gulf coast, and turning south to approach Pad 2 from over the water, with sonic booms expected to be audible across Cameron County. Transonic at T+22:29:34. The landing burn begins at T+22:32:16 with the flip to vertical on three engines, steps down to two at T+22:32:26 and to one at T+22:32:33, and ends at T+22:32:34 with the catch—an eighteen-second terminal maneuver, which for a window-open liftoff falls at about 3:17 p.m. Central time on Saturday, November 14. Even inside the corridor the profile retains exits: controllers can end the entry early, including tumbling the ship to ensure it burns up over the ocean, and a contingency water landing in the Gulf stands behind a late no-go on the tower.

Success on Friday comes in grades, and the briefing prints them in descending order because the program’s own history says the lower grades are the likelier news. Full success is both catches with the satellites deployed and the stack recovered intact at one pad. Below it: either catch achieved without the other—a first ship catch with the booster diverted or lost, or the first Block 3 booster catch with the ship disposed of at sea on a health call. Below that, conservative success: satellites deployed, both stages disposed of at sea on health calls, on a 22-hour profile that would still multiply the program’s longest orbital endurance by more than seven and return the boil-off record the transfer program needs. Failure is loss of the vehicle on ascent—the base rate is real, five of fourteen on the record’s accounting—or loss during entry over the corridor, the outcome the entire gate structure exists to keep from becoming a public-safety event. If the plan flies as published, it stacks five firsts in one mission: the first ship catch attempt, the first booster catch attempt since March 2025 and the first of a Block 3 booster, the first catch of any kind at Pad 2, the first attempt to recover both stages of an orbital system on one mission, and the longest Starship mission by a factor of about seven.

4. The Catch: Why the Tower, and Why There Are No Legs

Each Starbase pad pairs a launch mount with an integration tower carrying two large articulated arms—the chopsticks, on a tower the program calls Mechazilla. The arms ride a carriage up and down the tower, translate and rotate, and do three jobs with the same hardware: they lift and stack the ship onto the booster, stabilize the stack, and catch returning stages. Pad 2’s tower is a newer design than Pad 1’s, with shorter arms—two truss sections removed—electromechanical actuators in place of hydraulics, and no ship lifting pins. The booster catch, demonstrated three times, runs as follows: after hot staging the booster flips, fires a subset of its engines to aim itself back at the pad, coasts, steers by grid fin through the upper atmosphere, and lights its center engines for a landing burn that brings it to a near-hover beside the tower at essentially zero relative velocity—telemetry from the first catch showed under half a meter per second at capture—whereupon the arms close on the vehicle’s catch fittings and it ends hanging from the tower it launched from minutes earlier, ready to be lowered straight back onto the launch mount.

The ship catch runs the same play with a vehicle that arrives horizontally, belly-first, out of orbital reentry, and every element of it is unproven in flight.
