Third, the Iran damage: “a few months” against “many years,” from agencies of the same two governments within the same week, the assessments measuring different quantities and the underground halls unentered by any inspector, then or since. Fourth, the counts inside single events: fourteen GBU-57s agreed and Tomahawks at 24 against 30; fourteen missiles at Al Udeid with six hits, thirteen intercepted with one impact, nineteen launched. Fifth, the snapback’s effective date: September 27 on the Congressional Research Service’s account, September 28 on the European governments’ and the Arms Control Association’s. Sixth, the small numbers that carry larger filings: the Bulletin’s own statement gives atmospheric carbon dioxide at 150 percent of preindustrial in its summary and 152 percent of 1750 levels in its climate section; the Human Security Lab’s sole-authority figure stands at 32 percent in the university’s release and 30 percent in the Bulletin’s write-up, on different wordings; the sole-authority survey itself is a special population, 750 veterans and active-duty respondents, and is not filed in this report as a general-population measurement. Seventh, General MacArthur’s requested bombs: 26, 34, and 38, by source, from December 1950. Eighth, the Khamenei edict’s founding message: April 2010 in most scholarly citations, 2009 in some Iranian sources. Ninth and last, the report’s own method, stated once: where this file’s instruments conflict, the desk has printed both readings and named the bridge unknown rather than building one, because a bridge the record does not contain is a claim, and claims in this paper are labeled. The final paragraph of the report is the first paragraph’s restatement, as the form requires: no nuclear weapon has been used in war since August 9, 1945; the prohibition that record embodies is measured as strong in principle and conditional in the concrete, defended in print by scholars who call it fragile and by none who call it strengthening; it survived a testing directive answered by no test, a doctrine revision answered by no use, two wars against a threshold state that neither crossed the line nor left the treaty, and the lapse of the last strategic arms treaty into a silence of unilateral, unverified restraint; and through the autumn of 2026 it was argued about, at mass reach and in apocalyptic vocabulary, by broadcasters whose central allegation stands unverified against a presidential denial on the record—the argument itself now part of the record the next filing will inherit.

The File, Clipped

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective, a source with a position, printed because it is useful, and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Seventeen items.

Subjective
Nina Tannenwald—“The Nuclear Taboo: The United States and the Normative Basis of Nuclear Non-Use,” International Organization 53(3), Summer 1999; “Stigmatizing the Bomb,” International Security, Spring 2005; The Nuclear Taboo, Cambridge University Press, December 2007; “The Vanishing Nuclear Taboo?” Foreign Affairs, 2018

The naming file: the argument that non-use rests on a normative prohibition built by stigma, the case record from Japan to the Gulf War, and the author’s own later verdict that the norm remains widely shared and under pressure, printed in this report at her words and with her question mark.

Subjective
The Nobel Committee—the 2024 Peace Prize to Nihon Hidankyo, citation and press release, October 11, 2024, and the award lecture, December 10, 2024

The institutional sentence on the taboo’s condition before the period this report covers: the survivors “contributed greatly to the establishment of the nuclear taboo,” and “it is therefore alarming that today this taboo against the use of nuclear weapons is under pressure.”

Subjective
The survey-experiment literature—Press, Sagan & Valentino, “Atomic Aversion,” American Political Science Review 107(1), 2013; Sagan & Valentino, “Revisiting Hiroshima in Iran,” International Security 42(1), 2017; Dill, Sagan & Valentino, “Kettles of Hawks,” Security Studies 31(1), 2022; Schwartz, International Security 48(4), 2024; Carpenter & Montgomery, International Security 45(2), 2020

The concrete-scenario measurements and their rebuttal: effectiveness moving majorities, civilian-death counts moving them back, an ally’s use approved at rates near one’s own, and the demonstration that law-and-norm framing in the instrument restores majority opposition to civilian targeting.

Subjective
The abstract-principle survey series—PIPA/Knowledge Networks 2004; PIPA/CISSM 2007; the Chicago Council Surveys, including March 2022; YouGov, October 30–November 2, 2025; Pew Research Center, June 2–8, 2025; Economist/YouGov, October 31–November 3, 2025

The older instrument family and its modern administrations: two decades of only-in-response majorities, the 2022 retaliation ladder, the 2025 juxtaposition of 46 percent expecting nuclear war against 7 percent accepting first use, and the retrospective Hiroshima trend kept in its own file where it belongs.

Subjective
The testing sequence—President Trump, Truth Social post, October 29, 2025; 60 Minutes interview, recorded October 31, broadcast November 2, 2025; Secretary Chris Wright, Fox News, November 2–3, 2025; Congressional Research Service memorandum, December 2025; CNN reporting, November 14–15, 2025

The directive and its four-day half-life: the order to test “on an equal basis,” the televised affirmation of detonations, the Energy Secretary’s redefinition of the tests as noncritical, and the research service’s sentence that it is unclear what change of policy, if any, is to take place.

Subjective
The Kremlin record—President Putin’s addresses of February 24 and September 21, 2022, and the deterrence-forces order of February 27, 2022; the Fundamentals of State Policy in the Field of Nuclear Deterrence, Decree No. 991, November 19, 2024; the Security Council transcript of November 5, 2025; the televised Oreshnik address of November 21, 2024

The primary Russian texts the signaling sections are built from, in their own words, including the words that are not there: no use of “nuclear” in the February 24 warning, and no naming of nuclear weapons in the “not a bluff” sentence.

Subjective
International Atomic Energy Agency—Board findings and resolutions GOV/2025/38, GOV/2025/71, and the referral vote of September 9, 2026; Director General’s reports GOV/2025/50, GOV/2025/65, GOV/2026/8, GOV/2026/33, and GOV/2026/50; the Director General’s statements to Sky News, CBS, the Associated Press, and the Security Council

The verification file: the June 13, 2025, baseline of 440.9 kilograms at 60 percent, repeated unchanged in every report since; the inspectors’ withdrawal and non-readmission; and the sentence that governs the stockpile’s present state, that the Agency has not been able to verify that there has been no diversion.

Subjective
The Islamabad Memorandum—text of June 17, 2026, as carried by the American Presidency Project; the Pentagon briefings on Operations Midnight Hammer and Epic Fury; the Iranian statements of record, 2024–2026

The settlement that was signed and not executed: fourteen points, a permanent termination of operations, a reconstruction plan of at least $300 billion to be developed, and Article 8’s reaffirmation that Iran “shall not procure or develop nuclear weapons,” with the stockpile to be down-blended on site under Agency supervision, in a final deal that never arrived.

Subjective
SIPRI Yearbook 2026, Chapter 8, Kristensen & Korda—world nuclear forces at January 2026; and the Federation of American Scientists, Status of World Nuclear Forces 2026, with Russian Nuclear Weapons 2025

The arsenal counts and their warning label, printed in the report where the numbers stand: one analyst team in two venues, a shared headline table, and a 91-warhead disagreement between the two publications on Russia’s stockpile that neither instrument bridges.

Subjective
Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists—the 2026 Doomsday Clock statement, January 27, 2026

The Clock at 85 seconds, the closest setting in its history, and its stated grounds in full—three theatres under the nuclear shadow, a full-blown arms race, the treaty set to expire, and the accelerants beyond the nuclear file—filed in this report as the Bulletin’s judgment, never as the paper’s measurement.

Subjective
U.S. Department of Defense—Military and Security Developments Involving the People’s Republic of China, 2025, released December 23, 2025; China’s Arms Control, Disarmament, and Nonproliferation in the New Era, white paper of November 27, 2025

The two governments’ China file: the Pentagon’s low-600s count, its thousand-by-2030 track, and its counterstrike-posture assessment, set against Beijing’s own document reaffirming no-first-use and rejecting the arms-race characterization, each printed as its maker’s.

Subjective
The European texts—the Northwood Declaration, July 10, 2025; President Macron’s televised address of March 5, 2025, and Île Longue address of March 2, 2026; Chancellor Merz’s statements of February 2025 and February 13, 2026; Prime Minister Tusk to the Sejm, March 7, 2025

The movement from debate to documents, and the limit every document keeps: coordination announced, exercises opened, a warhead increase declared without a number, disclosure ended—and the decision, in each text, remaining in one national pair of hands.

Subjective
The Sean Penn file—Hannity, Fox News, April 5, 2022, transcript as carried by Grabien and corroborated by Variety and TheWrap; Newsweek interview, February 20–21, 2026; Face the Nation, CBS, September 17, 2023; Club Random, June 15, 2025; Shane Smith Has Questions, VICE, released July 16, 2026

The actor’s nuclear record in his own words across four years—intimidation, threat-monopoly, and the invention invoked—with the file’s two corrections carried on its face: the Blitzer appearance is March 1, 2023, not March 2026, and the word “bluff” in the August 2026 circulation is the commenters’, not his.

Subjective
The Carlson document—Tucker Carlson, posts on X, November 1–2, 2026, as republished in full by the Daily Caller; the Daily Caller News Foundation’s reporting and counter-reporting of November 2–3, 2026, including the Peters, Knopf, and Bleek statements

The allegation and its answers in one clip pair: a nuclear strike on Pickaxe Mountain within days, a decision by November 7, an observer who says the Israeli prime minister calls daily—and, against it, the President’s October 15 denial, a near-zero chance assessed by Heritage’s Peters, and the eighty-year tradition named by Middlebury’s Knopf.

Subjective
The Jones run—AlexJonesLive programme pages and headlines, October 26–November 8, 2026; podcast-feed transcripts as carried by Podscan, November 3 and November 8, 2026; the programme summaries of PodcastRex, November 6, 2026; Newsweek and CDM republications of the November 2 posts

The dated discourse at its documented density: nine dated instances in fourteen days, the 25th Amendment urged as the mechanism, the probability sentence attributed to the host and the genie sentence to his guest, and the November 8 program’s own billing—with the file’s limits stated, no full primary transcript recovered and the word Armageddon documented for November 3, not November 8.

Subjective
Arms Control Association—reporting on the New START expiry and its aftermath, February–September 2026

The post-treaty record kept by its monitors: no successor talks underway or planned, no informal no-upload understanding found, and the sentence the architecture section adopts as its verdict, that this is the first period since 1972 with no legally binding limit on the two largest arsenals and no inspection regime to watch them.

Subjective
KCNA and the Korean Central News Agency renderings—Kim Jong Un’s Supreme People’s Assembly speech of September 21, 2025, as reported by Reuters and the Associated Press; SIPRI and Federation estimates for North Korea, January 2025 and January 2026

Pyongyang’s position in its official English and the counters’ numbers beside it: never giving up the weapons, possession sacred and absolute in the constitution, a second mission beyond deterrence—and about sixty assembled warheads where the leader’s own visitor claimed fifty-seven.
items.summary: No state has used a nuclear weapon in war since Nagasaki on August 9, 1945. The desk files the state of the prohibition scholars call the nuclear taboo at November 2026: what the surveys measure and where they disagree, the American testing directive of October 29, 2025 and the verified absence of any explosive test that followed it, Russia’s signaling record since February 2022 and its doctrine of November 2024, the two Iran wars of 2025 and 2026 and the enriched-uranium stockpile the IAEA can no longer verify, the wider field from Pyongyang to Paris, the expiry of New START on February 5, 2026 and the first period since 1972 with no legally binding limit on American and Russian strategic forces, the President’s statements set against the record of what was done, and the public argument about use that ran through the autumn of 2026, attributed and graded throughout.

items.title: The Talks Open in Abu Dhabi, Asia Extends the Rally, and China Passes a Trillion
items.content_html:
The Night File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

The Talks Open in Abu Dhabi, Asia Extends the Rally, and China Passes a Trillion

The night file, while Washington slept: the Abu Dhabi table opened with Europe in the next room and Paris arguing it belongs inside; the two capitals on the Iran file repeated themselves exactly; Asia ran with Monday’s rally and oil walked back toward ninety; Beijing printed a trillion-dollar surplus built on the world’s AI demand; and every dated thing the week left open—the press conference, the inflation number, the oath in Jerusalem, the counts—stands dated today.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0400 ET, Tuesday, November 10, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 27, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, which filed the president’s readout, Tehran’s answer, and Monday’s close. The reports filed here are the night’s reports, taken after that edition closed; where they restate Monday’s facts, the restatement is identified. The midnight edition stands unrevised, as a log stands.

The Night in Brief

The night opened one table, extended one rally, and produced one very large number, and it settled no war, no coalition and no count. In Abu Dhabi, negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the United States sat down Tuesday for their first three-way meeting since February, two days on security guarantees, in the Associated Press account filed below; European officials are in the city for separate meetings and not at the table, and in Paris the G7 ministers spent Monday telling Secretary Rubio that Europe belongs at it. Washington and Tehran carried Monday’s opposite sentences through the night without either side moving: the war effectively over and the blockade standing, in the president’s words; seven conditions, and a warning that renewed attacks would bring a severe reply, in Tehran’s. Asia took Wall Street’s best day since April and ran with it—Seoul up more than 5 percent at the open, fast enough for the exchange to pause program buying; Tokyo back above 60,000; oil down again toward ninety dollars. Beijing’s customs put China’s trade surplus for the first ten months at $1.04 trillion, past the trillion a month earlier than last year, on the world’s demand for AI hardware. In Jerusalem the new Knesset is sworn in today and the speakership is still unsettled. In Kraków thousands marched in silence on Monday evening while the autopsies began. Tuesday holds the rest of the week’s appointments: Secretary Hegseth at the Pentagon at 0800, the inflation report at 0830, Alaska’s next count, Mississippi’s deadline, and the second day in both Paris and Abu Dhabi.

Abu Dhabi at 0400: The Table Opens, Europe in the Next Room

The talks the week has pointed at since Friday are open, and the first fact about them is who is in which room. The trilateral room holds three delegations: the Americans, envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner; the Russians, led by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky with Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and General Yuri Zhigarlovsky; and the Ukrainians, led by Rustem Umerov with Kyrylo Budanov, Davyd Arakhamia, Sergiy Kyslytsya and Vadym Skibitsky, in the delegations account and the opening account filed below. The subject, on the announcements, is security guarantees: the American proposals, per the BBC account carried in the briefs filed below, include security consultations, crisis hotlines, reciprocal de-escalation measures and a possible revival of the NATO-Russia Council. Before the three-way session, Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff meet separately with envoys from Ukraine, the European Union, NATO, Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Italy, in the AP account above. The stated positions have not moved for the opening: Kyiv rejects territorial concessions in the Donbas and asks for guarantees and an immediate ceasefire; Moscow asks for Ukrainian withdrawal from the Donbas, limits on Ukraine’s military and guarantees against NATO expansion. President Zelenskyy’s hope for the round is on the record from Berlin: that adviser-level talks open a path to a leaders’ meeting with President Putin, in the Berlin account filed below. No statement out of the room exists at 0400. The desk files the room, the names and the announced subject, and nothing beyond them.

Paris at 0400: The Second Day, and the Argument About the Table

The G7 foreign ministers close their two days in Paris on Tuesday with the argument they opened with, and it is the same argument as Abu Dhabi’s seating plan, heard from the other side. On Monday the European ministers told Secretary Rubio that Europe must have a say in any deal ending the war, in the Paris account filed below; German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul insisted Europe maintain an active seat, and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot confirmed European representatives will participate in the Abu Dhabi discussions, in the ministers account filed below. The Kremlin’s standing sentence is that the negotiations remain trilateral. Both sentences stand; the seating plan in Abu Dhabi at 0400 agrees with the Kremlin’s. Tuesday’s Paris programme carries Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, in a session on Ukraine—air defence, economic pressure, Black Sea navigation—and a session on instability in the Middle East, with ministers from Saudi Arabia, Egypt, South Korea and Brazil attending parts of the meeting. France has indicated the meeting may produce no joint statement. The desk files the difference as the day’s European fact: the ministers are united that Europe belongs at the table, and divided, with Washington and Moscow, on whether it is at one.

Washington and Tehran at 0400: Two Sentences, Carried Through the Night Unchanged

No new sentence from either capital entered the file in the night, and the night’s Iran file is therefore the standing one, restated by the morning papers in both capitals’ words. The president’s account stands as Monday’s: Iran militarily effectively over; the status quo kept at the behest of the neighbours; Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait preferring the continuation of the naval blockade and of Operation Iron Gate, land and sea; further strikes quite unlikely; forces locked and loaded if the position changes, in the Al Jazeera account filed below. Tehran’s account stands in its two registers: President Pezeshkian’s, negotiation with dignity and no surrender to force; and Mr. Rezaei’s, that the United States should stop manufacturing fake news about imaginary talks and accept the seven conditions, in the conditions account filed below. The conditions named publicly now run to six of the seven in the fuller lists: an end to hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon; the lifting of the naval blockade; the reopening of the strait’s lanes; the lifting of sanctions; the release of frozen assets; and an end to intervention in Iran’s internal affairs; the fuller lists in the accounts differ on the remainder, and the desk prints the count of named conditions as the accounts give it. Foreign Minister Araghchi’s warning stands beside them, that Tehran would “rain down hell” if the United States resumed attacks, in the briefing account filed below. Secretary Rubio’s sentence also stands: not on the verge of a breakthrough, and the demands not realistic, in the Washington account filed below. No agreement, text or confirmation from any second capital exists. What the two capitals agree on, physically, is the blockade: imposed in one’s account, demanded lifted in the other’s.

Hormuz and Khor Mor at 0400: No Unauthorised Transit, in Tehran’s Word; a Field Still Dark

The strait’s overnight state rests on one owner’s word, and the desk prints it as that. Navigational aid systems in the south of the strait were destroyed and no unauthorised vessels transited the route overnight, an unnamed Guards Navy official told Iranian media on Monday, in the Reuters account filed below. No tracker count for the night is in the file at 0400, and no tanker claim has been added to the weekend’s. Iraq’s understanding with the United States on a shipping lane near Oman, reported Monday, has produced no reported sailing under it. At Khor Mor, the position is the operator’s and it has not changed: production remains suspended while the damage is assessed, the fire extinguished, no injuries to personnel, and 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts off the Kurdistan grid, in the operator account filed below. One unconfirmed local account places the drone’s launch in the mountains near Tuz Khurmatu; no authority has attributed the attack, and no group has claimed it. Baghdad’s joint investigative committee is the file’s only open instrument.

Beijing at 0400: A Trillion in Ten Months, and the Monthly Gap Narrowing

China’s customs published the night’s largest single number, and it is a record approached from both sides of the ledger. The trade surplus for January through October stands at $1.04 trillion, past a trillion for the second consecutive year and a month earlier than in 2025, against $1.2 trillion for all of last year, in the Reuters account and the CNN account filed below. October’s exports rose 35.2 percent on the year to $412.3 billion, ahead of the 33.5 percent forecast and a touch below September’s 36.3 percent; the driver named in every account is the world’s race to build AI infrastructure and its demand for Chinese high-technology goods. Imports rose faster, 41.6 percent to $307.1 billion, far above the 32 percent forecast, on purchases of technology products, critical minerals and energy; the monthly surplus therefore narrowed to $105.3 billion, from $133.5 billion in September, the smallest since April, and below the $125.8 billion expected. The bilateral surplus with the United States narrowed slightly, to $32.71 billion from $34.01 billion. Two dates stand around the figures: on Monday Beijing announced a two-month extension of the trade truce with Washington that was due to expire today, and next week Presidents Xi and Trump are expected to meet at the APEC summit in Shenzhen. The desk files the customs figures, both directions of trade, and the narrowing month inside the record year.

The Markets at 0400: Asia Runs With Monday, Oil Walks Back Toward Ninety

Asia’s Tuesday session is Monday’s American session continued, with the chipmakers in front and the inflation report waiting at the end of it. At 0230 GMT Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 stood up 2.9 percent at 60,475.78 and Seoul’s Kospi up 4.1 percent at 5,223.87, in the AFP account filed below; the later prints run higher for Seoul—over 5 percent at the open, the rise so fast the Korea Exchange briefly paused program buying under its sidecar rule, in the open account filed below—and about 3 percent for the Nikkei in the Reuters account, against 2.6 percent to 60,279.37 in the AP print; Hong Kong rose 0.4 percent and Shanghai 0.4 percent. The regional index rose 1.5 percent on the Reuters print and 1.78 percent on another, off a seven-month low. Oil moved the other way in the same hours: Brent at $91.63, down 1.0 percent, at 0230 GMT; $91.56, down 1 percent, in the Reuters Singapore print; $91.74, down 0.9 percent, in the AP print; and $91 in the recap account, its weakest since early September. The accounts name the same two engines: cheaper oil after the president’s restraint on strikes, and the chip rebound from last week’s rout. Both engines meet their test at 0830 Eastern, when the October inflation report lands; the rally is a position taken before the number, and the desk files it as one.

Washington at 0400: A Press Conference at 0800, a Number at 0830, a Vote by Wednesday

Tuesday in Washington is two appointments and a deadline, all set on Monday. At 0800 Secretary Hegseth holds a Pentagon press conference, his first in more than six months—180 days in the Associated Press count—to address the eight articles of impeachment Representative Massie filed on Monday, in the briefing account filed below. The articles are allegations: the first three charge the Iran campaign was conducted in violation of the War Powers Resolution; the fourth cites the strike on the Shajarah Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab and a figure of more than 200 civilians killed or injured; the rest cover the vessel strikes—at least 243 dead in his office’s updated count—the Venezuela operation, Yemen, and alleged retaliation against Senator Kelly, in the articles account filed below. The secretary says he is not worried and intends to serve out the term. House leaders have until Wednesday to table, refer or vote. At 0830 the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes October’s consumer prices, the last inflation reading before the Federal Reserve’s December 8–9 meeting. The consensus is a 0.3 percent monthly rise in headline prices and 0.2 percent in core, down from September’s 0.6 and 0.3; no annual rate will be published, because the 2025 shutdown left no October 2025 index to compare against, in the consensus account filed below. Futures price a better-than-80-percent chance—84 percent in one print—of a quarter-point rise in December, to a 4.00–4.25 percent range; Bank of America’s economists hold that only an indisputably soft 0.1 percent reading would put that in doubt.

Jerusalem at 0400: The Knesset Sworn In Today, the Chair Still Open

The 26th Knesset convenes today for its inaugural session, 120 members taking the oath, 47 of them first-time members who spent Monday at orientation, and the day’s open question is the one the mandate has carried since Sunday: who chairs it, and when. The facts of the ceremony are settled: remarks from President Herzog and from Speaker Amir Ohana, who holds the chair until a successor is elected, and a separate event in the plaza, in the inauguration account filed below. The speakership facts are not settled, and they now run in three sentences: Mr. Eisenkot and Mr. Liberman agreed Monday that the next speaker will be a member of Yashar, unnamed; United Torah Judaism declined to back a replacement before a government is formed; and Mr. Ohana has said he will arrange a vote within a week if 61 members submit a formal request, while ruling out a vote on inauguration day, in the opening-day account filed below. Sixty-one is also the number Mr. Eisenkot does not have for a government: his bloc stands at 48, Mr. Netanyahu’s at 53, the Arab-led parties at 19, and the mandate runs to December 6 with a possible 14-day extension. Mr. Netanyahu remains prime minister while the negotiations run. The desk files today as a sitting, not a settlement.

Kraków at 0400: A Silent March, the Autopsies Begun, and a Gun Law Under Review

Poland’s national mourning ended Monday night, and Kraków ended it in the street. Thousands marched in silence through the city on Monday evening, the president and the prime minister among them, following part of the route the gunman drove while firing and lighting candles at the places where people were killed, in the march account filed below. The city’s own mourning runs to November 11. Behind the march, the investigation acquired two new items in the day’s accounts. The first is a flag: a yellow Gadsden flag—a snake, and the words “Don’t tread on me”—was found in the gunman’s room, Prosecutor Nowak told the press conference, describing it as associated with various meanings of freedom or rebellion and not widely known as linked to extremism; it is printed here as the prosecutors printed it, an object and not a motive. The second is a policy: the interior ministry announced a review of gun-licensing procedures, including more frequent medical updates for permit holders, after police data showed more than 50,000 new licences issued in 2025; both the gunman and his father held permits. The prosecutors’ limit stands where Monday placed it—no findings that would let them state responsibly that the man was inspired by any particular ideology—against the interior minister’s weekend reading, which stands unwithdrawn, and against the opposition leader’s sentence that the far-right claim is a blatant lie. Three positions, each with its owner. The autopsies of the nine victims began Monday and are expected to take about two days; the phones, computers and 11 firearms are under analysis, in the investigation account filed below. The criminal case against the dead man will in time be closed; the investigation around him continues.

The Count at 0400: No New Figure in the Night, and Tuesday Is the Day Both Files Named

Neither Senate race was called in the night and no new figure was published for either, and for the first time in a week that stillness is itself on schedule: today is the day both counts named for movement. Alaska holds its next scheduled count today, carrying early votes cast October 30 to November 2, absentee and questioned ballots, on a race standing at Mary Peltola 102,962 to Dan Sullivan 102,325, a margin of 637 first-choice votes with roughly a quarter of ballots outstanding; no candidate is near 50 percent, and the ranked-choice tabulation is set for November 18, in the delay account filed below. Mississippi’s deadline falls today: mail ballots postmarked by Election Day must arrive, and affidavit voters must cure their identification, on a race standing at Scott Colom 467,930 to Cindy Hyde-Smith 465,356, a margin of 2,574 on about 97 percent counted, with just over 2,800 mail ballots still out when the secretary of state last counted; counties certify by November 13, and Mississippi has no automatic recount provision. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide. Colorado’s 4th District stands uncalled with them.

Tuesday Opens: Tables, Numbers, Oaths and Deadlines

The day the night hands over is the heaviest appointment book of the week so far. In Abu Dhabi the talks run their first full day, with the European envoys in the adjacent rooms and a second day behind it. In Paris the G7 closes, Ukraine’s foreign minister in the room for the Ukraine session and the Middle East session behind it. In Washington the secretary of defense faces the press at 0800 and the inflation report lands at 0830, with the House’s impeachment clock running to Wednesday. In Jerusalem the Knesset is sworn in. In Alaska the count moves; in Mississippi the deadlines fall. In Kraków the autopsies run their second day and the city mourns through tomorrow. At Khor Mor the assessment continues with the field dark. Everything the week left open with a date still carries a date; the only file without one remains the president’s larger Iran decision, which both capitals described again in the night without either one dating it. The log proceeds to Tuesday.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On the war’s state, the president’s effectively over, the secretary of state’s not on the verge of a breakthrough, President Pezeshkian’s negotiate with dignity, and Mr. Rezaei’s imaginary talks—unchanged overnight, four bearings and no agreement beneath any of them. On the seven conditions, six named in the fuller lists and the remainder differing between accounts. On Abu Dhabi’s room, a trilateral table in every account, and Europe at it in the French foreign minister’s sentence and beside it in every delegation list. On Asia, the Nikkei up 2.6, 2.8 or 2.9 percent and the Kospi up 4.1, 4.3 or over 5 by the hour of the print; Brent between $91 and $91.74 in the same hours. On Kraków’s wounded, 15 in one Monday account against 17 in the prosecutors’ weekend count. On the count, no triangle at all: two margins standing exactly where the weekend left them, because the day named for their movement is today and has not yet run. Against the triangle, the night’s single-valued facts are these: the talks opened in Abu Dhabi with the three delegations named; China’s ten-month surplus passed $1.04 trillion on its customs figures; thousands marched in silence in Kraków; no unauthorised transit of the strait is claimed by the one voice that claims the strait; no Senate race was called; and Asia rose while oil fell. The log proceeds to Tuesday.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 34 items.

Subjective
Associated Press, via Europe Says — the three-way talks start in Abu Dhabi

ABU DHABI: the three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States start Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates, renewing a push for peace after several rounds of negotiations earlier this year. The two-day session, the first such meeting since February, will focus on security guarantees. China's customs put the ten-month trade surplus at $1.04 trillion on AI-driven exports. In Jerusalem the 26th Knesset is sworn in today with the speakership unsettled; in Kraków thousands marched in silence as the autopsies began; and neither Senate count moved in the night, both holding Tuesday deadlines. Collected at 0400.

items.title: The President Calls the War Effectively Over, Tehran Calls the Talks Imaginary, and No Agreement Exists
items.content_html:
The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

The President Calls the War Effectively Over, Tehran Calls the Talks Imaginary, and No Agreement Exists

The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: Monday’s meeting acquired a readout after the evening edition closed, and the readout is a claim, not an agreement—the war effectively over in the president’s words, the talks imaginary in Tehran’s, the blockade standing in both. The close stood as the market’s one completed verdict and oil fell further after it. The mourning ended in Poland, a speaker was agreed and refused in Jerusalem, a sentence was imposed in London, and the count held both its deadlines for Tuesday.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Tuesday, November 10, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 26, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Monday, and in Monday’s earlier editions, Nos. 24 and 25. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Monday Settled, What It Left Open

Monday settled the president’s word, the markets’ close and a sentence in London, and it left the war it described, the coalition it requires and the count it awaits all open, and the desk files the day in that order. The evening edition closed with no readout from the Oval Office; by midnight a readout exists, and it is the president’s own. In a Truth Social post and then in a surprise appearance in the briefing room, President Trump said “Iran, militarily, is effectively over,” that there is a “good chance” of a deal, that Tehran is “talking very politely,” and that renewed strikes are “quite unlikely,” in the Washington account and the running account filed below. The same sentences keep the naval blockade and Operation Iron Gate in place and keep American forces “locked and loaded.” Tehran answered in two voices: President Pezeshkian’s, that Iran will negotiate with dignity and not surrender to force, and Mohsen Rezaei’s, that the talks are imaginary. No agreement, no text and no Iranian confirmation exists in the file. In New York the close stood—the S&P 500’s best day since April—and after settlement Brent fell more than seven dollars to its lowest since late August. In Poland the national mourning ended with no ideology established for the dead gunman. In Jerusalem a speaker from Yashar was agreed, and one partner declined the replacement at Tuesday’s opening. In London Mr. Brand was sentenced to ten years and six months. Neither Senate race was called. Tuesday holds the Abu Dhabi table, the inflation report, the Alaska count, the Mississippi deadline, the Knesset’s first sitting and the secretary of defense’s press conference.

Washington at Midnight: A Readout at Last, and It Is the President’s Own

The meeting that produced no word by 1800 produced, by midnight, the day’s largest sentence, and the desk files it as a statement, not a settlement. Qatar’s prime minister presented Tehran’s two-day proposal in Washington, met the president and the vice president, and wrote afterward that he was grateful for positive discussions on reaching a deal, in the Reuters and Al Jazeera account filed below. The president’s readout names Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait as preferring the status quo—continuation of the naval blockade and of Operation Iron Gate, land and sea—and records agreement, in his words, that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. None of the governments he named has confirmed that account in the file. A diplomat briefed on the meeting, cited by one reporter and unnamed, said the president told the Qatari prime minister in private that he wants a deal but could reverse course if Tehran is not serious; that description rests on a single unnamed person. Secretary Rubio’s position stands unmoved: negotiators are not on the verge of a breakthrough, and Tehran’s demands are outrageous and not realistic. Settled: what the president said, in public, twice. Open: whether any other party says the same.

Tehran at Midnight: Dignity From the President, “Imaginary Talks” From the Security Council

Iran answered Monday in two registers, and midnight is the hour to print them side by side without joining them. President Pezeshkian said the Leader had instructed officials to end the state of neither war nor peace, that Iran can negotiate with dignity, and that it will not surrender to force, in the Tehran account filed below. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, wrote that Washington should fold its hand and “stop manufacturing fake news about imaginary talks,” and accept the seven conditions Iran has repeatedly set out, in the conditions account filed below. Three of the seven are named publicly: an end to the war on all fronts, the release of frozen funds and an end to the naval blockade. Tehran says it will not reopen Hormuz to normal traffic until the conditions are met. The two capitals describe the same evening in opposite words—momentum in Washington, imaginary talks in Tehran—and the blockade both sides invoke is the one physical fact they share.

The Price at Midnight: The Close Stood, and Oil Kept Falling After It

The markets gave the day its only completed verdict, and then enlarged it after hours. The close stands as the evening edition filed it, in two prints that differ in the third figure: the Dow up 1,104.02 to 52,389.75 on the Associated Press print and up 1,131.81 to 52,417.54 on the Reuters print, the S&P 500 at its best day since April on both, Nvidia down against the market on its board’s inquiry in every account. After settlement the move continued: Brent, settled down $5.75 at $92.57, fell more than seven dollars a barrel in post-settlement trade to its lowest level since late August, and in early Asian trading front-month Brent stood at $91.57, down 1.1 percent, with West Texas Intermediate at $85.78, in the early Asian account filed below. The driver named in every account is the same diplomacy that produced no agreement: a president downplaying renewed strikes. Tuesday’s test is fixed: the October consumer price report at 0830 Eastern, the last inflation reading before the Federal Reserve’s December meeting.

Kraków at Midnight: The National Mourning Ends, the Limit Stands

Poland’s file closed Monday where its prosecutors placed it: with a death, a limit and an investigation that continues without the man it concerns. The suspect died at about 0430 after at least three operations; autopsies of the nine victims began Monday and will take about two days; fifteen wounded remain in hospital, fourteen stable and one officer in serious condition. Prosecutor’s spokesman Przemysław Nowak said investigators do not have findings that would let them state responsibly that the gunman was inspired by any particular ideology, and that no obvious symbols associated with a particular political movement have been found, in the prosecutors’ account filed below. Government spokesman Adam Szłapka said assessments should be withheld until the services have full information. Those sentences stand against the interior minister’s weekend reading, which stands unwithdrawn; the desk prints the limit as the newest bearing. National mourning ended Monday night; the city’s own runs to November 11.

Jerusalem at Midnight: A Speaker Agreed, a Partner Declining the Opening Vote, and the Knesset at Noon

The mandate’s second day ended with its first agreement narrowed by its first refusal. Mr. Eisenkot and Mr. Liberman agreed the next speaker will be a member of Yashar, and Mr. Liberman told Mr. Eisenkot, in the Channel 13 report, “You will be prime minister. I’m not asking for that position for myself,” and asked for time to exhaust talks with the ultra-Orthodox parties first. Yashar invited Shas and United Torah Judaism to join in replacing Speaker Amir Ohana at Tuesday’s inaugural session, and United Torah Judaism declined the timing, saying replacement should come after a government is formed, in the speaker account filed below. The bloc in hand stands at 48 seats, 61 are required, and the mandate runs to December 6. The 26th Knesset is sworn in Tuesday. Settled: the speakership belongs to Yashar by agreement. Open: when it changes hands, and whether any coalition follows.

Abu Dhabi at Midnight: The Council Heard the War, Paris Stated Its Differences, and the Table Sits Tuesday

Nothing about the talks changed on Monday except the record around them, and that record grew heavier. The Security Council met in New York at Ukraine’s request and heard that at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured in Ukraine in September, an 85 percent increase over the year before, and that strikes on Kyiv’s three main power stations in October left 600,000 people without electricity, in the Council account filed below. Ukraine urged a resolution requiring an immediate ceasefire; Russia questioned the meeting’s purpose; China urged the parties to seize the Abu Dhabi opportunity. In Paris the G7’s first day ended with the differences stated—far apart on Ukraine, Iran and international organizations, agreed the conflicts should end quickly—and Germany’s foreign minister repeating that Europe must be part of any resolution. The eve’s fire stands as the evening edition filed it: 317 Russian drones in Ukraine’s count, four substations struck in Russia’s account, the KINEF refinery burning, and Zaporizhzhia’s power restored through a single line. On membership the two statements stand apart: the Kremlin’s exclusively three delegations, and France’s Europeans present, role unclear. The talks open Tuesday.

The House at Midnight: Eight Articles Filed, a Press Conference at 0800, a Vote by Wednesday

The impeachment file acquired its clock on Monday and nothing else; midnight files the clock. Representative Massie spoke for more than an hour on the floor, filed eight articles as a privileged resolution, and said the measure is more likely to pass after the election than before it. House leaders have two legislative days to vote, to table or to refer, with a vote expected as early as Wednesday. Secretary Hegseth said he is not worried and holds a press conference at 0800 Tuesday, his first in 180 days in the Associated Press count; the president said he will stand by him, and Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries supports the articles. The articles are allegations in a charging document; they are findings by no court, and removal would require two-thirds of the Senate. Mr. Miller’s first day as chief of staff closed without a statement from him in the file.

London and the Standing Files: A Sentence Imposed, a Field Still Dark

The day’s one completed legal act stands as imposed. Mr. Justice Bennathan sentenced Russell Brand to ten years and six months—nine years for rape and eighteen months for three counts of sexual assault, running consecutively—to serve two-thirds in custody, naming him a sexual predator. Files on two further women are with the prosecutors and a New York civil case proceeds; both stand open. At Khor Mor the operator Dana Gas said the fire is extinguished, no staff were injured, and production remains suspended pending assessment, with 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts off the grid and no claim of responsibility; the American envoy to Iraq, Tom Barrack, condemned the attack on Monday, in the envoy account filed below. In Hormuz the Guards’ claim stands—no unauthorised transit overnight—against the tracker’s two crossings; at Al-Ayyat no authority has stated a cause for the collision that killed seven.

The Count at Midnight: Nothing Called, and Tuesday Holds Both Deadlines

For a fifth day no Senate race was called and no new figure displaced Friday’s in Mississippi or Wednesday’s in Alaska. Mississippi stands at Scott Colom 467,930 to Cindy Hyde-Smith 465,356, a margin of 2,574 on about 97 percent counted, with just over 2,800 mail ballots still out; ballots postmarked by Election Day are due by 1700 Tuesday, and counties certify by November 13. Alaska stands at Mary Peltola 102,962 to Dan Sullivan 102,325, a margin of 637 on a count posted November 4; its next count is Tuesday, absentee ballots arrive through November 18, and the ranked-choice tabulation is set for that day if no candidate clears 50 percent, in the count account filed below. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On the war’s state, the president’s effectively over, the secretary of state’s not on the verge of a breakthrough, President Pezeshkian’s negotiate with dignity, and Mr. Rezaei’s imaginary talks—four bearings, no two the same, and no agreement beneath any of them. On the private meeting, one unnamed diplomat’s account against the public record. On the close, the two prints differing in the third figure, the rally single-valued and its exact size not. On Kraków’s motive, the prosecutors’ Monday limit against the ministers’ weekend readings. On the speaker, Yashar’s by agreement between two men, and not at Tuesday’s opening by the refusal of a third. On Hormuz, open, severely restricted and closed to the unauthorised, in three owners’ words. Against the triangle, Monday’s single-valued facts are these: the president spoke and kept the blockade in the same sentences; oil fell after settlement to its lowest since late August; eight articles were filed and action is due by Wednesday; Mr. Brand was sentenced; the national mourning ended; no Senate race was called. Tuesday holds the rest. The log turns.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 33 items.

Subjective
USA Today — military strikes, a peace agreement, or the status quo in Iran

WASHINGTON: President Trump said at a surprise news conference on November 9 that it “won’t be necessary” to escalate the conflict. “Iran, militarily, is effectively over. We’re just keeping it the status quo,” he said. He met Qatar’s prime minister privately the same day; Secretary Rubio said negotiators were not on the verge of a breakthrough and that Iranian demands were “outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.” The account puts the war’s cost to the American military at more than $47 billion as of October 16, on the Pentagon’s estimate, with about 50,000 troops deployed to Central Command’s area.

Subjective
The Business Standard, carrying Reuters and Al Jazeera — the president says the Iran conflict could end soon as Qatar presents Tehran’s proposal

President Trump said the campaign against Iran could end soon after meeting Qatar’s prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, in Washington, with Vice President Vance also attending. Qatar presented Iran’s two-day proposal aimed at ending hostilities, and the Qatari prime minister wrote that he was grateful for positive discussions on reaching a deal. Iranian officials rejected the president’s description: Mohsen Rezaei called the talks imaginary, and President Pezeshkian said Iran would negotiate under fair conditions but would not surrender to force. The account lists Tehran’s seven conditions as including the lifting of sanctions, the unfreezing of financial assets, recognition of a new shipping channel through Hormuz established alongside Oman, and an end to hostilities across the region.

Subjective
Israel.com — the president says the Iran war is effectively over militarily and that he wants a deal

The running account, updated at 02:07 Israel time on November 10: a diplomat briefed on the White House meeting said the president told Qatar’s prime minister he wants a deal and will give the negotiations a chance, but could reverse course if Tehran is not serious. At an impromptu press conference the president said there was a “good chance” of a deal and that Tehran was “talking very politely.” In his Truth Social readout he named Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait as preferring the status quo, defined as keeping the naval blockade and a new operation called Iron Gate, on land and at sea, and wrote that all agreed Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. The account notes the diplomat’s description is the only account of the private exchange and rests on a single unnamed person.

Subjective
Silent Dossier — the president says the Iran war is effectively over after the Qatar talks, while Tehran calls the talks imaginary

President Trump said on November 9 that the war with Iran is “effectively over” militarily, hours after meeting Qatar’s prime minister, and kept the naval blockade and the threat of new strikes in the same account: “We’re keeping it going. We have the greatest military blockade ever,” and “we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes.” Iranians, he said, “are talking to us, and they’re talking very politely.” Mohsen Rezaei wrote: “FOLD YOUR HAND. STOP manufacturing FAKE NEWS about imaginary talks.” President Pezeshkian struck a different note, saying Iran is open to further negotiations but will not be coerced.

Subjective
InvestingLive — Iran tells the United States to stop fake news on talks and demands acceptance of seven conditions

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Washington to stop publishing false reports about what he called imaginary negotiations and said it was time for the United States to accept the seven conditions Iran has repeatedly set out. Tehran conveyed the conditions through Qatar in September; the three named publicly are an end to the war on all fronts, the release of frozen funds and an end to the naval blockade. Tehran says it will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz to normal traffic until the conditions are met. The remarks contrast with the president’s view of positive momentum and his comment that Gulf states prefer to keep the blockade in place.

Subjective
Life News Agency — the president holds off new Iran strikes after the Qatar talks and says the war is effectively over militarily

WASHINGTON, November 9, 2026: President Trump said he would hold off on new military strikes against Iran for the time being after talks with Qatar’s prime minister, while keeping a naval blockade in place and warning that American forces remained ready if conditions changed. The White House Rapid Response account posted clips of the president in the briefing room: “Iran, militarily, is effectively over. We’re just keeping it the status quo… I don’t guarantee anything, but if we do have to go back in, we are locked and loaded.” His Truth Social post described an excellent conversation, further strikes as quite unlikely, and positive momentum toward an end to the conflict.

Subjective
New York Post — the president says the Iran war is effectively over militarily: keeping it the status quo

President Trump said Monday that the Iran war “is effectively over” militarily but that he will maintain the status quo of isolating Tehran economically, including with a naval blockade and a newly announced initiative to sever overland trading routes. “We’re just keeping it the status quo, and we’re doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbors,” he told reporters at a press briefing. He said he made the decision not to resume strikes following his conversation with Qatar’s prime minister, after announcing the new Operation Iron Gate effort.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine — the president says the Iran war is effectively over and signals a shift away from renewed strikes

President Trump told reporters on Monday that he believes the war in Iran “militarily is effectively over.” He made a surprise visit to the White House briefing room after meeting Qatar’s prime minister earlier in the day. “Iran militarily is effectively over,” he said. “We’re just keeping it the status quo.” The account is filed under the heading of a shift away from renewed military strikes.

Subjective
Press TV — the Leader ordered Iran’s officials to end the state of neither war nor peace, the president says

President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Monday that the Leader, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, has instructed Iranian officials to put an end to the current state of neither war nor peace. “We can engage in dialogue with dignity and bring this matter to a dignified conclusion,” the president said, adding that Iran will never surrender in the face of force, intimidation or bullying.

Subjective
Fox News — the president meets the Iran war mediator, and the Emirates reveal an oil export surge

President Trump met Qatar’s prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, on Monday at the White House as efforts to end the Iran war continue, with Secretary Rubio warning that negotiations remain far from a breakthrough and Tehran signalling willingness to negotiate without yielding to pressure. An Emirati official at the ADIPEC conference said the Emirates exported almost 4.4 million barrels a day now, against 3.1 to 3.2 million before the war began on February 28. Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment and did not receive a response before publication.

Subjective
The Courier Journal — Representative Thomas Massie moves to force a House vote on the Hegseth impeachment

Representative Thomas Massie reintroduced articles of impeachment against Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth on November 9, forcing Congress to decide whether to move forward. House leadership has two days to move to table the resolution, move it to committee or allow a floor vote. Hegseth announced he would hold a press conference, his first in 180 days in the Associated Press count, about the impeachment on Tuesday, November 10.

Subjective
New York Post — Representative Massie reintroduces impeachment articles against Secretary Hegseth over the Iran war

WASHINGTON: Representative Thomas Massie re-filed articles of impeachment against Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday, accusing him of illegally waging the Iran war without congressional authorization, and spoke for more than an hour laying out his case on the House floor. “I think it’s more likely to pass after the election than before the election,” he told the Post. A vote is expected as early as Wednesday. Republicans hold a five-seat majority in the House in this account. The secretary will host a press conference at 8 a.m. Tuesday to respond, and has said through a spokesman that he intends to serve through the end of the president’s term.

Subjective
WHRO — Representative Massie files articles of impeachment against Secretary Hegseth

Published November 9 at 3:52 p.m. Eastern and updated at 7:17 p.m.: Representative Massie has reintroduced articles of impeachment against Secretary Hegseth, setting up a vote in the House in the next two days. The resolution accuses the secretary of high crimes and misdemeanors and lists eight charges, including three charges for illegally waging war against Iran in violation of the War Powers Resolution. The account notes that there could be sufficient votes to impeach in the House, with all Democrats, Mr. Massie and a handful of Republicans, and that removal would require two-thirds of the Senate.

Subjective
Associated Press, via TV News Check — the Dow jumps 1,104, the Nasdaq climbs 674, the S&P 500 adds 173

NEW YORK (AP): the United States stock market rallied Monday and recovered most of last week’s losses as oil prices swung lower. The S&P 500 jumped 2.3 percent, its best day since April, the Dow leaped 1,104.02 points to 52,389.75, and the Nasdaq composite rose 673.71 to 25,253.14. A barrel of Brent crude fell 5.8 percent to $92.57.

Subjective
Reuters, via SRN News — Wall Street jumps back as the oil slide eases inflation worries; Nvidia slumps

NEW YORK, Nov 9 (Reuters): United States stocks rallied on Monday, as a drop in oil prices tempered inflation fears and helped the S&P 500 bounce off its biggest weekly drop since April 2025, and tech shares jumped even as Nvidia slumped. The Dow rose 1,131.81 points, or 2.21 percent, to 52,417.54, the S&P 500 gained 177.81 points, or 2.41 percent, to 7,554.67, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 656.06 points, or 2.67 percent, to 25,235.49.

Subjective
Market Briefer — the global close, November 9, 2026: the oil slide and chip rebound power the best day since April

The S&P 500 jumped 2.35 percent to 7,549.94 for its best day since April as January Brent fell 6.26 percent to $92.17 on receding Iran strike risks and chipmakers rebounded from last week’s rout, even as Nvidia fell 4.27 percent. The Dow climbed 1,104.02 points to 52,389.75 and the Nasdaq Composite rallied 673.71 points to 25,253.14. The catalyst named is energy: Brent down from above $112 at the start of the month, after the president said new strikes on Iran were highly unlikely if negotiations progress.

Subjective
Business Today, carrying Reuters — oil extends its slide, Brent sheds more than seven dollars after the president signals restraint

LONDON: Brent crude futures continued tumbling after settlement on Monday, losing more than $7 a barrel to hit their lowest level since late August, after President Trump downplayed the likelihood of renewed strikes on Iran. Brent settled down $5.75, or 5.85 percent, at $92.57 a barrel; West Texas Intermediate settled down $3.98, or 4.38 percent, to $86.85, and later fell more than $5 in post-settlement trade. Brent’s decline followed a 16 percent plunge last week, its steepest weekly drop since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic. A senior Iranian security official told state media Tehran has no plans to negotiate unless Washington takes practical steps to meet seven conditions set out in a June interim agreement.

Subjective
The Wall Street Journal — oil falls as the United States–Iran conflict risks ease

0159 GMT: oil weakens after President Trump played down the prospect of further strikes on Iran, the diplomatic signals driving a repricing of the geopolitical risk premium in the note quoted. Front-month West Texas Intermediate futures extend overnight declines in early Asian trading, falling 1.2 percent to $85.78 a barrel, and front-month Brent futures are 1.1 percent lower at $91.57 a barrel.

Subjective
The Bull Post — Polish prosecutors say it is too early to tell if the Kraków gunman was motivated by political ideology

Polish prosecutors have said they do not currently have any evidence tying the man who killed six people and injured 16 in Kraków to any particular political ideology. The 24-year-old Polish national died in hospital early on Monday after being critically injured in a shootout with police. “We do not have findings that we could, in a responsible way, categorically state that he was inspired by any particular ideology,” the National Prosecutor’s Office spokesman, Przemysław Nowak, said. “It is far too early to comment on the motives… We have not found any obvious symbols that are generally associated with a particular political movement, whether far right or far left,” he added. Mourners left candles in the square, which reopened late Sunday, and flags were lowered during two days of national mourning.

Subjective
Europe Says, carrying AFP — the Kraków shooting rampage suspect dies amid the hunt for a motive

A Polish man accused of carrying out a deadly shooting spree in Kraków died in hospital on Monday, two days after he was critically wounded in a gunbattle with police. Prosecutors said his reasons for killing nine people, including three family members, remained unclear. He was declared dead around 4:30 a.m. after three operations. Authorities had previously said the man had been “fascinated by far-right ideologies” and the prime minister called the shooting an act of “terrorism.” At Monday’s press conference prosecutors said there was no evidence tying the suspect to any particular political bent, and an interior ministry spokeswoman said the many emblems and patches on his clothing were being analysed.

Subjective
Reuters — the Kraków mass shooting assailant died in hospital, Polish police say

WARSAW, Nov 9: a gunman who killed six people in central Kraków on Saturday died in hospital on Monday, as grief mixed with a political dispute over his motives. Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said the investigation will continue, aiming to establish if he acted alone or was inspired by any group. Fifteen people injured in the attack remain in hospitals, fourteen stable, while a police officer who took part in apprehending the attacker remains in serious condition, Governor Krzysztof Klęczar told reporters.

Subjective
JFeed — Mr. Eisenkot and Mr. Liberman agree on the next Knesset speaker pick

Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot and Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman met on Monday and agreed that the next Knesset speaker will be a Yashar member, according to reports. The agreement marks a shift from Mr. Liberman’s original demand that the post go to Yair Lapid, which had caused friction among the bloc’s partners. Mr. Liberman is also willing to drop his call for an immediate vote to replace the speaker. Yashar has not said which of its members will be named. Mr. Eisenkot has until December 6 to present a government, with a possible 14-day extension.

Subjective
NewsCord — Mr. Eisenkot’s Yashar seeks Shas and United Torah Judaism support to replace Speaker Ohana

Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party invited Shas and United Torah Judaism on Monday to join an effort to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana during the inaugural session of the 26th Knesset on Tuesday. United Torah Judaism chairman Yakov Asher rejected the timing, saying the replacement should take place after a government is formed; the party said it had not received instructions to cooperate with replacing the speaker. Replacing the speaker requires at least 61 members to sign a request or vote to elect a new speaker. The two Arab-led parties together hold 19 seats and have said they will also vote to replace Mr. Ohana.

Subjective
Marc Schulman, Substack — November 9, 2026: Mr. Eisenkot and Mr. Lieberman find common ground

Israel spent Monday waiting to see whether Gadi Eisenkot can turn his election result into a governing coalition. Eisenkot met Avigdor Lieberman on Monday; this evening he addressed a gathering of party supporters. Following their meeting both men described the talks as positive and expressed confidence they were making progress toward a stable government. So far the only agreement made public concerns the next speaker of the Knesset, who will come from Eisenkot’s Yashar party. The two also reportedly agreed that Mr. Lieberman would first have an opportunity to negotiate with the ultra-Orthodox parties. Tomorrow, when the new Knesset is sworn in with 54 new members, the real work begins, in the account’s closing line.

Subjective
United Nations Meetings Coverage — the civilian toll mounts in Ukraine as attacks intensify, a senior official warns the Security Council

As the war in Ukraine grows increasingly “dangerous and unpredictable,” many Security Council speakers on Monday condemned attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure and warned against the weaponization of winter through strikes on Ukraine’s energy network, while expressing hope that the Abu Dhabi talks could yield humanitarian measures. Kayoko Gotoh reported at least 328 civilians killed and 2,105 injured in September, an 85 percent increase from 2025, and nearly 18,000 civilian deaths verified since 2022. She welcomed the six-day local ceasefire in Oleshky as an encouraging example. Ukraine’s representative asserted that Russia’s army has reached a dead end and urged a resolution requiring an immediate and unconditional ceasefire; Russia’s representative questioned the purpose of the meetings and alleged abuses not reflected in United Nations reports. China’s delegate urged the parties to seize the Abu Dhabi opportunity.

Subjective
UN News — Security Council live: strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, as peace talks loom

9 November 2026: the Security Council met in New York on Ukraine on Monday. Russian strikes on energy infrastructure are threatening millions with another cold, dark winter, and civilian deaths are climbing sharply. Strikes on Kyiv’s three main power stations in October left 600,000 people without electricity. Talks with Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi are slated for November 10–11.

Subjective
Associated Press, via Military.com — the G7 talks in Paris try to tackle unresolved global crises, with uncertainty high over the American approach

PARIS (AP): foreign ministers of the Group of Seven began two days of talks in Paris on Monday with clear differences on multiple unresolved global crises and questions about how President Trump will approach foreign policy after the midterm losses. Whether on the Russia-Ukraine war, Iran or international organizations, the sides appeared far apart, although all agreed on the need to end the conflicts as quickly as possible. Secretary Rubio was expected to face questions about whether the administration will shift its positions; German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul welcomed the Abu Dhabi talks and stressed that Europe must be part of any resolution.

Subjective
political.org — Russia and Ukraine trade long-range strikes on the power grid and oil refineries a day before the Abu Dhabi talks

Russia struck Ukraine’s electrical grid again and Ukrainian long-range drones set fire to one of Russia’s largest oil refineries, officials said Monday, November 9, hours before Russian and Ukrainian delegations were due to meet for new United States-brokered talks on November 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi. Russia’s Ministry of Defense said it targeted four electrical substations in Ukraine’s Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Cherkasy and Vinnytsia regions; Leningrad Governor Alexander Drozdenko said Ukrainian drones started a fire at the KINEF refinery near St. Petersburg.

Subjective
USA Today — Russell Brand sentenced to ten and a half years in prison for rape and sexual assault

Russell Brand, 51, received his sentence at London’s Southwark Crown Court on Monday, November 9, after a jury convicted him of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault against four women between 2004 and 2009. The judge said Brand would serve two-thirds of his sentence in custody before being released on licence. Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of the Metropolitan Police made a statement on November 9.

Subjective
People — Russell Brand sentenced to ten and a half years after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault

Russell Brand’s sentence was revealed at London’s Southwark Crown Court on Monday, November 9: ten years and six months in prison, per the BBC account carried. Judge Bennathan said Brand must serve two-thirds of his sentence before he will be eligible for release, according to The Guardian account carried. A jury found him guilty on Thursday, November 5, of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, after a trial of about four weeks; he had faced three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault, and was acquitted on three counts.

Subjective
Voice of Emirates — the American envoy condemns the attack on the Khor Mor gas field in Kurdistan

On Monday the American Special Envoy to Iraq, Tom Barrack, condemned in the strongest possible terms the missile attack targeting the Khor Mor gas field in the Kurdistan Region. On Sunday evening the field, in Chamchamal district of Sulaymaniyah Governorate, was subjected to an attack by a suicide drone; a massive fire followed and production and supply operations halted completely. The operator Dana Gas announced that emergency teams had extinguished the fire, with no human casualties reported, and that all production and supply operations remain temporarily suspended pending a full assessment of damage and verification of safety. The Kurdistan electricity ministry warned the interruption would cut generation by between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts.

Subjective
USA Today — why the Mississippi and Alaska Senate races are taking so long to call

Nearly a week after Election Day, it could still take several more days before the winners in the Mississippi and Alaska Senate races are known. By 11:42 a.m. Eastern on November 9, Scott Colom’s lead over Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi had grown to more than 2,500 votes, with about 97 percent counted in the Associated Press results. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day must arrive by November 10. In Alaska, by 12:07 p.m. Eastern on November 9, Mary Peltola led Senator Dan Sullivan by about 600 votes with about 74 percent counted; if no candidate reaches 50 percent, the ranked-choice tally would not start until November 18.

Subjective
Jamoke News — the Alaska and Mississippi Senate races, 2026: the latest count and what happens next

Facts checked November 9, 2026, at 6:30 a.m. Eastern: two Senate races from the November 3 midterms were still uncalled—Alaska, where Mary Peltola narrowly leads Senator Dan Sullivan, and Mississippi, where Scott Colom narrowly leads Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. Alaska stands at 102,962 to 102,325 in unofficial first-choice results last posted November 4; the next scheduled count is Tuesday, November 10, including early votes cast October 30 to November 2 and questioned ballots, and the ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled for November 18. Mississippi stands at a lead of 2,574 votes, 467,930 to 465,356, with about 97 percent counted; the secretary of state said 75 of 82 counties had uploaded unofficial results, 12,767 affidavit ballots had been processed with about 77 percent accepted, and just over 2,800 absentee mail ballots were still out.
items.summary: The midnight file for Tuesday, November 10, 2026: what Monday settled and what it left open. After meeting Qatar's prime minister, President Trump said Iran militarily is effectively over, that there is a good chance of a deal and that renewed strikes are quite unlikely, while keeping the naval blockade and Operation Iron Gate; Tehran's security council secretary called the talks imaginary and demanded acceptance of seven conditions, and no agreement, text or Iranian confirmation exists. Wall Street's best day since April stood at the close and oil fell more than seven dollars a barrel after settlement. National mourning ended in Poland with no ideology established for the Kraków gunman; in Jerusalem a speaker from Yashar was agreed and United Torah Judaism declined to replace the speaker at Tuesday's opening; and neither Senate race was called, with both counts holding Tuesday deadlines. Collected at 0000.

items.title: No Readout From the Oval Office, a Best Day Since April on Wall Street, and a Speaker Agreed in Jerusalem
items.content_html:
The Evening File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

No Readout From the Oval Office, a Best Day Since April on Wall Street, and a Speaker Agreed in Jerusalem

The day whole, at evening: the mediator came, met the president and the vice president, and left no public word behind him, and the war he mediates acquired a sentence from Tehran instead—its president said the Supreme Leader had ordered an end to the state of neither war nor peace. The House acquired a deadline: eight articles against the secretary of defense, refiled at mid-afternoon, with action required by Wednesday. The markets acquired a close: the best day since April, priced on oil down near six percent, with the two closing prints differing and both printed below. Kraków acquired a limit: its prosecutors said no ideology for the dead gunman had been established, as the national mourning ended on schedule. Jerusalem acquired an agreement: a speaker from Yashar, the ultra-Orthodox talks to be exhausted first, and full confidence stated by both men. Nothing was called in the Senate count. Tuesday holds the rest—the Abu Dhabi table, the inflation print, the next Alaska count, and the Knesset’s first sitting.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Monday, November 9, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 25, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 today, and closes the day begun in Edition No. 24, the Overnight Watch. Four special reports filed outside the watches today—on organ donation, on the Cornell 7 case, on the Russell Brand sentence, and on the Hegseth impeachment filing—stand on their own pages; this edition files the day’s record whole, including the facts those reports treat at length. Where the evening figures differ from the midday figures, the difference is stated here, in the open, and the earlier editions stand unrevised, as a log stands.

The Evening in Brief

Monday ended with its meetings held, its markets closed, its one new legal sentence imposed in London, its one new parliamentary clock started in Washington, and none of its open questions answered. In Washington, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, Qatar’s prime minister and foreign minister, met President Trump in the Oval Office at noon and Vice President Vance separately, and by 1800 no readout had been issued and no agreement announced, in the afternoon account and the evening account filed below. Tehran spoke for itself the same day: President Masoud Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had instructed officials to end the state of “neither war nor peace,” that Iran could negotiate with dignity, and that it would not surrender to force, in the Tehran account filed below, and Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei defended Tehran’s two-day proposal as the most reasonable offer on the table. In the House, Representative Thomas Massie refiled eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth as a privileged resolution; House leaders have two legislative days to act. In New York the Dow closed up more than eleven hundred points on the Associated Press print and the S&P 500 had its best day since April, as Brent crude fell 5.8 percent to $92.57. In Kraków the National Prosecutor’s Office spokesman, Przemysław Nowak, said investigators could not yet link the dead gunman responsibly to any ideology, in the evening brief filed below. In Jerusalem Mr. Eisenkot and Mr. Liberman agreed the next speaker of the Knesset will be a member of Yashar, in the speaker account filed below. In London Mr. Justice Bennathan sentenced Russell Brand to ten years and six months in prison. The desk files the day in that order.

Washington at Evening: The Mediator Leaves No Word, and the House Gets a Clock

The noon meeting produced, by evening, a fact of attendance and nothing else. The Qatari prime minister met the president behind closed doors and the vice president separately, having visited Tehran last week; the White House released no readout, and Fox News reported it had sought comment and received no response before publication. The terms on the table stand where the midday edition printed them: an end to the American blockade of Iran’s ports, the lifting of some sanctions and a halt to bombing, in return for Tehran stopping its own closure of the Strait of Hormuz, with nuclear talks to follow—a plan Washington has repeatedly rejected, and which Secretary Rubio, in Paris for the G7, again said was not near a breakthrough, its demands in part unacceptable, outrageous and not realistic. Tehran’s considered response arrived Monday in two voices. Mr. Baghaei defended the plan. President Pezeshkian, at a ceremony in Tehran, gave the day its fullest Iranian sentence: the Leader had ordered an end to the neither-war-nor-peace state; “we can negotiate with dignity and resolve the issue with dignity”; and Iran would not surrender in the face of force, intimidation or bullying. The president’s own Sunday sentence stands unwithdrawn beside them: fresh attacks are highly unlikely if talks produce a strong agreement. No side moved a term on Monday. The mediation moved a man between capitals, and the record of the day is the movement and the statements, not a settlement.

At mid-afternoon the House acquired the week’s hardest deadline. Representative Massie of Kentucky, a Republican, read a 34-page resolution on the floor re-filing eight articles of impeachment against Secretary Hegseth, as a privileged resolution, in the Louisville account filed below. The articles charge violations of the War Powers Resolution in the Iran war, failure to minimize civilian casualties, extrajudicial killings in the boat strikes, suppression of Senator Kelly’s speech, the seizure of Nicolás Maduro without authority, and an unlawful war in Yemen.
