The procedure is the fact: leaders must act within two legislative days—an up-or-down vote, a motion to table, or a referral to committee, each itself a vote—with a vote expected by Wednesday. The answers on the record are these: Mr. Hegseth said he is not worried and will defend his record at a Pentagon press conference on Tuesday, his first in 180 days in the Associated Press count; the president has backed him, and said on Sunday’s broadcast interview that he has confidence in him; Speaker Johnson opposes the effort; Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he supports the articles. Mr. Massie first filed the same articles on September 15; the House left for its campaign recess the next day and the notice expired. If the House impeaches, Mr. Hegseth would be the third Cabinet secretary impeached in the republic’s history, and removal would require two-thirds of the Senate. The articles are allegations in a charging document; they are findings by no court. Mr. Miller’s first day as chief of staff, the morning’s other Washington fact, closed without a statement from him in the file.

The Markets’ Close: The Best Day Since April, in Two Prints

New York kept the morning’s reading and enlarged it, and the close is the day’s largest single number. On the Associated Press print, carried in the closing account filed below, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,104.02 points, or 2.2 percent, to 52,389.75; the S&P 500 rose 173.08 points, or 2.3 percent, to 7,549.94, its best day since April, sitting 3.4 percent below its all-time high; and the Nasdaq Composite rose 673.71 points, or 2.7 percent, to 25,253.14. On the Reuters print, carried in the second closing account filed below, the Dow rose 1,131.81 points, or 2.21 percent, to 52,417.54; the S&P rose 177.81 points, or 2.41 percent, to 7,554.67; and the Nasdaq rose 656.06 points, or 2.67 percent, to 25,235.49. The two prints differ in the third figure on every index; the desk prints both, each under its wire, in the Cocked Hat. The driver named in both accounts is oil: Brent crude fell 5.8 percent to $92.57 a barrel, from above $112 at the month’s start, on the president’s stated unlikelihood of renewed strikes on Iran—the same diplomacy that produced no readout at noon was priced in New York as de-escalation. Inside the rise Nvidia fell against the market all day on its board’s inquiry into whether its chief executive was the target of a foreign intelligence effort: down 4.27 percent to $178.67 at the close in one account, down 6.2 and 6.3 percent in two others, each at its own hour, all filed below; the board said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, Mr. Huang remains chief executive and has pledged full cooperation, and Beijing rejected the espionage allegations. Tuesday’s test is named in every account: the October consumer price report at 8:30 a.m. Eastern.

Kraków at Evening: No Ideology Established, and the Mourning Ends

Poland’s file acquired its limit on Monday evening, stated by the prosecutors themselves. Przemysław Nowak, spokesman for the National Prosecutor’s Office, said investigators do not have elements that allow them responsibly and categorically to state that the gunman was inspired by a particular ideology, in the evening brief above. Government spokesman Adam Szłapka said such assessments should be withheld until the services have full information. Those two sentences stand against the weekend’s government reading—the interior minister’s far-right and ultra-nationalistic reading of the emblems on the man’s clothing, and the justice minister’s statement that he acted to intimidate a large number of people, making the offence a terrorist offence in the minister’s words—and the desk prints the limit and the readings side by side, unresolved. The day’s facts stand as the midday edition filed them: the suspect, 24, died at about 4:30 a.m. after at least three operations; autopsies of the nine victims—six in the Main Market Square and three at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski—began Monday and will take about two days; fifteen wounded remain in hospital, fourteen stable and one officer, Artur Morański, in serious condition after, in the evening brief’s figure, twelve hours of surgery; eleven firearms were recovered in the searches. National mourning, declared for November 8 and 9, ends Monday night; Kraków’s own mourning runs to November 11, which the city marks without a parade. School sessions with psychologists ran in Ostrowiec on Monday and continue Tuesday. The investigation proceeds on forensics, witness testimony, telephones, computers and weapons; the man who could have answered it is dead, and the prosecutors’ Monday sentence is that the evidence has not yet answered it either.

Paris and the Eve of Abu Dhabi: The Allies Apart in Public, the Guns Loud in Private Fact

The G7’s first day in Paris ended with the differences stated, not settled. The Associated Press account, in the Paris account filed below, records that on the Russia-Ukraine war, on Iran and on international organizations the sides appeared far apart, while agreeing the conflicts should end as quickly as possible. Secretary Rubio faced the allies’ questions on whether the midterm defeat changes the administration’s approach—his first trip abroad since the elections. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, meeting Mr. Rubio separately, welcomed the Abu Dhabi talks and stressed that Europe must be part of any resolution; Canada’s Foreign Minister Anita Anand said it remains an open question how Washington will proceed; and in a sideline meeting with Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, Mr. Rubio pressed the administration’s case against European Union trade preferences. France has said the meeting is not expected to produce a joint communiqué. The talks continue Tuesday, with a dedicated Ukraine session.

The table Paris is the antechamber to sits on Tuesday, and on Monday its membership was itself disputed. The Abu Dhabi round—the fourth of the American-brokered process and the first since February—brings Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner for Washington, Mr. Medinsky for Moscow and Mr. Umerov for Kyiv, on security guarantees, de-escalation and humanitarian questions, in the talks account filed below. On Monday Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov reiterated that the negotiations would take place exclusively between the Russian, Ukrainian and American delegations; Mr. Barrot had said on Sunday that officials from France, Britain, Germany, NATO and the European Commission would be present, and a European Union official said Monday that national security officials would be on site, with their role unclear. Both statements stand. The eve was marked, as eves of talks in this war are marked, by fire: Russia launched 317 drones overnight, 105 of them jet-powered, and struck four electrical substations in the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Cherkasy and Vinnytsia regions by its defence ministry’s account, leaving more than 600,000 people in Dnipropetrovsk region without power in the operator DTEK’s figure; Ukrainian long-range drones set fire to the KINEF refinery at Kirishi, one of Russia’s largest, in the Leningrad governor’s account; and the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant spent ten hours on emergency diesel after losing its last working external power line on Sunday, before power was restored through a single line, in the strikes account and the energy account filed below. President Zelenskyy said the European Union had agreed to activate a special emergency mechanism to speed funding for grid repairs. No ceasefire attends the talks; the talks are not one.

Jerusalem at Evening: A Speaker Agreed, the Ultra-Orthodox First, and Confidence Stated by Both

The mandate’s second day produced the file’s first agreements, and they are procedural in the way that decides governments. Mr. Eisenkot and Mr. Liberman met Monday and agreed that the next speaker of the Knesset will be a member of Mr. Eisenkot’s Yashar party, in the speaker account above—a shift from Mr. Liberman’s earlier demand that the post go to Mr. Lapid, which had caused friction in the bloc. Yashar’s statement after what it called a substantive and good meeting said the two “expressed their full confidence in the ability to form a stable government for four years,” in the statement account filed below; the account notes the statement did not say whether their differences were resolved. The Channel 13 report carried in the second Jerusalem account gives the meeting’s substance: Mr. Liberman told Mr. Eisenkot, “You will be prime minister. I’m not asking for that position for myself,” demanded time to work and the bloc’s preparation for compromises, and asked him to assist in contacts with the ultra-Orthodox parties; the two agreed those talks must be exhausted first, and only afterward should a minority government resting on the Arab-led parties be examined—which puts Mr. Liberman’s ruled-out option last rather than off the table, and negotiations with United Torah Judaism are reported already begun. The new Knesset convenes Tuesday. Mr. Eisenkot has until December 6, with a fourteen-day extension available; the bloc stands at 48 seats, 61 are required, and Mr. Netanyahu remains prime minister while the days run.

Hormuz and Khor Mor at Evening: No Unauthorised Transit, an Export Claim, and a Field Still Dark

The strait’s Monday record is a claim of control from Tehran, a tracker’s count from midday, and an export figure from Abu Dhabi, and the three do not sum. An unnamed Guards Navy official told Iranian media that navigational aid systems in the south of the strait were destroyed and that no unauthorised vessels transited overnight, in the Reuters account filed below. The tracker’s midday count stands as the midday edition filed it: two crossings visible on Monday, both inbound, against a seven-day average of 7.0 and a pre-crisis average of 84.8 a day. Against both, the Emirates’ account of its own bypass: an Emirati official at the ADIPEC conference said the country exported almost 4.4 million barrels a day now, against 3.1 to 3.2 million before the war began on February 28, through routes including the Fujairah pipeline outside the strait, in the Fox account above; Energy Minister Suhail Al Mazrouei had said on November 2 that exports had at times exceeded pre-war levels, without dates or volumes, and the pipeline’s own ceiling is 1.5 million barrels a day in the analysis filed below, so the figure, if it stands, runs substantially through the strait itself and the shuttle system around it. The president’s Sunday sentence—that the strait is open—stands beside the tracker’s severely restricted. At Khor Mor nothing moved by evening: production remains halted after Sunday’s drone attack, the operator’s damage assessment has produced no figure and no restart date, 2,800 megawatts stand off the Kurdistan grid, no group has claimed the attack, and Baghdad’s joint investigative committee has not reported.

London at Evening: Ten Years and Six Months

The day’s one completed legal act was a sentence. At Southwark Crown Court on Monday morning, Mr. Justice Bennathan sentenced Russell Brand, 51, to ten years and six months in prison: nine years for one count of rape, and eighteen months—the longest of three terms of nine, eighteen and eight months, running concurrently—for three counts of sexual assault, the two sentences running consecutively, in the sentencing account and the wire account filed below. A jury convicted him on Thursday, November 5, on four of seven counts, for offences against four women between 2004 and 2009, and acquitted him on three. The judge told him his offences were fuelled by “staggering arrogance,” named him a sexual predator, reduced the rape term by one year for his lack of previous convictions, the seventeen years since the last offence, and his work with people in addiction, and ordered that he serve two-thirds of the sentence in custody before release on licence. Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of the Metropolitan Police made a statement on Monday on the investigation. Files on two further women are with the prosecutors, and a New York civil case proceeds; both stand open. The full record of the case is filed on this paper’s special report page of today’s date.

The Count at Evening: Nothing Moves, and Tuesday Holds Both Deadlines

For the fourth day running no Senate race was called and no new vote figure was published for either. Mississippi stands at Scott Colom 467,930 to Cindy Hyde-Smith 465,356, a margin of 2,574, with just over 2,800 absentee mail ballots still out in the secretary of state’s accounting; mail ballots postmarked by Election Day are due by 5 p.m. Tuesday, and counties certify by November 13. Alaska stands at Mary Peltola ahead of Dan Sullivan by 637 first-choice votes, and its next count is Tuesday, carrying early votes cast October 30 to November 2 and questioned ballots; the ranked-choice tabulation stands on November 18. Colorado’s 4th District stands uncalled with them. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide, and control of neither chamber is in question. The standing files did not move: at Al-Ayyat the investigations ordered Sunday own the cause of the collision that killed seven, the driver of Train No. 134 among them, and no authority has stated a cause; in Asunción former President Peña’s pretrial detention stands, with no ruling on any charge, and he is presumed innocent.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On the close, the Associated Press print puts the Dow up 1,104.02 to 52,389.75 and the Nasdaq up 673.71, and the Reuters print puts the Dow up 1,131.81 to 52,417.54 and the Nasdaq up 656.06; the rally is single-valued, its third figure is not. On Nvidia, down 4.27 percent at the close in one account and down 6.2 to 6.3 percent in two others at their hours. On Kraków’s motive, the interior minister’s far-right reading of the emblems, the justice minister’s terrorist-offence statement, and the prosecutors’ Monday limit—no elements allowing a responsible and categorical statement of any ideology—with the government spokesman counselling withholding; the limit is the newest bearing and the readings stand unwithdrawn. On Abu Dhabi’s membership, the Kremlin’s exclusively-three-delegations against the French foreign minister’s European presence and the Union official’s on-site, role unclear. On Hormuz, open in the president’s word, severely restricted in the tracker’s, and closed to the unauthorised in the Guards’; on the Emirates’ exports, almost 4.4 million barrels a day in an official’s conference words against a 1.5-million-barrel pipeline ceiling and no dated volumes. Against the triangle, the evening’s single-valued facts are these: the mediator met the president and the vice president and no readout exists; Iran’s president stated the Leader’s instruction to end neither war nor peace; eight articles were refiled in the House and action is due by Wednesday; Mr. Brand was sentenced to ten years and six months; a speaker from Yashar was agreed in Jerusalem and the ultra-Orthodox talks go first; the autopsies began in Kraków and the national mourning ends tonight; no Senate race was called and no figure moved. Tuesday holds the Abu Dhabi table, the G7’s second day, the inflation report, the Alaska count, the Mississippi mail deadline, the Knesset’s convening and the secretary of defense’s press conference. The log proceeds to midnight.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Thirty items.

Subjective
Fox News — the president meets the Iran war mediator, and the Emirates reveal an oil export surge

President Trump met Qatar’s prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, on Monday at the White House as efforts to end the Iran war continue, with Secretary Rubio warning that negotiations remain far from a breakthrough and Tehran signalling willingness to negotiate without yielding to pressure. An Emirati official at the ADIPEC conference said the Emirates exported almost 4.4 million barrels a day now, against 3.1 to 3.2 million before the war began on February 28. Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment and did not receive a response before publication.

Subjective
Zark News — the president meets Qatar’s prime minister as Iran defends the truce offer Washington rejected

Qatar’s prime minister met President Trump and Vice President Vance at the White House on Monday. Tehran publicly defended the truce offer Washington has already rejected, the secretary of state said no breakthrough is near, and as of Monday evening the two sides remain apart on the same points and no agreement has been announced.

Subjective
Reuters — the president to meet the Iran war mediator Qatar, no imminent deal seen to end the war

CAIRO/ABU DHABI, Nov 9: President Trump will meet the prime minister of key mediator Qatar on Monday as efforts to end the Iran war ramp up following last week’s midterm elections, though senior American and Gulf officials cast doubt on the chances of an imminent deal. Iran’s proposal involves an end to the American blockade of its ports, the lifting of some sanctions and a halt to bombing in return for Tehran stopping its own blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, with talks on its nuclear programme and other sanctions to follow.

Subjective
Press TV — the Leader ordered Iran’s officials to end the state of neither war nor peace, the president says

President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Monday that the Leader, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, has instructed Iranian officials to put an end to the current state of neither war nor peace. “We can engage in dialogue with dignity and bring this matter to a dignified conclusion,” the president said, adding that Iran will never surrender in the face of force, intimidation or bullying.

Subjective
Anadolu, via Hathalyoum — Iran open to negotiations to end the no war, no peace situation, its president says

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday that Tehran remains open to negotiations to end the country’s “no war, no peace” situation, stressing that Iran seeks dialogue with the United States based on mutual respect but will not surrender to pressure. “We can negotiate with dignity and resolve the issue with dignity. We favor dialogue and negotiations,” he said.

Subjective
The Courier Journal — Representative Thomas Massie moves to force a House vote on the Hegseth impeachment

Representative Thomas Massie reintroduced articles of impeachment against Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth on November 9, forcing Congress to decide whether to move forward. House leadership has two days to move to table the resolution, move it to committee or allow a floor vote. Hegseth announced he would hold a press conference, his first in 180 days in the Associated Press count, about the impeachment on Tuesday, November 10.

Subjective
NationWire — Massie to force a Hegseth impeachment vote as the House returns

The House returns on Monday and Representative Thomas Massie intends to force a vote on eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. CNN reported that multiple Republican sources expect the measure to pass. Massie, who lost his Republican primary in May and leaves Congress in January, wrote on November 4 that the one contingency in which he would not reintroduce the articles is that Hegseth resigns.

Subjective
USA Today — three takeaways from the president’s 60 Minutes interview

The interview, which aired November 8: the president attributed the midterm losses to his not being up for reelection, cited the Iran war among the causes, hinted at cabinet changes before the chief of staff’s departure, and said he has confidence in Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. The House returned November 9, with the impeachment push expected to go forward.

Subjective
Associated Press, via TV News Check — the Dow jumps 1,104, the Nasdaq climbs 674, the S&P 500 adds 173

NEW YORK (AP): the United States stock market rallied Monday and recovered most of last week’s losses as oil prices swung lower. The S&P 500 jumped 2.3 percent, its best day since April, the Dow leaped 1,104.02 points to 52,389.75, and the Nasdaq composite rose 673.71 to 25,253.14. A barrel of Brent crude fell 5.8 percent to $92.57.

Subjective
Reuters, via SRN News — Wall Street jumps back as the oil slide eases inflation worries; Nvidia slumps

NEW YORK, Nov 9 (Reuters): United States stocks rallied on Monday, as a drop in oil prices tempered inflation fears and helped the S&P 500 bounce off its biggest weekly drop since April 2025, and tech shares jumped even as Nvidia slumped. The Dow rose 1,131.81 points, or 2.21 percent, to 52,417.54, the S&P 500 gained 177.81 points, or 2.41 percent, to 7,554.67, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 656.06 points, or 2.67 percent, to 25,235.49.

Subjective
Finance News Network — the ASX set to rise as Wall Street rallies and oil prices tumble

United States stocks rallied sharply on Monday. The Dow surged 1,104.02 points, or 2.15 percent, to close at 52,389.75; the S&P 500 jumped 2.35 percent to 7,549.94, its strongest session since April 8; and the Nasdaq Composite gained 2.74 percent to 25,253.14. Brent crude fell 5.85 percent to $92.57 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate dropped 4.38 percent to $86.85.

Subjective
Silicon Report — Nvidia shares drop nearly five percent premarket over the chief executive probe

Nvidia shares dropped nearly five percent in premarket trading on Monday after the chipmaker launched an independent board investigation into chief executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with an executive whom intelligence agencies describe as a Chinese spy. The board stated it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised; Mr. Huang remains chief executive during the inquiry and committed to cooperating fully.

Subjective
The Globuzz — Nvidia shares fall after the board opens the chief executive probe

Nvidia shares fell about five percent at the opening bell on Monday, November 9, after the company said its board had opened an independent investigation into reports that chief executive Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The board has not announced a finding, and Mr. Huang remains chief executive while the inquiry proceeds.

Subjective
Pollar — the evening brief, November 9: prosecutors probe the Kraków gunman

The suspect died in hospital, autopsies began, and prosecutors said no ideology had been established. Six people were killed, four women and two men, and fifteen others were wounded, including a police officer who remains in serious condition; the wounded officer Artur Morański underwent twelve hours of surgery. Przemysław Nowak, spokesman for the National Prosecutor’s Office, said investigators could not yet link him responsibly to any ideology.

Subjective
Infohandle — the Kraków suspect dies as Polish prosecutors keep the terror probe open amid motive questions

Michał Oksiński, the 24-year-old police seized after the mass shooting on Kraków’s Main Market Square, died in hospital early Monday, yet national prosecutors insisted their terrorism investigation will continue without him. At a Monday briefing the National Prosecutor’s Office spokesman said investigators still lack evidence to tie him to any particular political ideology. The interior ministry announced a review of gun-licensing procedures.

Subjective
Reuters — the Kraków mass shooting assailant died in hospital, Polish police say

WARSAW, Nov 9: a gunman who killed six people in central Kraków on Saturday died in hospital on Monday, as grief mixed with a political dispute over his motives. Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said the investigation will continue, aiming to establish if he acted alone or was inspired by any group. Fifteen people injured in the attack remain in hospitals, fourteen stable, while a police officer who took part in apprehending the attacker remains in serious condition, Governor Krzysztof Klęczar told reporters.

Subjective
Associated Press, via Military.com — the G7 talks in Paris try to tackle unresolved global crises, with uncertainty high over the American approach

PARIS (AP): foreign ministers of the Group of Seven began two days of talks in Paris on Monday with clear differences on multiple unresolved global crises and questions about how President Trump will approach foreign policy after the midterm losses. Whether on the Russia-Ukraine war, Iran or international organizations, the sides appeared far apart, although all agreed on the need to end the conflicts as quickly as possible.

Subjective
Reuters, via DevDiscourse — the G7 allies to assess the impact of the president’s midterm setback at the Paris talks

G7 foreign ministers gathered in Paris on Monday aiming to gauge whether a United States midterm defeat for President Trump alters the administration’s approach to Ukraine, the Middle East and ties with its closest allies, four G7 diplomats said. In a sideline meeting with French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, Secretary Rubio appeared to stick to the administration’s tough-talking approach toward allies in Europe, calling for an end to European Union trade preferences.

Subjective
political.org — Russia and Ukraine trade long-range strikes on the power grid and oil refineries a day before the Abu Dhabi talks

Russia struck Ukraine’s electrical grid again and Ukrainian long-range drones set fire to one of Russia’s largest oil refineries, officials said Monday, November 9, hours before Russian and Ukrainian delegations were due to meet for new United States-brokered talks on November 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi. Russia’s Ministry of Defense said it targeted four electrical substations in Ukraine’s Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Cherkasy and Vinnytsia regions; Leningrad Governor Alexander Drozdenko said Ukrainian drones started a fire at the KINEF refinery near St. Petersburg.

Subjective
Associated Press, via Military.com — Russia and Ukraine batter each other with long-range strikes a day before the talks

KYIV, Ukraine (AP): Russia battered Ukraine’s power grid again and Ukrainian forces hit another of Russia’s biggest oil refineries, officials said Monday. Russia launched 317 drones of various types including 105 jet-powered drones at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine’s air force said, and a strike on a warehouse holding food for schools and kindergartens in Odesa killed three people. The three-way talks in Abu Dhabi are due to start on Tuesday.

Subjective
Baltic Security Monitor — power at Zaporizhzhia, fire at Kirishi

Europe’s largest nuclear plant lost all off-site power for the 27th time in the war and spent ten hours on diesel before the grid came back through a single line, the IAEA reported. The same night drones set Russia’s Kirishi refinery ablaze; the governor confirmed impacts in the industrial zone, and damage to the refinery’s primary units and any halt in processing are not independently confirmed.

Subjective
AnewZ — the Russia-Ukraine peace talks return to Abu Dhabi

Russia and Ukraine are set to return to Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for a fourth round of United States-brokered peace talks, with European participation, security guarantees and territorial disputes expected to shape the negotiations. Delegations joined by envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are due on November 10 and 11. On Monday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov reiterated that the negotiations would take place exclusively between Russian, Ukrainian and United States delegations.

Subjective
Al Jazeera, via 234Radio — no concession: what to expect from the Russia-United States-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi

Officials from Ukraine, Russia and the United States are set to converge in Abu Dhabi for negotiations aimed at ending nearly five years of war, but analysts are not hopeful of much progress. A Ukrainian member of parliament told the outlet he expects no tangible progress, and the analysts quoted were certain no peace accord would emerge from this week’s session. Europe is not officially part of the trilateral talks; a European Union official said national security officials would be on site, their involvement unclear.

Subjective
JFeed — Eisenkot and Liberman agree on the next Knesset speaker pick

Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot and Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman met on Monday and agreed that the next Knesset speaker will be a Yashar member of Knesset, according to reports—a shift from Mr. Liberman’s original demand that the post go to Yair Lapid. In a statement after what it called a substantive and good meeting, Yashar said the two expressed their full confidence in the ability to form a stable government for four years.

Subjective
JFeed — Liberman tells Eisenkot: you will be prime minister, I will oust Netanyahu

According to a Channel 13 report, Mr. Liberman told Mr. Eisenkot in Monday’s meeting that he has no interest in the prime minister’s role but demanded that Mr. Eisenkot prepare his party and the bloc for compromises, and asked him to assist in contacts with the ultra-Orthodox parties. The two agreed that talks with the ultra-Orthodox must be exhausted first, and only afterward should other options be examined; negotiations between Mr. Eisenkot and United Torah Judaism have already begun, the report says.

Subjective
The Times of Israel, via DevDiscourse — Eisenkot and Liberman express full confidence in forming a stable government

Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot and Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Liberman expressed “full confidence” in their ability to form a stable government for a full four-year term following a meeting on Monday, the Yashar party’s statement calling the discussions constructive and productive. The account notes the statement did not indicate whether the two leaders had resolved their differences or reached concrete agreements.

Subjective
Reuters, via Hathalyoum — Iran says no unauthorised vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz overnight after navigation aids were destroyed

DUBAI, Nov 9 (Reuters): navigational aid systems in the south of the Strait of Hormuz were destroyed and no unauthorised vessels transited the maritime route overnight, an unnamed Revolutionary Guards Navy official told Iranian state media on Monday.

Subjective
Talay Insight — the Emirates say the Hormuz bypass has lifted exports back to pre-war levels

Energy Minister Mazrouei told ADIPEC on November 2 that exports had for a time exceeded pre-war levels, but gave no dates or volumes. According to Kpler, exports bottomed at 2.13 million barrels a day in March and reached 3.94 million in June. The Habshan-Fujairah pipeline is capped at 1.5 million barrels a day, and the minister’s claim comes without the dates or volumes that would verify it.

Subjective
USA Today — Russell Brand sentenced to ten and a half years in prison for rape and sexual assault

Russell Brand, 51, received his sentence at London’s Southwark Crown Court on Monday, November 9, after a jury convicted him of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault against four women between 2004 and 2009. The judge said Brand would serve two-thirds of his sentence in custody before being released on licence. Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of the Metropolitan Police made a statement on November 9.

Subjective
NPR Illinois — the British comedian Russell Brand sentenced to over ten years for rape and sexual assault

“The total sentence is one of ten years, six months,” Mr. Justice Bennathan said on handing down the sentence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Monday. A jury found Brand guilty last week on four of the seven counts against him.
items.summary: The evening file for Monday, November 9, 2026: the day's developments whole. Qatar's prime minister met the president and the vice president in Washington and no readout or agreement was announced by collection time, while Iran's president said the Supreme Leader had ordered an end to the state of neither war nor peace and Tehran defended its two-day proposal. Wall Street closed with its best day since April on falling oil, the two closing prints differing in the third figure. In Kraków prosecutors said no ideology had been established for the dead gunman as national mourning ended. In Jerusalem Mr. Eisenkot and Mr. Liberman agreed the next Knesset speaker will come from Yashar and said they were confident of a stable government. Representative Massie refiled eight articles of impeachment against Secretary Hegseth, forcing House action by Wednesday, and Russell Brand was sentenced in London to ten years and six months. Collected at 1800.

items.title: Pete Hegseth Impeachment: Thomas Massie Files Eight Articles and Forces a House Vote
items.content_html:
Special Report

Breaking News—The Impeachment File: Eight Articles, a Two-Day Clock, and the Vote It Forces

Objective

Pete Hegseth Impeachment: Thomas Massie Files Eight Articles and Forces a House Vote — Special Report

Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, refiled eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on the House floor on Monday, November 9, 2026, as a privileged resolution, starting a clock that requires House leaders to act within two legislative days, with a vote possible as early as Wednesday. The articles charge Hegseth with waging the Iran war in violation of three provisions of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties, extrajudicial killings in the strikes on suspected drug-trafficking boats, suppressing the free speech of Senator Mark Kelly, seizing Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro without authority, and waging an unlawful war in Yemen. Hegseth said on Monday that he is not worried and will defend his record at a Pentagon press conference on Tuesday; President Trump has backed him; Speaker Mike Johnson opposes the effort; House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries is a hard yes. If the House votes to impeach, Hegseth would be the third Cabinet secretary impeached in American history, and removal would require two-thirds of the Senate. The desk files the filing, the eight articles one by one, the procedure, the count, every answer on the record, the September first filing, and what remains open.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1549 ET, Monday, November 9, 2026.

The File in Brief

Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a Republican, stood on the House floor on Monday afternoon, November 9, 2026, read a 34-page resolution, and refiled eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth as a privileged resolution, and that single filing sets the week: House leaders must act within two legislative days, a vote on the articles themselves, on a motion to table them, or on a motion to refer them to committee is expected by Wednesday, and a simple majority of the House would impeach the secretary. The articles charge high crimes and misdemeanors. Three of them allege violations of the War Powers Resolution of 1973 in the war with Iran: waging the war with no declaration of war, no statutory authorization, no attack on the United States, and no imminent threat; continuing it after both houses of Congress directed the removal of United States forces in House Concurrent Resolution 86; and continuing hostilities past the resolution’s 60-day termination period and its further 30-day withdrawal period, a span Massie’s office states at more than 90 days. The remaining five allege ignoring the laws that minimize civilian casualties, extrajudicial killings in the lethal strikes on suspected drug-trafficking boats, retaliation against Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona for protected speech, the seizure of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores in Operation ABSOLUTE RESOLVE, and an unlawful war in Yemen in Operation ROUGH RIDER. The answers stand on the record beside the charges. Hegseth said on Monday, “We’re not worried about that,” and announced a Pentagon press conference for Tuesday, his first there since May. President Donald Trump has backed his secretary in public, in an Oval Office remark and in a “60 Minutes” interview broadcast on Sunday. Speaker Mike Johnson opposes impeachment while hostilities continue. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Sunday that he is “a hard yes.” Massie first filed the same eight articles on September 15; the House left for its campaign recess the next day, the notice expired, and Monday’s filing restarts the clock in a lame-duck House that Republicans still control until January, one week after midterm elections in which they lost both chambers. If the House impeaches Hegseth, he becomes the third Cabinet secretary impeached in the history of the republic, after William Belknap in 1876 and Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024, and conviction and removal would then require two-thirds of the Senate, where Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats. The articles are allegations in a charging document filed by one member of the House. They are findings by no court, no tribunal, and no inspector general, and the desk files them at that grade, with every answer the record holds.

1. What Was Filed on Monday

The filing was one of the first legislative acts of the lame-duck session, and it was made in person, on the floor. The House returned to Washington on Monday, November 9, for the final weeks of the Republican-controlled Congress elected in 2024. Massie told the New York Post shortly before he rose that he was re-filing the articles, and that “I think it’s more likely to pass after the election than before the election,” a reference to the November 3 midterms, in which Republicans lost control of the House and the Senate, with the new majorities to be seated in January. On the floor he read the resolution’s operative charge in its own words: “Secretary Hegseth abused the powers of his high office through the following means: Executing an unlawful order to commence hostilities despite the absence of a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization, or a national emergency created by an attack upon the United States, its territories or possessions, or its armed forces.” The resolution’s closing sentence on its sponsor’s reading is also in the record: “Hegseth, by such conduct, has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law.” Massie’s office issued its announcement the same day, under the headline that he is forcing the House to vote, stating that his actions “will force the House to vote on eight specific impeachment charges against the Secretary of Defense,” and publishing the summary of each article that Section 2 of this report follows. The New York Times carried the filing as its breaking news of 3:30 p.m. ET: Representative Thomas Massie had called up impeachment charges against Pete Hegseth, accusing him of violating the Constitution, and the move started a clock that will force lawmakers to vote on the question within two days. The desk’s file agrees with the Times’ two-day statement, and adds the instrument: the resolution was filed as privileged, a question of the privileges of the House, and privilege is what starts the clock.

Massie stated his own terms for stopping, and his own advice to the president, in the same release. On November 4 he had written on X: “There is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns.” Hegseth did not resign, and the filing followed. In Monday’s statement Massie cast the effort in comparative terms: “My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what’s coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year. They will hold hearings and trials. President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate.” He stated the question he puts to his colleagues in a post on November 9: “I’ve seen some of my colleagues say Hegseth has been effective and they agree with the war, so they’ll vote not to impeach. That’s not the question though. The question is whether he committed impeachable acts, and the answer is yes, eight times.” Massie is a member of the House Judiciary Committee, on his office’s statement. He lost his Republican primary in May to a challenger backed by the president, and he leaves Congress in January at the end of this term. Those two facts—the committee seat and the January departure—are the whole of his standing in the file: he files from inside the committee of jurisdiction, and he files as a member with no election left to contest.

2. The Eight Articles, One by One

The eight articles divide into three groups: three on Iran and the War Powers Resolution, two on the conduct of operations, and three on operations and authority beyond Iran. The summaries below are Massie’s office’s own summaries of November 9, printed in the resolution’s order. The desk prints them as the sponsor’s statement of his charges.

Article I—Waging War in Contravention of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, Section 2(c). The article charges Hegseth with waging the Iran war despite no declaration of war, no statutory authorization, no attack on the United States, and no imminent threat, and establishes, in the sponsor’s summary, that the war was unlawful from its inception.

Article II—Waging War in Contravention of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, Section 5(c). The article charges Hegseth with continuing the Iran war after both houses of Congress directed the removal of United States forces through H. Con. Res. 86, and focuses on his refusal to obey Congress’s express direction to terminate unauthorized hostilities.

Article III—Waging War in Contravention of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, Section 5(b). The article charges Hegseth with continuing hostilities in Iran after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period, and establishes, in the summary’s words, that he treated mandatory statutory deadlines as discretionary. Massie’s standing formulation of the first three articles is one sentence, repeated in his release: “By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable.”

Article IV—Ignoring Laws That Minimize Civilian Casualties. The article charges Hegseth with ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties. The reporting of the resolution adds its central instance: the articles describe a United States strike that hit an elementary school in Iran as a foreseeable consequence of the secretary’s direction, and they accuse him of fostering what the resolution calls a war-making culture at the department, quoting his stated preference for “maximum lethality, not tepid legality” and his dismissal of “stupid rules of engagement.” The desk files the school strike and the culture passage as the resolution’s allegations, stated in the resolution’s terms.

Article V—Extrajudicial Killings. The article charges Hegseth with replacing maritime law enforcement with unauthorized lethal military targeting of suspected drug traffickers, resulting in at least 243 deaths, on the sponsor’s count. The article also addresses denial of quarter, secondary strikes on survivors, failure to rescue shipwrecked persons, and the creation of artificial legal authorities for the campaign. CNN’s account of the same operations, filed below, counts at least 80 vessels destroyed and 243 people killed since the operations began last September, and states that the Pentagon has provided no public evidence for its claims against the people killed. The two counts of the dead agree at 243.

Article VI—Suppressing Free Speech. The article charges Hegseth with using Defense Department authority to retaliate against and intimidate Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat of Arizona, for constitutionally protected speech questioning unlawful military orders. Reuters’ file supplies the sequence beneath the article: last year Hegseth sought to prosecute Kelly after Kelly and five other members of Congress with military and intelligence backgrounds urged United States troops to refuse illegal orders; Hegseth accused them of sedition.

Article VII—Kidnapping of a Sovereign Foreign Leader. The article charges Hegseth with directing Operation ABSOLUTE RESOLVE to seize Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores in Venezuela without constitutional or legal authority. The resolution’s characterization of the January operation, as CNN reports its language, is “an act of war against a sovereign country executed under the guise of narcotics law enforcement.” The president’s own characterization stands in Section 4 of this report.

Article VIII—Unlawful War in Yemen. The article charges Hegseth with initiating Operation ROUGH RIDER in Yemen without congressional authorization or an imminent threat to the United States, while also violating war powers reporting requirements.

The resolution closes in the form the House’s charging documents use, and CNN prints the sentence. “In all of this, Secretary Hegseth has acted in a manner contrary to his trust as Secretary of Defense and subversive of constitutional government, to the great prejudice of the cause of law and justice, and to the manifest injury of the people of the United States.” One defense from the administration stands on the record from the first filing: Attorney General Todd Blanche said in September that Hegseth follows the law. No fuller administration answer to the eight articles, article by article, stands in Monday’s file.

3. The Clock: How a Privileged Resolution Forces a Vote

The procedure is short, and every step of it is a recorded vote. The Constitution gives the House “the sole Power of Impeachment” and the Senate the power to try all impeachments. A member may raise impeachment as a question of the privileges of the House. When a resolution is filed in that form, House leaders have two legislative days to schedule its consideration. Massie stated the mechanics in his own words before the filing: “The ball is in their court once I give notice, so they have two legislative days. They could deal with it tonight, tomorrow or the next day.” The accounts agree on the deadline the clock produces: action by Wednesday, November 11, with a vote possible as early as Wednesday and, on Massie’s own statement, as early as Monday night. At the hour of consideration, leadership has three courses, and the file names all three in the same order in outlet after outlet: the House votes directly on the articles; a member moves to table the resolution, a motion that is not debatable and that ends the resolution if a majority agrees; or the House refers the resolution to committee, where it would sit for the remainder of the Congress. A motion to table is a vote on the effort’s survival that carries no vote on the charges themselves, and it is still a recorded vote, taken in public, one week after an election. If the tabling motion fails and the House passes the resolution, Hegseth is impeached, and the matter passes to the Senate.

The Senate’s part of the procedure carries the higher bar, and the file states it without variation. Impeachment is the charge; conviction at a Senate trial requires two-thirds of the senators, 67 of 100 when the full Senate votes. No Cabinet official has ever been convicted. CNN’s file adds the Senate’s two shorter courses, on a Republican aide’s account: the Senate could move to dismiss the articles, or refer the matter to a committee for investigation, and each course requires a majority vote. No trial date exists, and none can exist before a House vote that has not yet been held. The resolution Massie refiled on Monday is, on his own description, “99.99% the same” as the September text, with minor corrections, and he was required to refile it because the September notice expired during the recess, a point Section 5 takes up.

4. The Count: The House as It Stands, and the Senate Behind It

No public whip count exists in Monday’s file, and the desk prints the arithmetic and the stated positions, and no prediction dressed as either. Impeachment in the House requires a simple majority of the members voting. Republicans hold the House until the new Congress convenes in January, by a margin the New York Post states at five seats, which makes a handful of Republican votes the whole question if the Democratic members vote together. Reuters reports that congressional sources say the resolution may have the simple majority needed to pass the Republican-controlled House before Democrats take over on January 3. ABC News’ arithmetic, as carried in the accounts filed below, runs the same way from the other side: if every Democrat supports the resolution, three Republican defections would be enough to pass it. Massie’s own estimates stand in two dated versions. Before Election Day he told Roll Call: “I give it better than a 50 percent chance of passing,” and he has said he expects a handful of Republicans. On Monday he said the chances are better after the election than before it. Two private expectations are in the file at a lower grade: MS NOW reported that two Republican lawmakers privately expect the measure to succeed if it reaches a direct floor vote, and CNN reported before the filing that several House Republicans expected the measure to pass. Private expectations are printed here as what they are; they are commitments by no one.

The stated positions on the record at collection time run as follows. For the resolution: Massie, its sponsor, a Republican. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader, announced his support on Sunday, November 8, on ABC’s “This Week”: “I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution. Pete Hegseth has got to go.” Jeffries is expected to become Speaker when the new House is seated in January. Representative Adam Smith of Washington, the senior Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, said: “I think there are enough Republicans who want him gone.” Against, or uncommitted, on the record: Speaker Johnson, whose position is in Section 5; Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska, retiring, who told ABC News he would weigh the debate before deciding, adding, “I do think the secretary has made some bad mistakes”; and House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, who declined to back the effort. In the Senate, conviction appears unlikely on every account in the file: two-thirds is required, and Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats in the chamber that would try the case, a Republican Senate sitting until January. Behind the arithmetic stands the midterm result that frames it: voter anger over the Iran war helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week’s elections, on Reuters’ account; the president and the vice president have attributed the losses to the conflict with Iran and the ensuing rise in gas prices, on USA Today’s account; and some Republican lawmakers have expressed concern, on Reuters’ account, that Hegseth’s strained relationship with Congress will undermine the administration’s push for a $1.5 trillion defense spending package, while others have urged the White House to replace him while a Republican Senate can still confirm a successor.

5. The Answers on the Record: The Secretary, the President, the Speaker

Hegseth answered on Monday in person, briefly, and in advance of a fuller answer scheduled for Tuesday. Asked whether he had enough Republican support to defeat the impeachment push, he said: “We’re not worried about that.” He said he is ready to defend his record at the Pentagon. He announced a press conference for Tuesday at the Pentagon, his first there since May, at which the accounts agree he will address the impeachment effort and defend his tenure. CNN adds two Monday statements to the file: Hegseth said he agreed with the president that he would again launch the Iran war if he had a do-over, and he described disagreements in Congress over policy decisions at the Pentagon as “disagreements with success,” saying that those who take issue with the military operations under his watch are “taking issue with the troops.” His fuller answer predates the filing by four days. In a video posted on November 5, filmed outside the Defense Department, he said: “A disgruntled, defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice. It’s all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.” In the same video he defended the Iran war as a “courageous and historic effort” and pressed Congress for a reconciliation bill of at least $350 billion for the department. His spokesman’s statement stands beside his own: Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told the New York Post last week that “Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists,” that the department will continue to drive the president’s agenda “despite threats of sham witch hunts from Democrats,” and that the secretary “is 100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump’s term in office.” Hegseth styles his office Secretary of War, a usage Reuters notes as part of his rebranding of the department; his constitutional title, and the title in the resolution, is Secretary of Defense.

The president’s backing stands in three dated statements, and the desk files all three. On Thursday, November 5, Trump told reporters that Hegseth has done a “fantastic job,” and he told ABC’s Jonathan Karl in a separate conversation: “I have every intention to keep him.” On Sunday, November 8, he told reporters: “He’s guilty of two things: basically winning two wars. I believe we saved the Middle East and Israel combined.” In the “60 Minutes” interview broadcast on Sunday, as CBS’s transcript carries it and Reuters reports it, he said of the impeachment push: “They want to impeach him. Very unfair. We had two wars, we won both,” referring to Iran, where Reuters describes the war as at an impasse, and to Venezuela, where United States forces deposed President Maduro in a January raid on his compound in Caracas. The White House’s social media account has posted messages praising Hegseth and his accomplishments at the Pentagon in recent days. Separate reporting in the same file states that the president had been asking advisers and allies whether Hegseth should stay on after the midterms; the White House has announced no change in his status, and the public statements above are the administration’s position as it stands.

The Speaker’s opposition stands in a September statement and a current one, and the two differ in their grounds. In September, Johnson said the resolution would “immediately be tabled” once members returned, called the effort “a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention,” and said the secretary had done “an extraordinary job at the Department of War.” His current ground, as Reuters reports it, is the timing: impeachment “in the middle of hostilities abroad” would be “a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see.” The Speaker controls the floor schedule within the two-day rule; the rule limits that control to two legislative days, and the September exercise of it is the subject of the next section.

6. The First Filing: September, the Recess, and the Expired Notice

Monday’s filing was the second filing of the same resolution, and the history of the first is short and complete in the record. Massie first introduced the eight articles on September 15, 2026, reading the 34-page resolution on the House floor and giving notice of his intent to raise a question of the privileges of the House. The vote the notice would have forced never occurred. On September 16, Speaker Johnson cancelled the remaining floor session and sent the House home a day early into its seven-week campaign recess, ahead of the midterm elections. The two-legislative-day clock ran out with the House away, the notice expired during the pro forma sessions that followed, and the resolution lapsed without a vote, a tabling motion, or a referral. Johnson denied at the time that the timing had anything to do with Hegseth. Massie’s account of the same week is that leadership cancelled Congress to avoid the vote, and he has said he had kept party leaders in the dark in September so they could not shut the House down early to stop him. Both accounts of the motive stand in the file; the sequence itself—filing on the 15th, adjournment on the 16th, a seven-week recess, an expired notice—is agreed by every account the desk read. A separate Democratic effort stands in the background of the same record: Representative Yassamin Ansari of Arizona filed a six-article impeachment resolution against Hegseth in April, with eight Democratic cosponsors, and no vote has been held on it. The resolution that will be voted on this week, if any is, is Massie’s.

7. The History the Vote Would Join

A Cabinet secretary has been impeached twice in 250 years, and the file states both cases in full, because they are the whole of the precedent. The first is William Belknap, Secretary of War under President Ulysses S. Grant, impeached by the House in 1876 on charges of taking kickbacks and corruption. Belknap resigned on the day of his impeachment vote, in a tearful meeting at the White House, and the House impeached him anyway; the Senate tried him and acquitted him, falling short of the two-thirds required. Belknap remains, on Reuters’ statement, the first and to date the only civilian leader of the United States military to be impeached, which is the narrower record Hegseth’s case would enter. The second case is Alejandro Mayorkas, President Joseph Biden’s Secretary of Homeland Security, impeached by House Republicans in 2024 by a narrow margin over his handling of immigration at the southern border; the Democratic-controlled Senate voted to kill both articles without a trial. CNN’s statement of the count is the one the desk adopts: if this week’s vote succeeds, Hegseth would be the third Cabinet secretary to be impeached. Two-thirds of the Senate has never convicted a Cabinet official. Hegseth’s answer to the precedent is on the record in his November 5 video, in his comparison of his case to the president’s: the effort was tried against Trump twice, he said, and failed twice, and it will fail with him.

8. What the Record Does Not Yet Hold

Five items stand open at the hour of collection, and the desk files them open. First, the vote itself: no vote on the articles, on tabling, or on referral had been held at 1549 ET on Monday, and no hour for a vote had been published; Massie’s own range runs from Monday night to Wednesday. Second, the count: no member outside the statements in Section 4 had published a position in the accounts the desk read, and no whip count from either party’s leadership stands in the file. Third, the administration’s article-by-article answer: the record holds the secretary’s general answer, his spokesman’s statement, the president’s backing, and the attorney general’s September statement that Hegseth follows the law; it holds no point-by-point response to Articles I through VIII, and the secretary’s Tuesday press conference is the next scheduled occasion for one. Fourth, the Senate’s course: dismissal, referral to committee, and trial are all described in the file as possibilities, and no Senate leader’s statement of intent stands in Monday’s accounts. Fifth, the underlying operations: the articles’ factual allegations—the school strike in Iran, the 243 deaths in the boat campaign, the operations in Yemen and Venezuela—stand in the file as allegations supported by the reporting cited in the clippings below, weighed against the administration’s position that the wars were won and the law was followed, and they have been adjudicated by no body. The contradictions in Monday’s record are small and the desk prints them in the open: the margin of the Republican House majority is stated at five seats by the Post and implied at a handful by every other account, with the defection arithmetic stated at three Republicans in ABC’s version and at a handful in Massie’s; the expected day of the vote is stated as Wednesday in most accounts and as early as Monday night in the sponsor’s; and the secretary’s title is stated as Secretary of Defense in the Constitution, the resolution, and most reporting, and as Secretary of War in the secretary’s own usage and in statements by his defenders. None of the three conflicts changes the filing, the clock, or the charges.

The final paragraph of the report is the first paragraph’s restatement, as the form requires. On Monday, November 9, 2026, Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican leaving Congress in January, refiled eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth as a privileged resolution, charging three violations of the War Powers Resolution in the Iran war and five further articles covering civilian casualties, the boat strikes, Senator Kelly’s speech, the seizure of Nicolás Maduro, and the war in Yemen; the filing starts a two-legislative-day clock, and the House will vote on the articles, on tabling them, or on referring them by Wednesday, in a lame-duck chamber one week after the midterms took both houses from the president’s party. Hegseth says he is not worried and will answer at the Pentagon on Tuesday; the president says his secretary has done a fantastic job and that he intends to keep him; the Speaker opposes impeachment in the middle of hostilities; the Democratic leader is a hard yes. A simple majority impeaches, and two-thirds of a Republican-held Senate would be required to remove, and no Cabinet secretary has ever been removed that way. The desk files the day settled where it settled—a filing made, a clock running, eight charges printed, every answer on the record beside them—and open where it stands open.

The File, Clipped

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective, a source with a position, printed because it is useful, and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Eleven items. The breaking-news alert that carried the filing to the desk—The New York Times, 3:30 p.m. ET, November 9, 2026, reporting that Representative Thomas Massie had called up impeachment charges against Pete Hegseth, accusing him of violating the Constitution, and that the move starts a clock forcing a vote within two days—is filed in the report’s first section, where the desk used it.

Subjective
Office of Representative Thomas Massie—the announcement of November 9, 2026, forcing a House vote on impeaching Secretary Hegseth

The sponsor’s own statement of the filing: that his actions force the House to vote on eight specific charges, that three of the charges allege specific violations of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, his sentence that by engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization the secretary is breaking the law, his statement that the effort is a gentler version of what is coming when the Democrats assume control, his advice that the president replace the secretary while a Republican Senate can confirm a successor, and the office’s summary of each of the eight articles in the resolution’s order. The desk’s Section 2 follows this summary.

Subjective
Reuters—Hegseth faces an expected House impeachment vote this week (November 9, 2026)

The wire’s full account of Monday: Massie’s filing and the two-day clock it set off; congressional sources saying the resolution may have the simple majority needed to pass the Republican-controlled House before Democrats take over on January 3; conviction appearing unlikely in a Senate where two-thirds is required and Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats; Speaker Johnson’s opposition, in his words that impeachment in the middle of hostilities abroad would be a terrible thing for allies and enemies to see; Hegseth’s Monday answer, “We’re not worried about that,” and his Tuesday press conference, his first at the Pentagon since May; the president’s “60 Minutes” answer, “They want to impeach him. Very unfair. We had two wars, we won both”; Jeffries’s hard yes; the Belknap precedent of 1876; and the concern among some Republicans that the secretary’s standing with Congress puts a $1.5 trillion defense spending package at risk.

Subjective
Reuters—Hegseth plays down impeachment risks, says he is ready to defend his record (November 9, 2026)

The wire’s short file of the secretary’s Monday remarks: Hegseth played down the risks of the impeachment push against him, said he was ready to defend his record at the Pentagon, and answered the question whether he had enough Republican support to defeat the articles with the sentence, “We’re not worried about that.” The remarks came as Massie attempted to force the House vote.

Subjective
CNN—why lawmakers are pushing to impeach Pete Hegseth (November 9, 2026)

The explainer’s file: the constitutional procedure, the simple majority in the House and the two-thirds in the Senate; Massie’s Monday introduction and the two legislative days now running; the leadership’s motion to table; the Senate’s shorter courses of dismissal or referral to committee; the eight articles and their contents, including at least 80 vessels destroyed and 243 people killed in the boat operations since last September and the Pentagon’s providing no public evidence against the people killed; the elementary school strike in Iran as the articles frame it; the Belknap and Mayorkas precedents and the statement that a successful vote would make Hegseth the third Cabinet secretary impeached; and the secretary’s Monday statements and his November video, quoted in full.

Subjective
USA Today—a Republican moves to force a Hegseth impeachment vote this week (November 9, 2026)

The account of the filing in the lame-duck context: the effort’s arrival days after Republican losses in the midterms, which the president and vice president attributed to the Iran conflict and the rise in gas prices; the charges as Massie stated them, including Yemen, the capture of Nicolás Maduro, and the Pentagon investigation used, on his charge, to retaliate against Senator Kelly; Representative Adam Smith’s sentence, “I think there are enough Republicans who want him gone”; Jeffries’s November 8 statement of support; the September history of the first filing and the early recess that avoided the vote; Massie’s November 9 post on the question his colleagues face; and the president’s November 8 answer, “He’s guilty of two things: basically winning two wars.”

Subjective
New York Post—Massie reintroduces impeachment articles against Hegseth over the Iran war (November 9, 2026)

The filing as the Post reported it from Washington on Monday: Massie’s pre-filing interview, in which he said a passage is more likely after the election than before it; the floor language the Post quotes from the resolution, on executing an unlawful order to commence hostilities and on the secretary as a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office; the statement that Republicans hold a five-seat majority in the House, so a handful of Republican votes decides the question, with a vote expected as early as Wednesday; and the spokesman’s statement of last week that the secretary intends to serve through the end of the president’s term.

Subjective
The Courier Journal—Massie will soon force a House impeachment vote against Hegseth (November 4, 2026)

The Kentucky paper’s account of the plan before the filing: Massie’s intent to force the vote as early as the House’s November 9 return, confirmed by his spokesperson in a November 5 email; his November 4 post stating the single contingency that would stop the refiling, the secretary’s resignation; the September 15 launch of the eight accusations; the 34 pages of the resolution; and the closing fact of his term, that after losing the primary for Kentucky’s 4th District he has only the lame-duck session in which to pursue it.

Subjective
The Democracy Advocate—the Hegseth impeachment vote forced as Massie refiles the Iran war charges (November 9, 2026)

A full procedural account of the Monday filing: the eight articles summarized from the sponsor’s release, the three leadership courses of a direct vote, a motion to table, or referral to committee, and Speaker Johnson’s September statement that the resolution would immediately be tabled; the September 16 cancellation and the seven-week recess that let the first notice lapse; the vote arithmetic as ABC News stated it, that three Republican defections pass the resolution if every Democrat supports it; Representative Don Bacon’s statement that he would weigh the debate and that the secretary has made some bad mistakes; Chairman James Comer’s declining to back the effort; and the closing statement that the articles are allegations in a political charging document, findings by no court, tribunal, or inspector general.

Subjective
The Washington Sun—Massie says the impeachment odds are up after the Republican midterm losses (November 9, 2026)

The account carrying the sponsor’s own mechanics and his own description of the refiled text: his statement that the ball is in the leadership’s court once he gives notice, that they have two legislative days, and that they could deal with it tonight, tomorrow, or the next day; his statement that he must restart the process because the September notice expired during pro forma sessions; his description of the updated articles as 99.99 percent the same, with minor corrections; the statement that a vote could come as early as Monday night; and the momentum in the file from Jeffries’s Sunday announcement of support.

Subjective
The Geneva Times—a Republican congressman will force a Hegseth impeachment vote (November 9, 2026)

The filing as reported from outside the United States: Massie’s plan to force the vote in the week of the House’s return, alleging a violation of the Constitution in hostilities in Iran continued for more than 90 days without congressional authorization; the expectation in that account that the effort will likely fail while Republicans remain in power until January; Massie’s stated wish to push the president to fire the secretary before the Democrats can launch an impeachment process; Hegseth’s statement that he was not concerned and his Tuesday news conference; the September first introduction; and the rule that once the resolution is introduced, the Speaker must schedule consideration within two days.

Subjective
Action Network—the Hegseth impeachment odds tracker (updated November 2026)

The market file on the same event: the tracker’s statement of the week-of-November-9 vote Massie announced, the eight articles’ center in the war powers of Congress during the Iran conflict, Massie’s pre-election estimate to Roll Call of a better than 50 percent chance of passing, the September attempt and the Speaker’s early recess that dismissed it, the sponsor’s single contingency of the secretary’s resignation, the statement that the vote happens in the outgoing Congress and the new one the Democrats won, the Senate’s two-thirds requirement of 67 of 100, and the market’s dated prices on impeachment and departure, filed here as the odds record and at no higher grade.
items.summary: Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, refiled eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on the House floor on Monday, November 9, 2026, as a privileged resolution, starting a clock that requires House leaders to act within two legislative days, with a vote possible as early as Wednesday. The articles charge Hegseth with waging the Iran war in violation of three provisions of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties, extrajudicial killings in the strikes on suspected drug-trafficking boats, suppressing the free speech of Senator Mark Kelly, seizing Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro without authority, and waging an unlawful war in Yemen. Hegseth said on Monday that he is not worried and will defend his record at a Pentagon press conference on Tuesday; President Trump has backed him; Speaker Mike Johnson opposes the effort; House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries is a hard yes. If the House votes to impeach, Hegseth would be the third Cabinet secretary impeached in American history, and removal would require two-thirds of the Senate. The desk files the filing, the eight articles one by one, the procedure, the count, every answer on the record, the September first filing, and what remains open.
