items.title: The Cornell 7 Case: The Chi Phi Allegations, the Signed Statement and the Transcript, Cornell’s Findings, the Civil Lawsuit, and the Special Prosecutor
items.content_html:
Special Report

The Case File—Allegations, Findings, Lawsuit, and the Reopened Investigation

Objective

The Cornell 7 Case: The Chi Phi Allegations, the Signed Statement and the Transcript, Cornell’s Findings, the Civil Lawsuit, and the Special Prosecutor — Special Report

On the night of October 19–20, 2024, a 20-year-old Cornell undergraduate went to the Chi Phi fraternity house at 107 Edgemoor Lane in Ithaca. What happened in that house is the contested center of this file. She alleges, in a civil complaint filed in September 2026, that she was pressured to take ketamine, incapacitated, and sexually assaulted over hours by seven members of the fraternity while a group chat summoned more men upstairs. The district attorney who declined to charge in 2024 states that the sworn statement she signed that November described her participation as voluntary, conscious, and consensual, and did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. The transcript of her police interview, excerpted in 2026 reporting, contains words the signed summary does not: “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped.” Cornell’s disciplinary panel, judging under a preponderance standard, expelled two of the men, suspended two, barred one from campus, and imposed lesser sanctions on two, and found none of them responsible for every allegation against him. No court has heard evidence on what occurred in the room, and no criminal charge has been filed against any of the seven as of November 9, 2026. Around that open center the institutions have moved: a civil lawsuit against Cornell, three Chi Phi entities, two Tri Delta entities, a bar, and the seven men; a reopened criminal case from which the governor removed the local prosecutor and installed the attorney general as special prosecutor; a university president who kept his board’s confidence and lost his faculty’s, 75 to 50; and a statute whose definition of incapacitation the whole criminal question turns on. The desk files the whole record, attributed and graded, in that order.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1405 ET, Monday, November 9, 2026.

The File in Brief

The case has produced three proceedings, two irreconcilable documents, and no criminal charge. Jane Doe—the name under which the complainant proceeds in every filing, her anonymity formally granted by the court on October 23, 2026—reported to the Cornell University Police Department on November 8, 2024, about three weeks after the night at issue. Campus police interviewed her over two days, November 14–15, 2024, producing a transcript reported at approximately 120 pages and an officer’s six-page written summary, which she read, edited in more than twenty handwritten notations, and signed under the false-statement penalty of Penal Law §210.45. The Tompkins County district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, decided within days not to pursue charges, and stated his reasons in full on September 28, 2026: the signed statement “did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped” and “described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual”; applying Penal Law §130.05, “the alleged facts as set forth in the statement do not constitute a crime.” The interview transcript, as reported by CBS News, The New York Times, and CNN from the same document, contains her statements that she was “completely and totally incapacitated,” that she was “physically hit very, very hard,” and the sentence the summary omits: “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped.” Whether the transcript reached the district attorney in 2024 is disputed by the university, the prosecutor, and the governor, and the public record does not settle it. That dispute, printed in Section 4 at its full length, is the hinge on which every later event swings.

The university’s proceeding ran to completion in 2025, under a different standard and a different record. A three-member Cornell panel heard the cases over hearings running May 2–29, 2025, under Policy 6.4’s preponderance-of-the-evidence standard, and concluded that Doe was too intoxicated to affirmatively consent that night, as the panel summaries are reported. Its decision is dated August 18, 2025. Of the seven men: Matthew Ingalls and Johnathan Newell were expelled, each found responsible for sexual assault; Winston Lee received a two-year suspension; Gillio Lopes a three-semester suspension; Diego Sarabia, already graduated, was made persona non grata and barred from campus for three years; Scott Norris received a no-contact order and education modules; and Scott Kretzschmar, found not responsible for sexual assault or sexual exploitation as charged and responsible only for attempted sexual exploitation, received a no-contact order, education, and a reflection paper. Cornell states that published accounts of individual punishments are inaccurate and that federal privacy law bars it from confirming individual records; the outcomes above are as reported by The New York Times from Cornell’s disciplinary summaries and corroborated by the Cornell Daily Sun and other outlets, and they are printed under Cornell’s caveat. The Chi Phi chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus; the national fraternity states the chapter voted to remove the accused members from its rolls three days after Doe’s police report, and that it permanently expelled the chapter. One accused man, Kretzschmar, sued Cornell to overturn his record; a state judge dismissed his petition on September 23, 2026, and his appeal is pending.

The civil lawsuit, filed September 16, 2026, is in its first motion practice, and no court has ruled on its merits. Jane Doe v. Cornell University, Inc., et al., Index No. 161704/2026 in New York County, pleads ten causes of action in 101 pages: sexual assault, sexual battery, and intentional infliction of emotional distress against the seven men; negligence and negligent supervision against Cornell, the Greek organizations, and the bar; breach of contract against Cornell and Tri Delta; claims against Cornell under the New York Human Rights Law and Education Law §6440; and a Dram Shop Act claim against Zareen Enterprise LLC, doing business as Moonies Bar & Nightclub. No entity connected to Lot 10, the second bar in the night’s narrative, is a defendant. One man originally named, Orazio Petito, was discontinued with prejudice on October 20, 2026, after reporting established he had been misidentified as chapter president; he was never accused of participating in the alleged assault. Diego Sarabia’s motion to dismiss, returnable November 16, 2026, and Moonies’ motion to dismiss are pending. The court declined on October 16 to sign a proposed order restraining counsel’s public statements, and ordered the filings containing addresses sealed on October 9, after an uninvolved man who shares a defendant’s name was served by mistake and his family threatened.

The criminal case reopened on September 28, 2026, changed hands on October 1, and is under investigation with no deadline. Van Houten announced the reopening in the same statement that defended the 2024 declination, assigning a senior sex-crimes prosecutor and planning a grand jury presentation. Governor Kathy Hochul signed Executive Order No. 64 on October 1, 2026, under Executive Law §63(2), its operative words to “displace and supersede” the district attorney, and appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor. James announced an active criminal investigation on October 2 and on November 4 appointed Jacqueline Kelly, a partner at Boies Schiller Flexner and a former federal prosecutor who oversaw the prosecution of Sean Combs, to lead it. Five of the seven men are parties to a proceeding, Lopes v. Hochul and James, asking a court to remove James for statements they say show prejudgment; it was heard October 29, 2026, and no ruling has issued. A separate motion in Tompkins County seeks to bar James from any grand jury proceeding in the case; a decision is expected November 13, 2026. The two-year limitations period for misdemeanors arising from October 2024 has run; New York sets no limitations period for the most serious sex offenses.

The university’s leadership has been judged twice in one week, with opposite results. On November 6, 2026, Cornell’s Faculty Senate passed the first no-confidence resolution in its history, 75 to 50 with 5 abstentions and 5 non-votes, resolving that it “has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University.” The Board of Trustees answered within hours that it “remains confident that President Kotlikoff and his administration are the right leaders” and “fully supports” him; President Michael Kotlikoff has told The New York Times he has no intention of resigning. A Board committee has retained Sally Yates, the former deputy attorney general, to review Cornell’s handling of the case and its systems entire; the review has no announced timeline and no findings. The City of Ithaca adopted a permit moratorium against Cornell on October 7, 2026, and let it lapse on November 5, on a single local source’s reporting, with three demands outstanding and revival threatened. Cornell has suspended all Interfraternity Council house parties through the end of the 2026–27 academic year and signed an agreement under which a survivor pursuing criminal charges may choose the New York State Police or the Cornell police as the investigating agency.

What the record does not establish is as much a part of this file as what it does. It does not establish what occurred in the room, in what sequence, or each man’s individual conduct; no court has heard that evidence. It does not establish whether ketamine was administered to Doe without her consent, the element New York’s definition of mental incapacitation turns on and the point the complaint and the district attorney’s reading of her signed statement divide over. It publishes no toxicology or rape-kit results: the only documented medical fact of that kind is that a rape kit was collected at an Ithaca emergency room on November 7, 2024. It does not support the circulated claim that the men’s only punishment was writing essays; reflection papers were components of packages that included two expulsions. And it contains claims this report corrects rather than repeats: no Lot 10 entity is sued; the New York Times text-messages presentation carries no verified November 7 date; the BBC’s explainer is dated September 30, 2026; a separately reported 2023 lawsuit against Cornell was not unsealed in 2026 and drew no response from any SUNY authority, Cornell being a private university. The grades used throughout are the file’s own: VERIFIED, established by a primary document or multiple independent reputable reports; DOCUMENTED, established by a single reputable report or a reputable report of a document; ALLEGED or CLAIMED, an assertion by a party, counsel, or a filing, which is not a finding. Where accounts conflict, this report prints the conflict and does not reconcile it. The final section is the first section’s restatement, as the form requires: three proceedings, two irreconcilable documents, no criminal charge, and an investigation now in a special prosecutor’s hands.

1. The State of the Case: No Charges, and the Standing Cautions of the File

No criminal charges have been filed against any of the seven men as of November 9, 2026, and that fact governs every line that follows. It is verified across all reporting the desk read. Each of the seven is presumed innocent in the criminal matter. The only adjudications to date are a Cornell disciplinary panel’s findings under a preponderance standard, which are not criminal verdicts, and procedural rulings in the civil case, none of which reaches the merits. All seven men deny wrongdoing. The complainant is identified only as Jane Doe, as in the filings; this report makes no attempt to identify her and reproduces no purported identification, and the documented efforts by others to name her are filed in Section 11 as events, because they caused documented harm to uninvolved people. The seven men are named only as the public record names them, in the civil complaint’s caption and in reputable reporting, with their denials and their individual disciplinary outcomes attached to their names wherever the names appear. The desk’s research file for this report rests on primary documents read in full or in part—the district attorney’s September 28, 2026 statement, the civil summons and complaint, Executive Order No. 64 and Executive Law §63(2), Penal Law §§130.00 and 130.05, the Ithaca Common Council’s moratorium resolution, Cornell’s statements, and the governor’s October 2 news-conference transcript—and on reporting by The New York Times, The New Yorker, CNN, CBS News, ABC News, the BBC, the Associated Press, Reuters, USA Today, NBC News, NPR, The Washington Post, the Cornell Daily Sun, New York Focus, Le Monde, and 607 News Now.

2. The Night as the Complaint Alleges It: October 19–20, 2024

The complaint’s account is a pleading, not evidence, and it is printed here in its own terms, at the grade ALLEGED. Doe was a 20-year-old Cornell undergraduate, a member of the Alpha Beta chapter of Delta Delta Delta, living in the sorority house. On October 19, 2024, the complaint states, she drank at the sorority house—it says she had “binged” vodka, and that on arrival at the fraternity house she “was visibly intoxicated as she had consumed about 10 standard drinks within the past 3 hours”—then attended an event at Moonies Bar & Nightclub, where she alleges she was served alcohol despite markings on her hand indicating she was under 21, and then went to a second bar, Lot 10. At about 11 p.m. she left and walked alone, roughly a mile, to the Chi Phi house at 107 Edgemoor Lane to see Matthew Ingalls, a friend, on CNN’s timeline drawn from the complaint. The complaint alleges that Ingalls proposed a threesome with Johnathan Newell, the proposition pleaded as having been made when Doe was already “incapable of consenting”; that she was pressured to snort a substance described as ketamine; that she became incapacitated; and that over the following hours multiple fraternity members sexually assaulted her, snorted ketamine off her body, took photographs of her, and posted them to a fraternity group chat. A message in the “Chi Phi Actives” Snapchat group announced “free pussy” upstairs; the complaint reproduces a screenshot of the message and says it was meant to draw other members to the room. A man identified in the complaint’s room sequence as Alex Vega is named in the narrative and is not a defendant. Newell is alleged to have performed a ketamine-on-body act. The final alleged assault is placed in a smaller room, and the complaint alleges the assaults continued until approximately 5:45 a.m.

Against the institutions, the complaint pleads a failure before the night and a failure after it. It alleges Cornell knew or should have known of drug use at the fraternity and of risks of sexual violence in its Greek system, failed to supervise or warn, failed to discipline adequately afterward, “shelter[ed]” the accused students “from speaking to law enforcement,” and allowed suspended students “the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell”—the essay-mitigation claim Cornell expressly denies, at Section 5. It describes Cornell’s conduct as “so outrageous, shocking, despicable, and contemptible that it exceeds the reasonable bounds of decency.” The complaint states that Doe reported to the Cornell University Police Department on November 8, 2024, about three weeks after the night, and that Cornell suspended the Chi Phi chapter the same day. Both of those dated facts are verified independently of the pleading.

3. The Two Documents: The Signed Statement and the Interview Transcript

The central evidentiary conflict of the case is documentary, and both documents are in the record. The first is the six-page sworn statement Doe signed for the campus police in November 2024: single-spaced, typewritten, carrying more than twenty handwritten notations by Doe, signed under Penal Law §210.45. Its full text is not public. What is public is District Attorney Van Houten’s account of it in his September 28, 2026 statement, verified as his account: the statement describes Doe texting Ingalls and planning to meet at the house; it rates her own intoxication “5 out of 10” on arrival; it describes an agreed threesome; her refusal of a proposed foursome—“Hell No”—which was honored; a man’s hand swatted away; and her decision to take a second use of ketamine. Per Van Houten, it states that when she said stop, the conduct stopped, and that events ended at about 5:45 a.m. His conclusion, in his words: the statement “did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped” and “described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual.”

The signed statement was not devoid of non-consent content, and the file prints that precision because it narrows the dispute to its true size. Per NPR and ABC reporting on the statement’s contents, the signed statement retained language that the encounter “felt like coercion,” that Doe described herself as “pretty incapacitated,” that she was physically hit, and references to “eightsome” bragging. The documented dispute is therefore not whether the statement contained any non-consent element; it is whether the summary omitted the explicit rape characterization that the interview record carries. Printed so, neither side’s framing is overstated.

The second document is the transcript of the campus police interview of November 14–15, 2024, reported at approximately 120 pages and obtained by CBS News in 2026. In the transcript, per the reporting of CBS, The New York Times, and CNN from the same document, Doe said: “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped.” She said she was “completely and totally incapacitated.” She said she was “physically hit very, very hard.” She said the encounter “felt like coercion.” The six-page signed summary does not contain the “100 percent” statement; that is verified as a fact of the two documents’ comparison, per the same reporting and the governor’s October 2 remarks. Per documents ABC News reviewed, Doe’s initial intake report to the campus police recorded that she reported she “was recently raped by 8-10 men at the Chi Phi fraternity house”—a phrase that likewise does not appear in the six-page statement sent to prosecutors. The full transcript is not public. The conflict is printed, not reconciled: the complaint alleges coerced ketamine use, incapacitation, and gang rape; the district attorney’s summary of the signed 2024 statement describes voluntary, conscious, consensual participation with refusals honored. Both documents exist. No public record reconciles them. Doe’s counsel’s position is that the summary omitted what she told interviewers orally; the dispute over who held the transcript in 2024 is filed at Section 4.

The messages of the night and the weeks after are documented in the Title IX record, the complaint, and the reporting, and they are filed here with their senders only where the record fixes them. The complaint reproduces a screenshot from the “Chi Phi Actives” Snapchat group, which the complaint’s image indicates had 57 members. At about 1:42 a.m. a message announced there was “free pussy” upstairs; the Times’ interactive rendering reads “Free pussy in alum pu[—],” apparently a room designation, and a photograph of Doe was posted in the thread. Further messages, as reproduced in the Times interactive and verified against multiple reproductions: a member asked whether the “shop” was still open and was told “Yeah”; another wrote “Boys come whip it out”; members joked about a named member being with her. ABC News separately verified small-group-chat messages among members. Attribution, as documented: the complaint attributes the “free pussy” message to Newell; CBS News and Wikipedia’s synthesis attribute “Boys come whip it out” to Ingalls; and Kretzschmar and Norris each acknowledged sending a message in the thread, without the thread’s worst content being attributed to either by those acknowledgments. Beyond those items, the record does not fix senders, and this report does not. A dating caveat attaches to the Times’ presentation of the thread, the interactive titled “Read the Text Messages at the Center of the Cornell Rape Inquiry”: no Times Cornell text-messages piece bearing a November 7 dateline was located; the interactive surfaces in a push notification logged November 8, 2026, at 22:54 UTC, and the substantive Times text corpus is its October 1, 2026 article. This report therefore prints no November 7 date for it.

On October 21, 2024, one of the two men of the initial encounter apologized by text, and Doe’s reply is in the record entire. CBS News obtained the full exchange. The man—identified by CBS as “MALE 2”; the Times and Cornell records context identifies the two as Newell and Ingalls, and Doe’s own reply names “u and matt”—texted at 6:54 p.m.: “I just wanted to apologize for how things went down the other night. My memory’s kinda fuzzy abt a lot of it but me and [MALE 1] both feel like s[—]t for being too f[—]ed up to shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand… I’m so so sorry.” Doe replied at 10:05 p.m.: “my memories super clouded too. i think we were all way to f[—]ing drunk and high… but at the end of the day non of the sexual stuff was illegal and honestly i really liked being w u and [MALE 1]. so anything anyone has to say about the gamgbang is out of their jurisdiction. i don’t think we should feel any shame for the part. our body our choice asf.” The exchange is verified as published by CBS News and Wikipedia’s synthesis of the Title IX documents. Each side’s interpretation of it is filed at Section 9: Doe’s counsel calls the reply a textbook response to assault; the defence treats the contemporaneous messages as contradicting the 2026 lawsuit.

The remaining documented messages run from the night itself to the day of the report. During the night, at about 3:05 a.m., Doe answered a roommate’s text—“You coming home tn?”—with “idk”; one accused man contends the exchange shows she could read and respond. On October 22 she wrote to one of the men that in two months it all would be a “funny memory.” In late October, messages in the Title IX record show Ingalls assuring her “chi phi is your house and you are welcome here” ahead of the chapter’s Halloween party, relaying the chapter president’s view; Doe answered, “thank u i really appreciate that… i’ll bring my cigs tomorrow.” She was then disinvited by phone; per the texts, the president said it was for her own good. Doe to Ingalls: “I knew this was going to happen. The woman will always get the short end of the stick. Yall aren’t my friends. Yall are covering your asses.” An October 28 phone apology by one of the men is also reported in the Title IX record. On November 3, 2024, Doe texted two of the accused men: “let’s be clear that 90% of what happened that night was not consensual. i was given more key than i can remember [and] i know that i told u i felt uncomfortable and i didn’t know anyone in the room.” One replied that if he had been “less f[—]ed up and even somewhat aware of the situation and how out of hand it got I would’ve shut it down,” adding “i’m so so sorry.” On November 7, 2024, in a call she recorded and ABC News obtained, Doe told Winston Lee she was “completely and totally intoxicated and then given multiple sedatives,” that she was “surrounded by upwards of 8 to 10 men,” and “this is classified as gang rape.” Lee first apologized for “all the backlash you’re getting from this” and said he had been told not to message her; pressed, he asked, “What’s the purpose for why you decided to call me?”, said there was “nothing to say that… anything was happening in that room,” and, in ABC’s reporting of the call and a second call with Ingalls, the men’s account was that the door was unlocked and the house was crowded with a party. On November 8 she texted Ingalls, “I know you lied,” and reported to the campus police the same day. Per the Title IX record as reported by the Times, the morning after the night Doe told her roommates she had consumed ketamine and had sex with multiple men; one roommate testified she seemed in shock and was trying to laugh it off; another recalled Doe saying, “I wasn’t comfortable.”

The medical record is two contacts and a caution. On October 22, 2024, Doe went to Cornell Health for a urinary tract infection and STD testing and told the provider she had contracted the UTI in a “traumatic way.” Her attorney states she was advised to “speak with somebody” and was not offered a rape kit or a physical exam to document injuries; counsel’s statement continues: “Critically, two days after the assault, a rape kit would likely have revealed DNA… By the time she went for the rape kit on 11/7 all of the DNA evidence was gone.” The underlying facts are documented as counsel’s account; Cornell Health has not publicly answered this specific claim in the record the desk found. On November 7, 2024, Doe obtained a rape kit at an Ithaca emergency room. Secondhand summaries state it recovered no DNA. The desk’s caution is printed with it: a dedicated check found no public toxicology or rape-kit results in the record; only the November 7 collection is itself documented. The “no DNA” statement is therefore carried in this report as a reported summary, not as a verified result, and no finding of that kind is printed anywhere in this file.

One further allegation of the night’s aftermath is filed at its grade. ABC News reported that the campus police received an anonymous tip alleging Chi Phi leaders held a meeting after the night and urged members and witnesses to stay silent and protect the house’s reputation; police interview clips reviewed by ABC show witnesses recalling they were told the event was a “consensual orgy” but not to spread it. The tip and the meeting are alleged, not established. What is not established by any public document is listed here, at the head of the file, because everything after it depends on the reader holding it: what occurred in the room, in what sequence, and each man’s individual conduct; whether ketamine was administered to Doe without her consent, the element New York law turns on, at Section 10; and whether Doe’s November 2024 account as she gave it orally matches the complaint’s 2026 account. The excerpts suggest overlap—the “100% confidence” line, incapacitation, being struck—and the district attorney’s summary suggests material difference. Both suggestions stand in this file as an open conflict.

4. The First Criminal Decision: The Declination of November 2024 and the Dispute Over the File

The local handling ran on a short clock. Doe reported on November 8, 2024; Cornell issued a public-safety alert and temporarily suspended the Chi Phi Xi chapter the same day, both verified. The alert, per Wesley Lowery’s account, said a student reported she had been coerced into consuming ketamine and marijuana and sexually assaulted “by multiple males” at a fraternity house in the 100 block of Edgemoor Lane. A date conflict attaches to the alert and is printed unresolved: the alert as reproduced in the research record gives the incident date as October 25, against October 19–20 in every other account, including the complaint and the district attorney’s statement; no source reconciles the discrepancy, and this file does not assume it an error. The campus police interviewed Doe on November 14–15; she read, edited, and signed the officer’s six-page written statement on November 15. On November 15 the campus police also drafted letters to Verizon and T-Mobile seeking phone records in a sexual-assault investigation, drafts obtained by CNN in 2026; whether the district attorney’s office knew of the records requests is not established. In November 2024 the campus police asked the Tompkins County district attorney’s office to review Doe’s statement for criminality. Van Houten has said he decided within days of the interviews not to pursue charges. His office received, on his account, the six-page signed statement and a Snapchat screenshot; he told CNN his office “never received more than the Snapchat messages and a six-page investigative report.” Times-obtained records show the district attorney’s office declined to review additional evidence the campus police offered after the decision, an investigator’s note recording: “Criminal charges would not be pursued in this case.” Van Houten later characterized the additional material offered around November 25, 2024 as “not pertinent,” on the ground that his office already had “Jane Doe’s comprehensive account,” and stated the extra interviews were of fraternity members declining to speak on counsel’s advice; he told NBC News the same of the file’s interviews. His characterization sits beside, and does not settle, the dispute below. The Ithaca Police Department, the municipal force, says it never received a report and learned of the allegations from the media; the civil complaint initially stated, incorrectly per the department, that Ithaca police were investigating.

The district attorney’s stated reasons are a primary document, and they are printed in his words. Van Houten’s September 28, 2026 press statement, issued when he reopened the case, is the fullest statement of the 2024 reasoning. “Jane Doe’s sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual.” Applying Penal Law §130.05, he wrote that the statement established none of the routes to lack of consent: no forcible compulsion; no mental incapacitation, a term the statute defines around a substance “administered to him without his consent”; no physical helplessness; and “no evidence… indicating that she clearly expressed that she did not consent”—noting that, per the statement, each time she asked that conduct stop, it stopped. “The alleged facts as set forth in the statement do not constitute a crime,” and the November 2024 decision “was legally correct.” Of the men’s conduct he wrote in the same period, as reported by ABC: “She never says that she was drugged without her knowledge. She admits to taking drugs and alcohol voluntarily and with knowledge”; the behavior of some fraternity members was “without question disgusting and morally reprehensible,” but “criminal prosecutions must be based upon evidence and not emotion.” He stated his office “obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later.” He has said he never personally told Doe or her lawyer of the decision and asked the campus police to convey it. Her counsel, Thomas Giuffra, says Doe was left believing a criminal investigation was continuing while Cornell’s internal review ran: “I think she was misled. She was told it was still—they weren’t going to prosecute, but they were still investigating.” The parties’ accounts compete; the record does not establish what the campus police told Doe.

Three positions on what the prosecutor was sent are on the record, and the record does not settle between them. First, Van Houten: his office received the six-page signed statement and the Snapchat material and never received the interview transcript. When CBS put the “100 percent” line to him, around September 30, 2026, he called it “news to me”: “If she had said those words, we certainly would want to have explored that more… that wasn’t provided to me.” After the governor’s intervention he said, on October 2: “I support the appointment of Attorney General James and I trust that she will examine the facts and apply the law. It has become clear that we were not provided the full picture by the University. The focus has been and should continue to be on the victims. My office will cooperate fully with the Attorney General.” Second, Cornell and its police: the university initially said campus police shared “all investigatory information” with the district attorney’s office in 2024; in later formulations reported by CNN, Cornell said police shared the victim’s sworn statement and a Snapchat screenshot. Cornell has not specified publicly whether the transcript was transmitted. The conflict sharpens on the image itself: Cornell’s FAQ states the statement and a Snapchat screenshot were shared with the district attorney, while Van Houten told ABC News, as reported by the Cornell Daily Sun, that his office “was never provided with an image of a Snapchat group titled ‘Chi Phi Actives.’” The two statements may concern different images—a screenshot, and the group image as such—but no source establishes that, and the conflict is printed unresolved. Third, Governor Hochul, on October 2, 2026: the words “never made it into the account that the Cornell police sent to prosecutors”; the district attorney “then declined to pursue charges after reviewing that incomplete account and never interviewing her… In what world does the District Attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript?” She also noted Doe “sat for hours and told them exactly what happened to her.” Whether the transcript was offered and declined, or never transmitted, is unknown on the public record. The Times documents show the district attorney’s office declined additional materials after deciding; they do not settle whether the transcript itself was among what was available before the decision.

5. The University’s Proceeding: Title IX, the Panel, and the Seven Outcomes

Cornell’s proceeding ran from a formal complaint in November 2024 to a panel decision in August 2025, and two of its dates stand unharmonized in the record. From the court record in the Kretzschmar litigation, Cornell issued its formal Title IX complaint on November 22, 2024, revised in January and March 2025; Doe’s civil complaint and CNN’s timeline use a January 14, 2025 investigation-opening date beside it. Both dates are documented in their respective records; no source harmonizes them, and this report prints both rather than choosing. Doe filed her complaint with Cornell’s Title IX coordinator in January 2025, the same month the 2024 federal Title IX rule was vacated nationwide. Cornell’s Office of Civil Rights states that the 2024 regulations “were never implemented at Cornell due to legal challenges” and that Cornell “continues to utilize and comply with” the 2020 regulations; on Cornell’s own account, the 2020 framework governed, and the standard of proof was Cornell’s Policy 6.4 choice within it: preponderance of the evidence. The investigation ran January to May 2025 and encompassed roughly 50 interviews and 32 witnesses on the litigation record; reported counts vary—one account counts 48 interviews across December to February, CNN’s reading of the redacted panel summary says more than 50, including all of the accused men except one who declined—and the range is printed because the exact count is not fixed in the public record. Six of the seven men were interviewed in the Title IX process; all who were interviewed denied wrongdoing. A three-member panel of trained faculty and staff heard the cases over hearings running May 2–29, 2025, conducted by Zoom; the panel’s report runs 99 pages in redacted form and the hearing transcript 1,732 pages. The panel’s written decision is dated August 18, 2025, and later entered the public record as an exhibit in the Kretzschmar litigation. People reported the last of 16 responsibility findings—multiple charges per respondent—was still pending appeal at one point in October 2026. Per the panel summaries as reported, the panel concluded Doe was too intoxicated to affirmatively consent that night: a policy finding under Policy 6.4’s standard, not a criminal determination.

The seven outcomes, individually, are as reported by The New York Times from Cornell’s disciplinary summaries, corroborated by the Cornell Daily Sun and repeated consistently across the Associated Press, CNN, ABC, and others, under Cornell’s standing caveat. Matthew Ingalls, class of 2027: expelled; found responsible for sexual assault; the panel found he manipulated, exploited, and endangered Doe. Johnathan Newell, class of 2027: expelled; found responsible for sexual assault; disciplinary records note the allegation that he struck Doe during intercourse and manipulated her into ingesting ketamine. Winston Lee, class of 2027: a two-year suspension, disciplinary probation on return, a no-contact order, sexual-harassment education, and reflection papers; the civil suit alleges he snorted ketamine off her body and forced oral sex, and the panel’s per-charge findings for Lee are not public in the material the desk reviewed. Gillio Lopes, class of 2027: a three-semester suspension plus two years’ probation, a no-contact order, education, and reflection papers; one account by his counsel describes a “one-year suspension,” and the conflict is printed. Diego Sarabia, class of 2025: persona non grata, barred from campus for three years; he had already graduated when the panel ruled, and the policy then in force did not withhold an otherwise-earned degree pending adjudication. Scott Norris, class of 2026: a no-contact order, education modules in sexual harassment, social media, and bystander intervention, and a reflection paper; per his counsel, he was not found responsible for sexual activity or drug use. Scott Kretzschmar, class of 2026: a no-contact order, education, and a reflection paper; the panel found him not responsible for sexual assault or sexual exploitation as charged, and responsible only for attempted sexual exploitation. No man was found responsible by the panel for every allegation against him, and the panel did not find all seven responsible for sexual assault. Two of the seven, Lee and Lopes, remained enrolled as of an October 2026 Cornell webinar reported by CNN, a fact administrators confirmed on the record in that session. One conflict in this table does not resolve: the Times and Sun summaries record a three-year campus bar imposed on Sarabia, while President Kotlikoff told student government on September 29, 2026, that the graduated man had left “before any sanction could be imposed.” Both statements are in the record; they cannot both be literally correct, and no source reconciles them.

The chapter’s end is verified at both levels. The Xi chapter was temporarily suspended on November 8, 2024, the day Doe reported; it was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus, and the university-owned house at 107 Edgemoor Lane remains closed. Chi Phi’s national organization states the Cornell chapter voted unanimously to remove the accused members from its rolls three days after Doe’s police report and recommended the national fraternity permanently expel them, and that the national fraternity permanently expelled the chapter.

One accused man sued the university, and his lawsuit is how much of the internal record became public. Scott Kretzschmar sued Cornell in state court to overturn his disciplinary record: John Doe v. Cornell University, a CPLR Article 78 proceeding in Tompkins County, Index No. EF2026-0292, commenced March 30, 2026, filed anonymously, with media reports identifying the petitioner as Kretzschmar. It followed an internal Cornell appeal denied in full on January 14, 2026; the appeal grounds included a panelist participating by video while driving for roughly 45 minutes and a responsibility finding on an offense not charged. He challenged the attempted-sexual-exploitation finding, arguing the university’s process was fundamentally unfair, as reported. Justice Mark G. Masler dismissed the petition on September 23, 2026, reported at 2026 NY Slip Op 26172, upholding Cornell’s decision. As of October 5, 2026 reporting, he was appealing to the Appellate Division, Third Department; the appeal is pending as of November 9, with no ruling found. The litigation unsealed extensive internal records, including the August 18, 2025 hearing panel decision. No other accused man’s lawsuit against Cornell was found.

The process drew criticism from both directions, and Cornell’s standing position is on the record beside both. From Doe’s side, Giuffra said the punishments “did not reflect the severity of the charges”: “With the exception of [Ingalls and Newell], all of them will be able to graduate with a Cornell diploma and live their lives reaping the benefits of this coveted degree. In contrast, as of today, it is doubtful whether Doe will even graduate college or ever live a normal life due to what these men did to her.” The complaint’s claim that students could mitigate sanctions by writing essays is denied by Cornell: its September 28, 2026 statement says sanctions “included expulsions and suspensions” and that “no individual charged was offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement.” From the accused’s side: Kretzschmar’s petition attacked the process as fundamentally unfair; Ingalls’s February 2025 email, at Section 9, accused the investigation of gender discrimination; defence counsel have criticized the preponderance standard and the Zoom process in commentary. Cornell’s position, through Vice President for University Relations Kyle Kimball on September 21, 2026: the offices “investigated and adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies”; “Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students and we therefore are unable to make a public statement on any other disciplinary response… We will respond in detail through the legal process.”

6. The Civil Lawsuit: Defendants, Causes, and the First Motion Practice

The defendant list is verified from the summons, and one name on the circulated version of this case is not on it. Jane Doe v. Cornell University, Inc., et al. is assigned to Justice Phaedra F. Perry-Bond. The summons is dated September 14, 2026, and the summons-and-complaint was filed through NYSCEF on September 16, 2026; some reputable coverage says “filed September 14,” Doe’s counsel’s October 14 letter says “On September 16, 2026, we filed a lawsuit,” and the Cornell Daily Sun first reported it September 18. Both dates are in the record; the filing stamp is September 16. The defendants are: Cornell University, Inc.; Chi Phi Chapter House Association; Chi Phi Fraternity, Inc.; Chi Phi Educational Trust; Alpha Beta House Corporation of Delta Delta Delta; Delta Delta Delta Sorority; Zareen Enterprise LLC, doing business as Moonies Bar & Nightclub; the seven men—Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell (spelling as in the complaint), Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris, Scott Kretzschmar; John Doe (Faculty); John Doe (Alumni); John Does (Executive Board); and, until October 20, Orazio Petito. No Lot 10 entity is a defendant. Lot 10 appears in the narrative—Doe’s second bar stop, and the area the district attorney’s statement places her walk from—but no Lot 10 business entity is named in the summons. The only bar defendant is Moonies. The complaint is 101 pages, carries more than 590 numbered paragraphs, and demands a jury trial; Doe was permitted to proceed under the pseudonym, formally granted on October 23. Her counsel are Rheingold Giuffra Ruffo Plotkin & Hellman LLP, with Thomas P. Giuffra the public-facing attorney, and Cochrun & Seals, LLC.

Ten causes of action are pleaded, and the relief sought is damages, in an amount the complaint does not specify. The prayer seeks judgment on the first through the tenth causes of action. As enumerated by Doe’s own firm, consistent with the complaint and reporting: against the seven men, sexual assault, sexual battery, and intentional infliction of emotional distress; against Cornell, the Greek organizations, and the bar, negligence and negligent supervision, with reporting also describing premises-liability claims; against Cornell and Tri Delta, breach of contract; against Cornell only, violations of the New York Human Rights Law, Executive Law §296 et seq., and of the New York Education Law, §6440, with negligent infliction of emotional distress also pleaded against Cornell per reporting; and against Moonies, a claim under the New York Dram Shop Act for unlawful service of alcohol, including to a person under 21. In the original complaint’s text the count headings jump from “Fourth” to “Sixth,” with the Education Law claim pleaded in the Nature of the Action as the fifth; the prayer demands judgment on all ten counts, and later filings renumber—a filing irregularity, recorded as such, not a discrepancy in substance. The relief is compensatory and punitive damages plus attorneys’ fees, costs, and prejudgment interest, the amount stated to exceed “the jurisdictional limits of all other courts” and to be proved at trial. No injunctive or institutional-reform relief is pleaded in the prayer; the reform objectives Doe’s counsel describes publicly, at Section 9, are not part of the filed relief.

The case’s first two months produced a sealing order, a refused restraint order, a granted anonymity motion, and two pending dismissal motions. On October 9, 2026, Justice Perry-Bond ordered the complaint and other filings containing addresses sealed and directed redacted refiling, after an uninvolved man who shares a defendant’s name—an active-duty Marine, at Section 11—reported threats arising from an address wrongly listed in a filing. The court wrote that it “strongly condemns the reported acts of threats and doxing, which can only be characterized as brash, reckless, and ultimately dangerous internet vigilantism.” The redacted complaint was refiled October 19 as NYSCEF Document No. 71. On October 12–16 came the restraint fight: counsel for Sarabia sought an order restraining extrajudicial statements by parties and counsel, arguing Giuffra’s media statements created “a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing prospective jurors” and coincided with threats against defendants; Giuffra’s October 14 letter opposed, asserting the Title IX leaks came from the defence “to attempt to create a perception that the rapes and assaults were somehow consensual.” On October 16 the judge declined to sign the proposed order, holding it did not meet First Amendment requirements for a prior restraint, calling the application a possible “side show,” sealing an email exhibit she characterized as “mudslinging,” warning counsel about sanctions, and urging cooperation against doxing. On October 23 the judge granted Doe’s unopposed motion to proceed as “Jane Doe,” citing compelling circumstances, notoriety, and reported threats, harassment, and doxing attempts. The same day, Sarabia’s counsel filed his motion to dismiss, NYSCEF Document Nos. 87–90: Sarabia “categorically denies” the allegations and moves under CPLR 3211(a)(5) and (a)(7) to dismiss the complaint in its entirety as to him, with prejudice, return date November 16, 2026—after this report’s date, so the motion is pending and undecided. His arguments, labeled here as defence argument: as to Sarabia the complaint alleges only that he grabbed her face and kissed her without consent, which she pushed away, and snorted ketamine off her body—not that he supplied drugs or alcohol or participated in the sexual encounters described elsewhere; the assault, battery, and emotional-distress claims are therefore barred by the one-year limit in CPLR 215(3), and CPLR 213-c and 208 do not save them because an unconsented kiss is not a listed sex offense; the negligence claim fails for want of a duty. Moonies has likewise asked the court to dismiss the complaint against it entirely, as reported October 7. A low-reliability item claiming the judge “rejected” Sarabia’s motion on October 25 is not verified and is inconsistent with the Associated Press’s contemporaneous report and the November 16 return date; it is filed at Section 11. Appearances noted: Scott Norris, through Sher Tremonte LLP, on October 26; Chi Phi Fraternity, Inc. and Chi Phi Educational Trust, through pro hac vice counsel admitted November 4. No merits answer by Cornell, the Chi Phi entities, or the Tri Delta entities was found in reputable reporting as of November 9.

One defendant is out of the case, by a correction the case made against itself. Orazio Petito was named as the Chi Phi chapter president “at the time.” On October 20, 2026, all parties stipulated to discontinue the claims against him with prejudice, the stipulation signed October 19 as NYSCEF Document No. 82. Reporting by ABC states he was mistakenly identified as chapter president at the time of the incident. He was never accused of participating in the alleged assault; his role in the complaint was supervisory, responsibility for the house and members. His attorney, Eric Bernstein: “My client deserved to be released from this case. They had the wrong guy, and justice was served as far as Mr. Petito was concerned.” The discontinuance is verified; the misidentification account is documented. Any account still listing Petito as a current defendant is out of date.

The institutional defendants’ responses are on the record, and they are not interchangeable. Cornell’s statements are at Sections 5 and 7. Chi Phi’s national organization made two distinct statements, which this report does not merge: on September 24, 2026, to CBS News, that the allegations are “deeply concerning”; “Anyone who reports sexual violence deserves to be heard and treated with compassion, dignity, and respect. Chi Phi unequivocally condemns sexual violence… We cannot discuss the specific allegations during pending litigation”; and around October 1, through Interim Executive Director Trey Robb, the account of the chapter’s removal vote and the national expulsion, with “These actions went beyond anything the law or Cornell University required of us” and “Chi Phi condemns sexual assault and drug and alcohol abuse in the strongest possible terms.” No separate statement by the local Xi Chapter or Chapter House Association was found. Tri Delta’s on-record position, stated on behalf of the Alpha Beta Chapter, is: “Tri Delta does not comment on pending litigation,” and “As an organization, we are committed to supporting women and victims of sexual violence.” The organization did not respond to the Cornell Daily Sun’s request at filing, and no separate statement by the Alpha Beta House Corporation was found. Moonies denies serving Doe while underage: in its statement to the Sun, her claim of being served at Moonies is “completely inaccurate.” The bar’s position, as reported: the October 19 event was a private Tri Delta function, about 9 to 11 p.m., with about 185 guests; underage guests’ hands were marked, wristbands went only to guests 21 or older, and “no alcohol was served to guests who had marks on their hands.” The bar has moved to dismiss, and told Fox News Doe later worked for the company, in February–March 2025, and did not then say she had been served or intoxicated at Moonies. Giuffra responded that Moonies is “a minor player in the case” and the claims against it are limited, while standing by the allegation that she was served. The service question itself is contested and unresolved.

7. The Reopening: A Governor Displaces a District Attorney, and a Special Prosecutor Takes the Case

The sequence is eight dated steps. First, September 28, 2026: Van Houten reopened the case in the same press statement that defended the 2024 decision; his office had begun conversations with Doe and her attorneys, assigned a senior sex-crimes prosecutor, and planned to present the case to a Tompkins County grand jury; he stated that neither Doe nor her attorneys had contacted his office in the intervening two years and that he reached out to them after the lawsuit. Second, the same day, Attorney General Letitia James posted on her official X account, linking the Times’ reopening story, a text verified word for word: “What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.” Third, September 29: before acting on the prosecution itself, the governor called for an outside-counsel review of the local handling; Cornell agreed the same day. Fourth, October 1: Governor Hochul signed Executive Order No. 64—“Last night, I signed an executive order,” per her October 2 remarks—issued under Executive Law §63(2), appointing James as special prosecutor and expressly superseding the Tompkins County district attorney in the matter. Section 63(2) provides that when the governor so requires, the attorney general manages the specified criminal proceedings and the district attorney exercises only such powers as the attorney general requires. The order’s operative language, read in full, is to “displace and supersede” the district attorney; its recitals state that the district attorney declined charges “without speaking to Jane Doe” and that Doe’s statement as transmitted “reportedly omitted key portions”—the governor’s stated factual predicates, printed here as recitals, not as this report’s findings. Fifth, October 2, at a news conference: Hochul said Doe “had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable and then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her… That is why I’m invoking the power conferred to me as the Governor of the State of New York to enlist Attorney General James as an independent special prosecutor in this case.” She criticized the campus police for the omission of the “100% confident” statement and the district attorney for deciding without interviewing Doe or requesting the full transcript, and said she had lost confidence in the local handling. James announced an “active criminal investigation”: “Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, it will be investigated fully and fairly, that they will be seen and heard.” At the same conference Hochul said at one point that Doe was gang raped “by five men,” where seven are alleged; NPR noted the discrepancy, and no explanation is in the record; it is filed at Section 11. Sixth, October 2: Van Houten’s response, supporting the appointment and pledging full cooperation, at Section 4. Seventh, a policy rider on October 2: Hochul attacked the voluntary-intoxication limit in New York law—“If someone is too intoxicated to consent, it should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol. Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape, period. I support closing this loophole and will work with the New York State Legislature to accomplish this.” Cornell publicly supported the law-change effort. The statute and the bill are filed at Section 10.

The appointment is challenged in two courts, and both challenges are pending. The first is Lopes v. Hochul and James, Index No. 911974-26, filed in Albany County Supreme Court on October 7, 2026, by Gillio Lopes through attorney Andrew Miltenberg of Nesenoff & Miltenberg LLP. Justice James R. Farrell signed the order to show cause on October 9; the State responded October 22 through Assistant Attorney General Kaitlin Vigars; and the hearing was held October 29, 2026, in Monticello, Sullivan County—which is why reporting variously placed the case in Albany County, its filing, and Sullivan County, its hearing. At the hearing Farrell pressed both sides and made no bench ruling; joinder papers from the other accused were due November 5. Miltenberg’s stated grounds: James’s September 28 post and other public statements show she has prejudged the matter. His framing: “My issue is not political, and it is not personal… Several days before her appointment, Letitia James made some comments on X, and those comments are such that I think it’s fair to look at them and say it appears that the person making those comments [is] biased”; “It’s OK to offer compassion and be empathetic to survivors… I do not believe she can be fair. Had she made a statement that was empathetic or compassionate towards a victim, that’s fine. I don’t think that person can become a neutral investigator or prosecutor.” He says the defence welcomes an investigation, just not one run by James. For the governor and the attorney general, Vigars argued the bias claim is premature, that no charges have been filed, and that the appointment is lawful. On November 5, Diego Sarabia, Scott Kretzschmar, Scott Norris, and Winston Lee joined the petition, so five of the seven men—Lopes plus four—are parties to the effort; Matthew Ingalls and Johnathan Newell did not join, and reporting states they lack representation in the civil case and did not respond to Lopes’s attorneys. Some headlines phrase this as “four of the accused joined the bid,” counting the four who joined the original petitioner; both phrasings describe the same five-man participation, and this report uses the five. The second challenge is separate: an attorney for Winston Lee filed a motion in Tompkins County Supreme Court seeking to prevent James from participating in any grand jury proceeding in the case; reporting on November 6–7 stated a decision is expected November 13, 2026. As of November 9 both challenges are pending, no ruling has issued on either, and James remains special prosecutor. A third track is not a court challenge: on October 9, 2026, the National Legal and Policy Center filed a bar and grievance complaint against James arising from the same statements, a professional-conduct complaint, documented as such.

The investigation has a named leader, no deadline, and one printed conflict about her authority. On November 4, 2026, James announced that Jacqueline Kelly will lead the investigation as outside counsel. Kelly is a partner at Boies Schiller Flexner, which she joined in 2025, a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York, and the first chief of that office’s Civil Rights Unit in the criminal division; she oversaw the prosecution of Sean “Diddy” Combs, and the Peter Nygård and Dr. Robert Cruciani cases. She is a Cornell graduate. Her team is drawn from the attorney general’s office and her firm. The authority conflict, printed as found: CNN’s November 4 account describes Kelly as holding “decision-making authority,” while the attorney general’s own primary release states that her team “will report to OAG.” The two characterizations differ on where final authority sits; the record does not resolve the difference. James’s statement pledged an investigation “guided only by the facts, the evidence, and the law.” The attorney general’s office has set no deadline. Context noted by the Associated Press: the two-year limitations period for misdemeanors arising from October 2024 has run; New York sets no limitations period for the most serious sex offenses. James was re-elected attorney general on November 3, 2026, the day before the Kelly announcement.

Cornell’s independent review is constituted, scoped, and silent so far. It was announced October 6, 2026, by a newly formed Special Committee of the Board of Trustees, chaired by Board Chair Anne Meinig Smalling, and Sally Yates—partner at King & Spalding, former deputy attorney general and acting attorney general—was retained to lead it. Its scope, in Cornell’s statement: a comprehensive review of how Cornell prevents and responds to sexual harassment, assault, and related misconduct—report intake and investigation; student support; hearings, discipline, and appeals; the campus police role and coordination with law enforcement and prosecutors; campus safety reporting; Greek and student-organization oversight; and the Board’s own oversight—including a detailed review of the university’s response to the Jane Doe allegations and whether Cornell followed its policies. Its benchmarks are Title IX, the Clery Act, the VAWA Campus SaVE Act, New York law, and best practices. The review has full independence and reports to the Special Committee. The Board has said it intends to share the review’s “results and recommendations”; it has not committed to publishing the full report. No timeline has been announced, and there are no findings as of November 9, 2026.

8. The Leadership Crisis: No Confidence, a City Moratorium, and the Policy Changes

The Faculty Senate’s resolution is one sentence, and it is printed whole. “Resolved: That the Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University.” It passed on November 6, 2026, 75 yes, 50 no, 5 abstentions, 5 non-votes—verified; Cornell’s own November 6 statement frames the same result as 55.6 percent in favor, 37 percent against, 7.4 percent abstaining or not voting, of 135 senators excluding Weill Cornell Medicine. The path: posted October 7; debated October 14 and October 28, when the Senate voted 76–48 against postponing the ballot until the Yates review ends; electronic voting ran from October 29 or 30 to November 6. Its lead sponsor was Paul Ortiz of the ILR School, a labor historian, with 13 faculty cosponsors per the Ithaca Voice. The resolution is non-binding, names the “central administration” rather than President Kotlikoff personally, and does not call for any resignation; only the Board of Trustees can remove the president. Per Cornell’s AAUP chapter, it is the first no-confidence resolution in the Faculty Senate’s history—its “56-year history,” per USA Today. Before the vote: at the closed October 14 session Kotlikoff acknowledged he had not read the Cornell police report, on audio obtained by the Associated Press; in an October 13 Times interview he said he had never followed up on Doe or on the criminal investigation; his public silence on the case lasted more than two weeks after the lawsuit. Dean of Faculty Chris Schaffer opposed the resolution, writing that it “falls short” because it does not spell out the administration’s specific failures. The Board’s response came the same day, within hours, from Chair Smalling: “Today’s Faculty Senate vote reflects the deep anger across our campus and sends a clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable… The Board of Trustees remains confident that President Kotlikoff and his administration are the right leaders to thoughtfully and comprehensively address the serious problem of sexual assault on our campus… The Board fully supports President Kotlikoff and his administration.” Since the vote: Kotlikoff has told the Times he has “no intention” of resigning; AAUP chapter president David Bateman asked the Board to “affirm the Faculty Senate’s vote”; the full Board’s next scheduled meeting is January 30, and its executive committee meets by Zoom on December 3 and can exercise most Board powers between meetings. No leadership change has occurred. One posture note completes the record: Reuters reported on November 6 that Kotlikoff had not yet responded to the vote itself and has 30 days to respond in writing; no formal post-vote statement by him was located through November 9, and his “no intention” remark attends the vote coverage rather than answering the result.

The president’s own statements, and one disputed remark, are filed separately from the vote. In a video statement on the weekend of October 3–4, 2026, Kotlikoff called the allegations “deeply disturbing,” said they raise questions about the investigations conducted, and welcomed an independent review. In an October 13 letter to the community: “I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community.” He also apologized in his State of the University address, per the Cornell Daily Sun of October 19. The disputed remark: Doe, in a letter to faculty leaders transmitted through counsel, said her sorority president told her Kotlikoff had asked why she waited until the following month to report; Doe said the account left her feeling “unsupported and disbelieved.” Cornell disputes the characterization: it says Kotlikoff was asking why bystanders had not reported what they knew. The conflict is printed, not resolved.

Public pressure ran on a dated calendar of its own. A demonstration at Ho Plaza on October 5, 2026, as protests began. Faculty joined students at a rally on October 6–7 with signs reading “Justice for every Jane Doe” and “Cornell admin betrays survivors resign now.” A seven-hour sit-in on October 7, roughly 80 students at the Toni Morrison dining hall; students also hosted a town hall, and administrators, pressed at a webinar, confirmed two accused students remained enrolled. The City of Ithaca acted against the university, then let its act lapse with demands attached. Cornell’s policy changes since September 2026 are announced, dated, and in one place stated two ways. Announced October 13, 2026, in the president’s letter: all parties and social events at Interfraternity Council houses suspended through the end of the 2026–27 academic year, covering more than twenty IFC fraternities, under a “zero tolerance” rule by which a violating chapter faces immediate emergency suspension; Kotlikoff: “These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue.” New York State Police criminal investigators, independent of Cornell and trauma-informed, to have a role in campus sexual-assault investigations. 10. The Standards: Three Forums, Three Burdens, and the Statute the Case Turns On

Three forums have handled this case or will, under three standards, and the divergence of their outcomes is a function of those standards and their different records. In the criminal forum, a grand jury decides probable cause to indict and a trial jury decides guilt beyond a reasonable doubt; no charges have been filed, and the special prosecutor’s investigation is open. In Cornell’s discipline, a three-member panel decided under Policy 6.4 by a preponderance of the evidence—more likely than not; that proceeding completed in 2025, its outcomes are at Section 5, and one respondent’s court challenge was dismissed with an appeal pending. In the civil forum, a jury, demanded, would decide by a preponderance at trial; at the current CPLR 3211 stage, the complaint’s allegations are taken as true for motion purposes, and the case is in early motion practice. Every serious account of the case makes this point, the Associated Press’s October 14, 2026 Title IX explainer among them. This report states the divergence; it does not resolve it.

The criminal question turns on a definition, and the definition is printed from the statute. Penal Law §130.00(6): “mentally incapacitated” means rendered temporarily incapable of appraising or controlling one’s conduct by a narcotic or intoxicating substance “administered to him without his consent,” or by another act committed without consent. Section 130.00(7): “physically helpless” means unconscious or otherwise physically unable to communicate unwillingness to act. Section 130.05(2)–(3): lack of consent results from, among other things, forcible compulsion, or incapacity to consent, including being mentally incapacitated or physically helpless; for specified offenses it also results from clearly expressed non-consent that a reasonable person in the actor’s position would understand. The consequence, as documented in legal commentary and the governor’s October 2 statement: voluntary intoxication, without more, does not satisfy the “mentally incapacitated” definition, because the substance must have been administered without consent. That is the analytical core of Van Houten’s 2024 decision and of the reform debate. A bill first introduced by then-Senator Biaggi in 2019 would add voluntary-intoxication incapacity with a knowledge element; it passed the New York Senate in 2020, 2021, 2023, 2024, and 2025 and never received an Assembly vote. The current vehicle is S10632 (Fernandez) and A101 (Dinowitz): it passed the Senate on June 4, 2026, no Assembly floor vote is recorded, and it is not law as of November 9, 2026; the governor’s October 2 pledge stands behind it. Two further provisions belong to the landscape. The “Rape Is Rape” Act, effective September 1, 2024—six weeks before the night at issue—brought vaginal, oral, and anal contact under the rape rubric, repealing and folding in the former criminal-sexual-act provisions, so any charging analysis of October 2024 conduct proceeds under the post-September 2024 numbering. And §130.10(1) provides an affirmative defense in prosecutions premised on incapacity: that the defendant did not know of the facts or conditions responsible for the victim’s incapacity. The defense is statutory and would be for the defence to prove; no defendant here has been charged, so it is an element of the legal landscape, not a live pleading.

The limitations record is printed with its open question left open. On the civil side, CPLR 213-c gives claims premised on specified sex offenses a twenty-year limitations window and expressly provides that no criminal charge or conviction is required; it is the provision Sarabia’s motion argues does not reach the narrower conduct alleged against him. CPLR 215(8)’s extension, by contrast, is contingent on a criminal action having been commenced, which has not occurred as of November 9, 2026; it is not established here. The Adult Survivors Act, CPLR 214-j, revived only claims already time-barred as of its 2022 effective date; it is not clearly applicable to October 2024 conduct, and Doe’s suit does not appear to rest on it. On the criminal side, under CPL 30.10, first-degree rape carries no limitations period, other felonies default to five years, and misdemeanors to two years—the two-year misdemeanor period for October 2024 conduct has run. Whether §30.10(2)(a-1)’s twenty-year period or the five-year default governs §130.30(4)–(6) conduct after the 2024 renumbering was not found on the sources the desk retrieved; this report does not assert an answer. The procedural instrument of the reopening, Executive Law §63(2), and its precedent use in Executive Order 147, are at Section 7.
