items.title: The Kraków Suspect Dies in Hospital, the Mediator Comes to Washington, and Asia Buys Back Friday
items.content_html:
The Night File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

The Kraków Suspect Dies in Hospital, the Mediator Comes to Washington, and Asia Buys Back Friday

The night file, while Washington slept: the one man who could have answered the Kraków questions will not answer them, and Poland’s second day of mourning opened with the investigation turned from a questioning to a reconstruction. The region’s other fire acquired an operator’s statement: the Khor Mor fire is doused, the damage is being assessed, and no restart is promised. The Iran mediation acquired a room and an hour: the Oval Office at noon, closed, with Qatar’s prime minister inside it and Tehran’s foreign minister on the record waiting for an answer. Asia’s markets, handed the same weekend, bought back part of Friday. The Senate count did not move for a third day. Monday holds the meetings; Tuesday still holds the talks and the deadlines.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0400 ET, Monday, November 9, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 23, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, which filed the fourth tanker claimed in Hormuz, the halt at Khor Mor, and the count frozen at Friday’s figures. The reports filed here are the night’s reports, taken after that edition closed; where they restate Sunday’s facts, the restatement is identified. The midnight edition stands unrevised, as a log stands.

The Night in Brief

The night closed one file by death, priced another by the barrel and the index, and moved no count, no coalition and no tanker claim from claim to confirmation. In Kraków, Małopolska police announced early Monday that the suspect, a 24-year-old man wounded in the shootout with police on Saturday, died in hospital, in the Guardian account and the second police account filed below. The dead of the case therefore stand at ten on the accounts that count him with his victims: six in the Main Market Square, three at his home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, and the man himself. Prosecutors pursue the terrorism investigation on the sequence, the weapons and the emblems on his clothing; no motive has been established, and the man who held it is dead. In Iraqi Kurdistan, the operator Dana Gas said Monday it was assessing damage at Khor Mor after dousing the fire, with no injuries to staff, in the operator’s statement filed below; production stands halted and 2,800 megawatts stand off the grid. In Washington, the day’s schedule is the news: Stephen Miller takes the chief of staff’s office, and at noon the president meets Qatar’s prime minister behind closed doors on the Iran file, the vice president meeting him separately, in the schedule account filed below. In Paris the G7 foreign ministers meet Monday and Tuesday. In Tokyo the Nikkei closed its morning up 3.44 percent. The desk files the night in that order.

Kraków at 0400: The Suspect Is Dead, and the Questions Stay With the Living

Poland’s second day of national mourning began with an announcement from the police who shot the man. “We would like to inform you that the perpetrator of the tragic events died in hospital early this morning,” Małopolska police wrote on X, in the accounts filed below. The man, 24, named in Polish media as Michał O., had been in critical condition since Saturday, when officers shot him within minutes of the first shots in the Main Market Square. He had not been formally arrested and had not been questioned; prosecutors had said both waited on his medical condition. That waiting is now permanent. The investigation the national prosecutor’s office opened as a terrorist offence covers two acts, the killing of six people in the square with the attempted killing of many others including police officers, and the killing of the three at the home; with the suspect dead, its work is the work the overnight accounts list: the full sequence, the source of the weapons, the meaning of the emblems, and whether anyone else took part in planning.

The morning’s new evidence is clothing and guns, and both arrive attributed and unfinished. Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Galecka told TOK FM radio on Monday that the man’s clothes carried many different emblems, partly examined and interpreted, the patches associated with various motifs that specialists are still analysing; she would not say more while the investigation runs. The minister’s Saturday reading stands where it stood: fascination with far-right ideology and very radical, ultra-nationalistic views, in the interior minister’s words, and a reading is what it remains. On the weapons, one Monday account counts 11 firearms recovered in all, four from the man or his car in Kraków and seven from the family home, in the victims and firearms account filed below; Polish media report he held a firearms permit and may have obtained guns from the home, and police have not confirmed that account. The wounded stand at 17 injured in the prosecutors’ count carried in the morning accounts, against 15 and 16 in the weekend’s files, with the two officers’ conditions divided in the accounts between regained consciousness in the evening file and one officer in a coma in the Monday account; both are printed in the Cocked Hat. The six of the square stand as the midnight edition named them by age and nationality, and the three at home stand at father 53, mother 52 and sister 21 in the Sunday confirmation the morning accounts repeat. Kraków’s own mourning runs through November 11; the national mourning ends Monday night.

Khor Mor at 0400: The Fire Is Doused, the Assessment Begins, and No Hand Is Claimed

The gas field’s operator has spoken, and its statement is the night’s firmest new document in the region. Dana Gas, joint operator of Khor Mor, said in a Monday statement that production was halted on Sunday following a suspected drone attack, that it was assessing the damage after dousing a fire sparked by the attack, and that there were no injuries to staff. The statement confirms the halt from the party that runs the field; it gives no restart date and no damage figure. The rest of the file stands as Sunday left it: a single drone struck a liquefied petroleum gas storage tank, in the electricity ministry sources’ account; employees were evacuated to shelters; gas supply stands suspended to power plants in Erbil, Sulaimaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal and Duhok; the loss stands at 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts, with more than 70 percent of the region without power in the regional accounts, in the Al Jazeera account and the Press TV account filed below. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s joint investigative committee is ordered; an initial assessment found no casualties. No group has claimed the attack, and no authority has named a hand. The field was shut once before this year, in July, on security threats, and restarted later that month; that history is in the operator’s account, and it is a history, not a forecast.

Hormuz at 0400: The Claims Restated, the Lane Near Oman, and Still No Confirmation

No tanker fire of the weekend acquired an independent confirmation in the night, and the morning files are restatements with one new sentence about a lane. The Guards’ Navy’s position stands in its fuller morning form: three oil tankers struck mines and caught fire extensively in a prohibited lane on Sunday, in the Antara account filed below, beside the Iranian Navy’s fourth tanker in the eastern strait, in the IANS account filed below; the two services’ counts differ by one ship, as the midnight edition printed them. One morning summary states the limit plainly: the reports do not establish that a fourth tanker incident occurred on November 9, and no flag or destination has been given for any of them, in the summary account filed below. The weekend’s maritime record that rests on incident reports rather than claims also stands: two tankers hit within an hour on Saturday evening in the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reports, one burning eight nautical miles northwest of Khasab with its crew evacuated, open-source analysts tentatively naming it the Navig8 Messi, and the American disabling of the bulk carrier Huda in the Gulf of Oman, in the maritime account filed below. The new sentence is Iraq’s: Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said Iraq reached an understanding with the United States on Sunday to facilitate crude exports through the strait using a shipping lane near Oman, in the market accounts filed below. A lane agreed is not a lane used; no sailing under it is in the file at 0400.

Washington at 0400: A New Chief of Staff, a Mediator at Noon, and an Answer Owed

Monday in Washington is a handover and a meeting, and both were set before the weekend. Stephen Miller, 41, deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, takes the chief of staff’s office today, succeeding Susie Wiles, who moves to the Trump Political Operation; the president’s announcement of Friday stands as the record of the change, and the opposition’s answers stand as the midnight edition filed them, Senator Schumer’s and, on Sunday, Representative Jeffries’s statement on ABC that his party will not work with Mr. Miller, in the Sunday account filed below. At noon Eastern the president meets Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, Qatar’s prime minister and foreign minister, in the Oval Office in a session the White House schedule marks closed press; Vice President Vance is due to meet him separately, an American official told Reuters, in the schedule account above. Mr. Al Thani is the principal channel between Washington and Tehran; the vice president has spent roughly a fortnight in near-daily contact with him on the indirect Iran channel, in the backchannel account filed below.

What the mediator carries into the room is a sequence, and what he carries out of it is not yet in any file. The proposal described by the mediation sources runs in two days: on day one the United States lifts its naval blockade and releases some frozen Iranian funds while Tehran invites International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to the bombed nuclear sites; on day two the strait reopens and nuclear talks resume on Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on X on Sunday that Tehran was still waiting for Washington’s answer to that proposal. Against the sequence stand two American sentences from Sunday: the president’s, to CNN, that fresh attacks are highly unlikely if talks produce a strong agreement, with further targets mapped if fighting resumes; and Secretary of State Rubio’s, before the G7 talks in Paris, that he would not call the negotiations close to a breakthrough and that Iranian demands are in part unacceptable. No readout of any Monday meeting exists at 0400, because the meetings have not happened. The desk files the schedule, the proposal as its sources describe it, and the two sentences, and nothing beyond them.

Paris and Abu Dhabi at 0400: The Ministers Sit Monday, the Table Sits Tuesday

The G7 foreign ministers meet in Paris on Monday and Tuesday, and the Abu Dhabi round opens Tuesday, and the connection between the two rooms is Europe’s seat. The Paris gathering, among the last major events of France’s G7 presidency, takes up air defence and energy support for Ukraine ahead of winter, in the Paris account filed below; Secretary Rubio is expected on both days. Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot’s Sunday statement stands: Europeans will be well represented in Abu Dhabi and France will take part, he told RTL radio, and he cannot yet say who will represent France, in the Reuters account filed below. Russia has said there would be no place for European representatives at the table; France says they will participate; both statements stand, as the midnight edition printed them. The delegations stand as reported and not as settled: Russia’s led by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky in the accounts, Ukraine’s named differently among the files, the Americans Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner. No agenda, draft or text has been published by any side. In Ukraine the file did not move in the night: the Komyshuvakha toll stands at at least 55 dead, the missing at 45 in the regional administration’s Sunday figure and about 50 in the intelligence agency’s, the search continuing in intervals under drone threat, in the toll account filed below; and President Zelenskyy’s reading of Friday night’s barrage, pressure ahead of the talks, stands as his reading.

Jerusalem at 0400: The Mandate’s First Working Day

Mr. Eisenkot’s 28 days began Sunday at the President’s Residence, and Monday is the first working day inside them. The mandate’s facts stand as the weekend filed them: 48 seats in his four-party bloc, 61 required, 67 recommendations to 46, four conditions published for joining his government, and no coalition. The expected meetings are the day’s file: Mr. Bennett on Sunday evening, its outcome not taken in by midnight and not supplied in the night’s accounts, and Mr. Liberman on Monday. The contest underneath stands in the positions the accounts carry: Mr. Liberman prepared for painful compromises, including on conscription, to build 61 without the Arab-led parties, and ruling out a minority government resting on their abstention, in the compromise account filed below; the arithmetic that account prints is the only road to 61 yet drawn on paper, 48 plus United Torah Judaism’s 7 and Shas’s 6, and it runs through the draft law his bloc campaigned on. On Tuesday the new Knesset is scheduled to convene. Mr. Netanyahu remains prime minister while the negotiations run. Nothing in the night’s file adds a seat, removes a condition, or names an agreement.

Al-Ayyat and Riyadh at 0400: Two Files That Did Not Move, and One That Moved Sideways

Egypt’s railway file rests where Sunday’s late count left it, and the morning accounts are the Sunday accounts carried forward. Seven dead in every later account; the injured at 112 in the Health Ministry’s count, 114 in the prosecutors’ provisional estimate, and at least 125 in the chief prosecutor’s late Sunday statement; the Giza-to-Fayoum train against the stationary Cairo-to-Aswan train between Kafr Ammar and Raqqa; President al-Sisi’s order for an urgent investigation and accountability for anyone found negligent; and no cause stated by the railway authority, the prosecutors or the ministry, in the wire account and the ministry account filed below. The dead have not been named. The investigation owns the cause, and it has not spoken.

Riyadh’s file moved sideways in the night: the damage, not the event, is now the disputed item. The Saudi Energy Ministry’s account stands, debris from an intercepted attack, minor damage to an Aramco administrative building in the financial district, no casualties. Against it stands a later filing reporting footage verified by BBC Verify in which one floor of the building is severely damaged and window glass is broken across several floors, in the intercepts account filed below. The coalition’s interception count stands at three ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles destroyed, with two ballistic launchers in Saada destroyed in answer; the Houthi spokesman’s operations stand at four in one account and six in another, in the daily brief filed below; and the Sanaa toll stands unmoved at 33 killed, among them eight women and thirteen children, and 39 wounded, in the Houthi-run health ministry’s count, which Saudi Arabia’s communications center said it was investigating. Every figure keeps its owner. The desk prints the ministry’s word and the verified footage’s picture side by side, and reconciles neither.

The Count at 0400: A Third Day Without Figures

Neither Senate race was called in the night, and no new figure was published for either, for the third day running. Mississippi stands at Scott Colom 467,930 to Cindy Hyde-Smith 465,356, a margin of 2,574 on the tally stamped Friday evening; Alaska stands at Mary Peltola ahead of Dan Sullivan by 637 first-choice votes on a count posted Wednesday, in the count guide and the delay account filed below. Monday is the first day on which either count is scheduled to move: Alaska’s next update is due Monday or Tuesday, November 9 or 10, and is expected to carry early votes and a large batch of absentees. Tuesday remains the heavier date in both states: Mississippi’s mail ballots postmarked by Election Day must arrive by 5 p.m. Tuesday and its affidavit voters must cure identification by then, counties certify by November 13, and Alaska’s ranked-choice tabulation is set for November 18 if no candidate reaches 50 percent. The estimates of Mississippi’s remainder still run from about 3,139 mail ballots to the state Republican chairman’s 23,000 to 25,000, with a tracker’s roughly 30,498 in its own model. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide. Colorado’s 4th District stands uncalled with them.

Asunción and Shizuoka at 0400: A Detention’s Second Night, a Count Settled

Paraguay’s file carried one long explanatory account in the night and no new ruling. Former President Santiago Peña spent a second night in pretrial detention at the Presidential Escort Regiment, former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo in detention beside him, 27 people charged in the Ueno case in all, the repayments at $160 million to nearly 1.2 million savers in the central bank’s reporting and $153.5 million on the same savers in the guarantee fund’s second accounting, in the collapse account and the detention account filed below. Mr. Peña’s plea stands at not guilty through his attorney, Ricardo Preda; he declined to testify; no court has ruled on the substance of any charge, and he is presumed innocent. President Pedro Alliana is naming the cabinet that serves through 2028. Ueno froze the accounts of nearly three million customers in a country of 6.5 million; how much of the roughly $850 million in public money it administered can be recovered is not established.

Central Japan’s file is settled at the figures the midnight edition closed with, and Monday is its assessment day. The injured stand at 22 in the prefectures’ division, 19 in Aichi with one serious and three minor in Shizuoka, against 21 in the updated Jiji Press count and 24 in a local papers’ tally no official account carried forward, in the correction file filed below. The earthquake stands at magnitude 5.7 by the Japan Meteorological Agency and 5.5 by the United States Geological Survey, 1:04 a.m. Sunday beneath western Shizuoka, upper 5 in Chita, no tsunami, no deaths. The agency’s guidance stands for about a week, the risk highest in the next two to three days, its landslide thresholds lowered for the hardest-shaken municipalities, and its further investigation of the quake set for a meeting on Monday in the television accounts. No overnight aftershock of consequence is in the file.

The Markets at 0400: Oil Down, Asia Up, and the Two Readings of One Weekend

Asia’s markets opened the week by buying back Friday, and oil opened it by selling the weekend’s claims, and the desk files both prices without choosing between their readings. Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 closed its morning at 59,411, up 1,976 points or 3.44 percent, recovering just over half of Friday’s fall, with Taiwan’s index up between 5.3 and 5.9 percent across the morning accounts, South Korea’s Kospi up between 1.4 and 1.8 percent, and the regional index outside Japan up 0.8 percent after a 4.6 percent fall last week, in the Reuters market account and the recap account filed below; the chipmakers led, and the accounts carry an inquiry at Nvidia over its chief executive as the sentiment item the rebound shrugged off. Oil’s prints moved through the morning rather than settling: Brent at $97.48, down 84 cents, at 0138 GMT, $97.67 in the later Perth print the midnight edition filed, $96.91 down 1.5 percent at 0629 GMT in one account, and $98.35, up 3 cents, at 0427 GMT in another, in the Reuters oil account filed below. The prints are an hour-by-hour movement under two opposing weights, the president’s sentence that fresh attacks are highly unlikely while talks progress, and a strait in which four tanker fires are claimed and none confirmed. Brent fell 17 percent last week, its steepest weekly drop since 2020 on the LSEG figures in the accounts. What New York does with the same file on Monday is not yet in the record.

Monday Opens: Handovers, Meetings, and a Second Day of Mourning

The day the night hands over is a working day built of other days’ appointments. In Poland it is the second and last day of national mourning, with Kraków’s mourning running to November 11 and the terrorism investigation now running without its suspect. In Washington Mr. Miller takes his office and the Qatari prime minister is in the Oval Office at noon. In Paris the G7 ministers sit, with the Abu Dhabi table set for Tuesday and Wednesday. In Jerusalem Mr. Eisenkot meets Mr. Liberman inside a 28-day clock that started Sunday. In Iraqi Kurdistan the assessment at Khor Mor begins with the field dark. In Alaska the count may move today or tomorrow; in Mississippi nothing moves until Tuesday’s deadlines. Everything the week left open with a date still carries Tuesday’s date in the main: the talks, the American inflation report, the mail and cure deadlines, and the president’s larger Iran decision, which has no date at all. The log proceeds to Monday.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On Kraków’s wounded, the counts run 15, 16 and now 17 injured in the prosecutors’ morning count, counting different sets at different hours; on its two officers, regained consciousness in Sunday’s evening account and one in a coma in Monday’s account, the desk prints both and resolves neither. On the three at the home, the ages now agree at 53, 52 and 21 in the repeated confirmation, against the two other sets the weekend’s files carried. On Hormuz, the Guards count three tankers and the Navy counts a fourth, no party that did not claim a fire has confirmed one, one name is offered tentatively by analysts, and a morning summary states that no fourth incident on November 9 is established. On Khor Mor, the halt and the 2,800 megawatts are confirmed by the ministries that lost them and now by the operator that runs the field, and the hand is claimed by no one. On Riyadh’s tower, minor damage in the ministry’s word and a severely damaged floor in verified footage. On oil, four prints between $96.91 and $98.35 in one morning, a movement and not a level. On Asia, Taiwan up 5.3 or 5.9 and the Kospi up 1.4 or 1.8 by the hour of the print. Against the triangle, the night’s single-valued facts are these: the Kraków suspect is dead, announced by the police who shot him, and the investigation continues without him; the Khor Mor fire is doused and its damage is being assessed by its operator, with no staff injured and no restart promised; the Qatari prime minister is scheduled at noon in the Oval Office and Tehran waits for an answer; the G7 sits in Paris and the Abu Dhabi table sits Tuesday; no Senate race was called and no figure moved; and Asia bought back part of Friday while oil moved both ways under it. The log proceeds to Monday.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Thirty-three items.

Subjective
The Guardian, via World Right Now — Poland opens a terror inquiry as Kraków mourns six victims

Polish prosecutors have opened a terrorism investigation into the weekend shooting in Kraków, as the country began two days of national mourning and police confirmed that the suspected gunman had died in hospital. The suspect, a 24-year-old Polish man, died early on Monday morning in hospital, according to police in Małopolska. The national prosecutor’s office said it was examining the killing of six people with a firearm and the attempted killing of many others, including police officers, in an act it described as a terrorist offence. Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Galecka told TOK FM on Monday that his clothes carried many different emblems, partly examined and interpreted, associated with various motifs specialists are still analysing.

Subjective
VidiaNews — the Kraków shooting suspect who killed six has died, say police in Poland

A gunman suspected of killing six people in a popular market square in Kraków has died in hospital, Polish police said early on Monday. The suspect, a 24-year-old named in local media as Michał O. who authorities say was probably inspired by far-right ideologies, had been wounded in a shootout with police and had been in critical condition. “We would like to inform you that the perpetrator of the tragic events died in hospital early this morning,” Małopolska police wrote on X. Prosecutors had opened a terrorism investigation after the man opened fire on Saturday afternoon, killing six including a Briton and injuring 17. Police confirmed on Sunday that the three people found dead at his home were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21.

Subjective
DunyaDesk — Kraków shooting update: victims identified, 11 guns seized

Polish authorities have identified the six people killed in Saturday’s attack on the Main Market Square, seized 11 firearms linked to the suspect and his father, and confirmed that one of the two wounded police officers remains in a coma while the other has regained consciousness. Investigators recovered four firearms from the gunman or his car at the scene in Kraków and seven from the family home. The suspect, 24-year-old Michał O., remains in critical condition in hospital in this account, and Poland is observing the second day of national mourning. The National Prosecutor’s Office has opened a terrorism investigation, and the defence minister clarified that the suspect is not a soldier and has never had a connection to the military.

Subjective
AnewZ — Poland mourns the victims of the Kraków mass shooting

Monday marks the second of two days of national mourning in Poland as police bolstered security after six people were killed in a mass shooting in Kraków. Sixteen people were wounded in the attack, including two police officers and the suspected gunman, a 24-year-old Polish man who remained in critical condition in hospital in this account. One of the dead was a British citizen, and five foreign nationals from Austria, Germany, Portugal, Russia and Britain were among the wounded. Prosecutor’s office spokesperson Daniel Prokopowicz said it was “highly likely” the killings in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski and Kraków were carried out by the same person, and that seven firearms and a significant quantity of ammunition were recovered from the home.

Subjective
The Daily Lens — Kraków mourns six as the Main Market Square reopens

Kraków reopened its historic Main Market Square to the public on Sunday, just over 24 hours after a gunman killed six people and injured more than a dozen in the Old Town, as the country began two days of national mourning. Police identified the suspect as a 24-year-old Polish man who held a firearms permit and had no previous criminal record; he was shot during his arrest and remains in critical condition in hospital in this account. Three bodies found at his home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 150 kilometres northeast of Kraków, were confirmed on Sunday as his father, 53, his mother, 52, and his 21-year-old sister. The mayor declared city mourning until Wednesday, November 11, while the national mourning covers Sunday and Monday.

Subjective
Reuters, via DevDiscourse — Iraq’s Khor Mor gas field suspends output after the drone attack, the operator says

Production was halted on Sunday at Iraq’s Khor Mor gas field, one of the largest in the Kurdistan region, following a suspected drone attack, joint field operator Dana Gas said in a statement. The company said in Monday’s statement it was assessing the damage after dousing a fire sparked by the attack, with no injuries to staff. About 2.8 gigawatts of power generation in the Kurdistan region was taken out by the attack, the region’s electricity ministry said. There was no claim of responsibility for Sunday’s attack. Two sources in the region’s electricity ministry said a single drone strike hit the LPG storage tank in the field, causing the fire, and employees were evacuated to shelters.

Subjective
Al Jazeera, via 234Radio — the drone attack suspends production at Iraq’s Khor Mor gasfield

A drone attack on the Khor Mor gasfield has caused a fire at the facility and cut power to the region, according to Iraqi and Kurdish officials, and the Sunday night attack left more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region without power. It was not clear who was responsible or whether it was related to the war between the United States, Israel and Iran. Al Jazeera’s fact-checking agency Sanad verified footage of smoke and flames rising from the vicinity of the gasfield in Sulaimaniyah governorate. Electricity ministry spokesperson Omid Ahmed said the attack suspended gas supply to power plants in Erbil, Sulaimaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal and Duhok and knocked between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts off the grid. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said there were no casualties, based on an initial assessment.

Subjective
Press TV — the drone attack in Iraq’s Kurdistan region halts production at a major gas field

A drone attack on Iraq’s Khor Mor gas field in the Kurdistan region on Sunday forced a halt to production, triggered a fire at an LPG storage tank and disrupted nearly 2.8 gigawatts of electricity generation, according to regional officials and security sources. Two sources quoted by Reuters at the region’s Ministry of Electricity said a single drone struck an LPG storage tank at the facility, setting it ablaze. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said an initial assessment indicated no casualties. The region’s ministries of Natural Resources and Electricity described the incident as a “terrorist attack” in a joint statement.

Subjective
Antara, via Jawawa — three tankers catch fire after striking mines in the Strait of Hormuz

Three oil tankers struck mines and caught fire in a shipping lane restricted by Iran in the Strait of Hormuz, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said on Sunday, November 8. “From this morning until now, three oil tankers that violated the rules have struck mines and caught fire extensively in a prohibited lane in the Strait of Hormuz,” the statement said.

Subjective
IANS, via HiIndia — Iran’s Army says a violating oil tanker hit mines in the Hormuz Strait

Tehran, November 9: the navy of Iran’s Army announced that a violating oil tanker caught fire after hitting naval mines east of the Strait of Hormuz. In a statement on the army’s website, the navy said on Sunday the tanker had turned off its identification systems and was transiting the forbidden region east of the strait when it hit the mines, and it warned the strait will remain closed to vessels unless all threats are lifted. Earlier in the day, the Guards’ Navy said an oil tanker caught fire after colliding with naval mines in the unauthorized route, the third oil tanker to hit naval mines in the strait’s unauthorized route since the beginning of the day in its count.

Subjective
Splash 247 — Hormuz suffers a weekend of fire

Merchant shipping has been caught in an escalation of the war around the Strait of Hormuz over the past 72 hours, with tankers set ablaze, the American military bombing a bulk carrier, fresh Iranian warnings about naval mines and explosions reported along Iran’s southern coastline. On Saturday a United States military aircraft fired precision-guided munitions at the stern of the St. Kitts and Nevis-flagged bulk carrier Huda in the Gulf of Oman; Central Command said the vessel had repeatedly ignored warnings while attempting to leave regional waters after visiting an Iranian port. Two tankers were hit within an hour of each other on Saturday evening in United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reports, the first eight nautical miles northwest of Khasab, its crew evacuated, open-source analysts tentatively identifying it as the Navig8 Messi. The Guards’ Navy subsequently claimed two tankers had struck naval mines on unauthorized routes with their navigation systems off, and a third tanker was reported suffering an explosion and catching fire; the Iranian claims have not been independently substantiated.

Subjective
EL7.AI — Iran reports three tanker fires in Hormuz; Reuters could not confirm

The Revolutionary Guard said two tankers caught fire on November 8 after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Fars later reported that a third tanker caught fire, and Reuters was unable to confirm the reported strikes. Twenty-two people were rescued from a burning vessel in the Gulf of Oman, according to Emirati media. Available reports do not establish that a fourth tanker incident occurred on November 9. The Iranian military did not identify the tankers’ flags or destinations in its account of the two fires, according to the Associated Press.

Subjective
Clash Report — Trump meets Qatar’s prime minister for closed Iran diplomacy talks

The White House schedule places the session at noon Eastern in the Oval Office and marks it closed press, with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani set to see President Donald Trump behind closed doors on Monday. Al Thani, who also serves as Qatar’s foreign minister, has been the principal channel between Washington and Tehran in recent weeks. A United States official told Reuters that Vice President JD Vance is also due to meet him separately. Sources described a sequenced idea: on day one the United States would lift its naval blockade and release some frozen Iranian funds while Tehran invites International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to bombed nuclear sites; on day two the Strait of Hormuz would reopen and nuclear talks would resume. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday on X that Tehran was still waiting for Washington’s answer to that two-day proposal. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that he would not call the negotiations close to a breakthrough.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine — JD Vance leads the backchannel talks with Iran to revive a ceasefire and nuclear negotiations

United States Vice President JD Vance has spent the past fortnight directly engaged in indirect negotiations with Iran aimed at brokering a new ceasefire and resuming stalled nuclear discussions, Axios reported, citing two sources with knowledge of the matter. Behind closed doors, Vance has maintained daily discussions with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, Pakistan’s Army Chief Asim Munir and other mediators. The sources revealed that Vance, alongside Qatari and Pakistani interlocutors, has evaluated setting up a working-level technical meeting involving American and Iranian delegates soon, though such a meeting has not yet materialised.

Subjective
US News Pulse — Trump to host Qatar’s prime minister at the White House on Iran

President Donald Trump will meet Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani in a closed-door session in the Oval Office on Monday, November 9, 2026, as efforts to end the nine-month war between the United States and Iran reach a delicate moment. Vice President JD Vance is also scheduled to meet the Qatari leader before Trump does. Qatar has carried messages between Washington and Tehran for months, and Iran is now reviewing proposals presented by chief mediator Qatar, the Associated Press reported. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Sunday, November 8, that negotiations had made little progress and he did not see an imminent breakthrough.

Subjective
USA Today — Jeffries says Democrats will not work with Trump’s new chief of staff

Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said that his party will not work with Stephen Miller, President Donald Trump’s new chief of staff, during an appearance on ABC’s “This Week” on November 8. Miller was tapped to replace former chief of staff Susie Wiles on November 6 and will step into the role on November 9. Jeffries is likely to be the next Speaker of the House when Democrats assume the majority in January.

Subjective
JournalArta — G7 ministers press for a role in the United States-led Ukraine talks

G7 foreign ministers are meeting in Paris on Monday and Tuesday as Europe presses for a role in United States efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine. Their gathering coincides with talks between Moscow and Kyiv scheduled to begin in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, while ministers are also expected to discuss Iran. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said France would join the Abu Dhabi talks: “Europeans will be represented and France will participate in these talks,” he told RTL radio. Barrot said he did not know the details of United States plans for a possible agreement. United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio is expected to attend both days of the Paris meeting.

Subjective
Reuters, via EuropeSays — Europeans will join the Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, the French foreign minister says

PARIS, November 8: Europeans will participate in talks on Ukraine in Abu Dhabi this week, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on Sunday, as President Donald Trump said he believed the war would end soon. United States envoy Steve Witkoff said Washington would bring together delegations from Ukraine and Russia on November 10 and 11 to discuss ending Moscow’s war against Ukraine, post-war security pacts and de-escalation. “The Europeans will be well represented. France will be in Abu Dhabi to take part,” Barrot told RTL radio in an interview.

Subjective
WHRO — Europe to join the United States-brokered Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi

European officials will turn up for the United States-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in the United Arab Emirates this week, France’s foreign minister said Sunday, days after the Kremlin had insisted there could be no role for European powers at the meeting. “France will be there and will ensure that Europe’s voice is heard,” Jean-Noël Barrot told French radio. He did not say who would represent Paris, or whether French or other European officials would take part directly in negotiations, or simply observe. The meetings, set for Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, had previously been presented as a three-way session between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv, and will be the fourth round brokered by the Trump administration and the first since Geneva in February.

Subjective
All Israel News — Liberman announces support for a government with an ultra-Orthodox party, in the Eisenkot bloc

The Change Bloc, led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, is reportedly considering forming a coalition with the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism, despite months of campaigning for universal military service. Yisrael Beiteinu chairman Avigdor Liberman publicly announced his support for the move on Friday, soon receiving backing from The Democrats and United Torah Judaism. For the bloc to reach the necessary 61-seat majority, it would need to add the seats of both United Torah Judaism, 7, and Shas, 6, to its own 48 seats. Declaring that he is prepared for “painful compromises,” Liberman said his three main conditions were ending the Netanyahu era, preventing new elections, and ruling out a minority government that relies on the abstention of the Arab parties, the Joint List and Ra’am.

Subjective
ZarkNews — the death toll in the Komyshuvakha aid-center strike rises to 55 as a drone hits rescue crews

Ukrainian authorities said on Sunday that at least 55 people were killed in the November 2 bombing of Komyshuvakha, and that a Russian drone struck rescue crews working at the site on Sunday, damaging equipment; no rescuer was injured. The confirmed death toll from the bombing of a school used as a humanitarian aid distribution point has risen to 55, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said, and the search of the rubble is still going on. Mykhailo Semikin, the acting head of the Zaporizhzhia regional military administration, said 45 people were still listed as missing on Sunday afternoon. Russia’s Defense Ministry offered a different account, saying its forces had targeted Ukrainian military units in areas around Komyshuvakha and two other settlements.

Subjective
Malay Mail, via Bangsar — two trains collide south of Cairo, killing seven

AL AYYAT, November 9: two trains collided south of the Egyptian capital yesterday, derailing several carriages, killing seven people and injuring more than 100 others, according to the authorities. Egypt’s railway authority said a train travelling from Giza to Fayoum crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to the city of Aswan. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said he was following the accident “with great concern” and had directed authorities to conduct an urgent investigation to “hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent.” Authorities said they had launched an investigation into the cause of the crash, which occurred in Giza’s Al-Ayyat area, the site of Egypt’s worst-ever rail disaster.

Subjective
AsiaOne — the Egypt train crash leaves seven dead and 112 injured

An Egypt train crash killed at least seven people and injured 112 others on Sunday. Two passenger trains collided about 76 kilometres south of Cairo; Egypt’s health ministry confirmed the casualties. The accident occurred near Al-Ayyat village in Giza Governorate; one train was traveling from Giza to Fayoum. Officials have not yet explained what caused the crash. The collision disrupted services on the Cairo–Upper Egypt railway line. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi ordered a swift investigation, and the public prosecutor confirmed investigations were underway, examining the technical reasons behind the collision.

Subjective
LankaNewz — the Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed missiles aimed at Riyadh as the Houthis claim Aramco strikes

The Saudi-led coalition says its air defences destroyed three ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles launched by Yemen’s Houthis on Sunday, two of them aimed at the capital Riyadh, as the group claimed a fresh round of attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure. Coalition spokesperson Major-General Turki al-Maliki said the three ballistic missiles were destroyed, with two launched towards Riyadh, and the coalition also intercepted and destroyed two cruise missiles over Riyadh and the southern region and a further ballistic missile fired towards the Eastern Province. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had carried out six operations targeting Aramco oil facilities, Riyadh airport and Saudi military positions. An update on November 9 reports video footage verified by BBC Verify showing the Riyadh building sustained considerably more serious damage than the “minor damage” the Saudi energy ministry described: one floor was severely damaged in what appears to have been a missile or drone strike, and window glass was broken across several floors.

Subjective
Addis Standard — the daily brief: the Houthis claim a wave of missile and drone attacks on Riyadh

Yemen’s Houthi group claimed it launched a series of missile and drone attacks targeting Saudi Arabia on Sunday, November 8, including King Khalid International Airport, Aramco facilities and other strategic sites in Riyadh and the kingdom’s oil-rich Eastern Province. The group’s military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said the operations involved ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones targeting multiple locations, including Aramco installations in Khurais and Abqaiq, a pumping station in Dawadmi, and Saudi military positions in the kingdom’s southern regions, described as retaliation for recent Saudi airstrikes in Yemen. Saudi officials said air defence systems intercepted and destroyed several incoming projectiles, including two ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles heading towards Riyadh. The Energy Ministry said falling debris from an intercepted attack struck an administrative building belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh, causing minor damage but no casualties. The attacks followed reported Saudi airstrikes near al-Shariya village outside Sanaa, which Houthi authorities said killed at least 33 people, mostly women and children, with dozens more wounded.

Subjective
Jamoke News — Alaska and Mississippi Senate races 2026: the latest count and what happens next

As of November 7, two United States Senate races from the November 3 midterms were still uncalled: Alaska, where Democrat Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, and Mississippi, where Democrat Scott Colom narrowly leads Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. In Alaska, Peltola led Sullivan 102,962 to 102,325, 48.0 percent to 47.7 percent, in unofficial first-choice results last posted November 4; roughly 60,000 early and absentee ballots were still uncounted, with the next count due November 9 or 10, and ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled for November 18. In Mississippi, Colom led Hyde-Smith by 2,574 votes, 467,930 to 465,356, or 49.1 percent to 48.8 percent, with an estimated 96.9 percent of votes counted as of Friday, November 6; the secretary of state estimated 12,000 to 20,000 affidavit ballots were still uncounted.

Subjective
Al Jazeera — what is delaying the United States Senate election results in Mississippi and Alaska

Two United States Senate races remain undecided. In Mississippi, the contest between incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith and her Democratic challenger, Scott Colom, remains too close to call, with both candidates holding about 49 percent of the vote according to the Associated Press; 96 percent of the ballots have been counted so far. Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson counted roughly 3,600 mail-in ballots still to be tallied, along with an unknown number of affidavit ballots, and wrote that counties have 10 days from the date of the election to submit their certified results, which is November 13; Mississippi is the only state with no formal provision that would automatically authorise a recount. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola leads incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan by 637 votes as of Wednesday night according to the Associated Press, nearly a quarter of the votes remain uncounted, and ranked-choice results will not be published until November 18.

Subjective
Reuters, via The Business Standard — how a digital bank’s collapse toppled Paraguay’s president

For years, Paraguay’s digital bank, ueno, attracted roughly half the country’s population to open accounts and gave many people the opportunity to hold a bank account for the first time. But over just five days this week, the bank collapsed, freezing the savings of nearly 3 million customers in a country of 6.5 million people and triggering the country’s deepest political crisis in more than a decade. On Friday evening, President Santiago Peña was impeached after attempting to resign, and his vice-president, Pedro Alliana, was sworn in as his replacement. Authorities quickly arrested Peña; prosecutors charged him on Saturday with breach of trust and administration for personal gain, and a judge ordered him held in pre-trial detention at a military facility. Peña has denied wrongdoing, and his attorney, Ricardo Preda, told journalists that he was pleading not guilty. The central bank said on Saturday that the equivalent of $160 million had since been paid out to nearly 1.2 million savers under the state deposit guarantee scheme.

Subjective
AsiaToday — Peña’s pretrial detention ordered in the Ueno Bank probe

A Paraguayan judge on Saturday ordered former President Santiago Peña to remain in custody before trial, holding him at a military facility as prosecutors examine his links to the failed digital lender Ueno. Judge Humberto Otazú said the measure was needed to make sure Peña stayed in the country while the case moved forward. The ruling came one day after Congress removed Peña from office over the bank’s collapse, which froze the accounts of nearly three million customers. Prosecutors charged Peña with breach of trust and administration for personal gain. Judge Otazú also ordered former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo held in pretrial detention. Prosecutors have charged 27 people in total in connection with the Ueno case, and President Alliana has begun naming a new cabinet.

Subjective
NewsCubby — the Japan earthquake injures at least 22; more shaking is possible

The Associated Press reported at least 22 injuries from Sunday’s earthquake beneath western Shizuoka, while an updated Jiji Press account gave 21. Aichi’s second official report, with a 3:30 p.m. Sunday cutoff, recorded 19 injured within the prefecture, including one serious injury. The Japan Meteorological Agency’s event bulletin places the source beneath western Shizuoka, within the Philippine Sea plate; the United States Geological Survey identifies its reviewed location as 10 kilometres northwest of Hamakita, with an origin time of 16:04:35 UTC on November 7, which is 1:04 a.m. Sunday in Japan. The agencies’ magnitude estimates, 5.7 and 5.5, are separate estimates for the same earthquake. The agency’s advice calls for attention to further strong shaking for about a week, particularly during the first two or three days.

Subjective
Reuters — oil falls as Trump says new Iran attacks are unlikely

PERTH, November 9: oil prices fell at Monday’s open after President Donald Trump said he was highly unlikely to order new Iran attacks while talks to end the conflict make progress, despite both nations’ reports of attacks on ships in or near the Strait of Hormuz. Brent was down 84 cents, or 0.85 percent, to $97.48 a barrel by 0138 GMT, while West Texas Intermediate fell 32 cents, or 0.35 percent, to $90.51 a barrel. The fall reversed minor gains made on Friday’s settlement as the market assessed the possibility of further United States strikes on Iran, although Brent fell 17 percent last week, the steepest weekly drop since the start of the COVID pandemic on LSEG data dating back to 1988. “It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump told CNN in a phone interview. “The answer is, highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary.”

Subjective
Reuters, via BusinessToday — Asian stocks steady as Middle East jitters recede

Asian markets and United States equity futures made a steady start on Monday, November 9, wobbling into positive territory after a wild week where doubts about demand for computer chips sent tech-heavy markets in Asia into some of their steepest falls in years. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan rose 0.8 percent after sliding 4.6 percent last week. Japan’s Nikkei index added 2.5 percent while Korean shares made small gains. Taiwan’s benchmark rose about 2.5 percent after notching its heaviest weekly drop for two decades last week, when fears about AI profitability and infrastructure demand turned into a rout following wins by Democrats at the United States midterm polls.

Subjective
CoinEdition — Asia market recap: Asian stocks recover from the midterm-driven tech rout while the Nvidia inquiry weighs on sentiment

Asian equities rose on Monday as a bounce on Wall Street helped the region recover part of last week’s heavy losses, although an inquiry at Nvidia kept investors wary. Japan’s Nikkei 225 climbed 3.45 percent and the broader Topix opened 2.82 percent higher. Taiwan’s Taiex jumped 5.33 percent, South Korea’s Kospi added 1.68 percent, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng edged up 0.19 percent, and MSCI’s index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan gained 0.8 percent, recovering part of last week’s 4.6 percent drop. The rebound follows a Friday in which the Kospi tumbled about 9 percent, the Nikkei lost roughly 6 percent and the Hang Seng fell more than 1 percent. Nvidia’s board launched an independent probe into its chief executive, the account reports.
items.summary: The overnight file for Monday, November 9, 2026: Małopolska police said the 24-year-old Kraków suspect died early Monday in hospital as Poland began its second day of national mourning and prosecutors pursued the terrorism investigation without the man who could have answered it, Dana Gas said it was assessing damage at Khor Mor after dousing the fire with no staff injured, Qatar's prime minister was scheduled at noon in the Oval Office in the Iran mediation while Tehran waited for an answer to its two-day proposal, and Asian markets bought back part of Friday's rout while the Senate count stayed frozen. Collected at 0400.

items.title: A Fourth Tanker Is Claimed in Hormuz, Khor Mor Goes Dark, and the Count Still Waits
items.content_html:
The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

A Fourth Tanker Is Claimed in Hormuz, Khor Mor Goes Dark, and the Count Still Waits

The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: Sunday settled the toll at Al-Ayyat at seven dead, settled the hurt in central Japan at 22 in the prefectures’ own division, named the six of the Kraków square and reopened it, and put a price on Monday—oil down at the open. It left open everything with a deadline: a fourth tanker claimed in Hormuz and none confirmed, a gas field dark in Iraqi Kurdistan with no one claiming the drone, a mandate in Jerusalem exercised in conditions and not yet in a coalition, a Senate count frozen since Friday, and the Abu Dhabi table, enlarged on Sunday, still two days from sitting.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Monday, November 9, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 22, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Sunday, and in Sunday’s earlier editions, Nos. 19 and 21, and its special reports. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Sunday Settled, What It Left Open

Sunday settled counts, names and a price, and it left causes, claims and coalitions open, and the desk files the day in that order. At Al-Ayyat the dead settled at seven in every later account, and the injured reached their last Sunday figure late in the day, when the chief prosecutor’s office put them at at least 125, in the updated running account filed below; no authority has stated a cause. In Kraków the six killed in the Main Market Square stand named by age and nationality, the square reopened late Sunday, and the joining of the square to the three dead at the suspect’s home stands at a prosecutor’s spokesman’s “highly likely,” in Reuters’ evening account filed below. In the Strait of Hormuz the claims grew after the evening edition closed: an Iranian Navy statement raised the day’s tally of tankers said to have struck mines to four, in the Navy’s account filed below, and no tanker fire of Sunday has been confirmed by a party that did not claim it. In Iraq a drone halted the Khor Mor gas field and took 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts off the Kurdistan grid, with no casualties in the first assessment and no claim of responsibility. In Jerusalem Mr. Eisenkot’s mandate produced four conditions and the week’s meetings, and no coalition. In the United States the Senate count posted nothing new for a second day. And at Monday’s open in Perth, oil fell, in Reuters’ market file filed below. Monday holds the handovers and the meetings; Tuesday holds the talks and the deadlines. That is the day whole, as it stands at midnight.

Al-Ayyat at Midnight: Seven Dead, 125 Injured in the Late Count, and No Cause

The railway file closed Sunday with its numbers at their highest and its central question unanswered. The Health Ministry’s staircase ran four dead and 88 injured, then seven dead and 112 injured, and late Sunday the chief prosecutor’s office put the injured at at least 125, with more than 70 of them discharged after treatment, in the Associated Press account filed below. Prosecutors who inspected the site said the Giza-to-Fayoum train, No. 134, hit the last carriage of the Cairo-to-Aswan train, No. 2010, which was stationary on the same track between Kafr Ammar and Raqqa stations; a conductor was among the dead, and the dead have not been named. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi ordered a prompt investigation and accountability for anyone found negligent. No cause has been stated by the railway authority, the prosecutors or the ministry. Settled: the place, the two trains, the seven dead. Open: the 125 against the 112 and 114 also printed under official names during the day, and the cause, which the investigation now owns.

Kraków at Midnight: The Square Reopened, the Six Named, the Joining Still a Spokesman’s Word

Poland’s second day of mourning is Monday, and Sunday ended with the case in its legal shape and its human shape both on the record. The six of the square are counted by age and nationality: a 51-year-old Austrian woman, a 32-year-old British man, three Polish women aged 47, 53 and 61, and a Polish man of about 50. Prosecutors have opened the investigation as a terrorist offence covering two acts, the six murders in the square and the three murders at the home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, and are preparing six murder charges that could rise to nine. The spokesman Daniel Prokopowicz said it was “highly likely” the same person carried out both; highly likely remains an assessment, not a finding, and the suspect, in critical condition and not yet formally arrested or questioned, has answered nothing. The wounded stand at 16 in Reuters’ evening count, including the two officers and the gunman, and at 15 in other accounts; the three at home stand at 52, 51 and 21 in the evening brief and at 53, 52 and 20 in the prosecutors’ account, and the desk prints both triangles. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński declined on Sunday to withdraw his Saturday reading of the attacker’s views, and the opposition’s demand that he produce its basis stands unanswered. The square reopened late Sunday. National mourning runs through Monday.

Hormuz at Midnight: A Fourth Tanker Claimed, One Tentative Name, and Qeshm Unsettled

The strait’s tally grew by one after the evening edition closed, and its confirmation count did not grow at all. The Iranian Navy said a further tanker struck a mine in the eastern strait before noon on Sunday, its identification systems off in a prohibited area, and called it the fourth tanker to hit mines on Sunday; the Guards’ Navy’s own statement of the day counts three, exploded and on fire along an unauthorized route. The two statements are both Iranian, they differ by one ship, and the desk prints both. Against the claims stand the day’s firmer items, none joined to the tally by any authority: the Emirates’ rescue of 22 crew from a burning cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman, and the American disabling of the M/V Huda on Saturday, explained by Central Command. One name has been offered for one ship, and it is offered as tentative: open-source analysts identify the tanker that caught fire off Khasab, its crew evacuated and firefighting tugs alongside, as the Navig8 Messi, in the maritime account filed below. No owner, flag authority or coast guard has confirmed that identification. On Qeshm the record also disagrees with itself: the Tasnim agency reported two missiles struck the island, Iranian state television said officials had not confirmed any missile strikes and suggested the explosions might be related to Iranian military activity, and Reuters, in its Sunday file filed below, said it was not able to confirm any of the reported strikes. Three projectiles reported launched from Sirik toward vessels stand likewise unconfirmed, with no hit established.

Khor Mor at Midnight: 2,800 Megawatts Gone, and No Claim

The evening’s one confirmed interruption became, by midnight, the region’s largest measured fact. A single drone hit a liquefied petroleum gas storage tank at the Khor Mor gas field in Sulaymaniyah province on Sunday night; production halted, the fire was still raging in the first reports, and crews were ordered into shelters. The Kurdistan electricity ministry put the generation lost at 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts, gas supply was suspended to power plants in Erbil, Sulaimaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal and Duhok, and accounts put more than 70 percent of the region without power, with hospitals and water stations given priority and hydroelectric stations called on. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said an initial assessment found no casualties, and Baghdad directed a joint investigative committee, in the accounts filed below. The region’s ministries called the attack a terrorist attack in a joint statement. No group has claimed it, one reporter at the scene could not say whether the projectile was a drone or a rocket, and a security source’s claim about its launch place is unconfirmed. Settled: the field is stopped and the megawatts are counted. Open: the hand, the damage, and the restart.

Riyadh and Sanaa at Midnight: The Launchers Destroyed, the Toll Standing at 33

The Saudi–Yemen ledger did not move in its figures on Sunday night, and its two sides stand as far apart at midnight as at noon. The coalition said it destroyed two ballistic-missile launchers in Saada that it said were used in Sunday’s attack on Riyadh, after intercepting three ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles. The Energy Ministry’s account of the Aramco Tower stands: damage from falling debris, no casualties. The Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree’s claims stand against it: the financial district and King Khalid International Airport targeted, in operations the movement counts at four in one account and six in another, and a tally of coalition attacks over 24 hours that stands at 91 in one file and 105 in another. The Sanaa figure did not move: at least 33 killed, among them eight women and thirteen children, and 39 wounded, in the Houthi-run health ministry’s count for Saturday’s strikes on homes at al-Shariyah, east of the capital, which Saudi Arabia’s Center for International Communication said it was investigating. Every figure in this paragraph has its owner attached; none has been verified by a party that did not issue it.

Komyshuvakha at Midnight: 55 Dead, and the Missing at 45 or About 50

Ukraine’s file closed Sunday on a disagreement of five names. The toll of Monday’s bombing of the former school and the shelter at Komyshuvakha stands at at least 55 dead in every Sunday account, and Sunday’s drone strike on the rescue crews there injured no one and damaged specialized equipment, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said. The missing do not agree: the military intelligence agency HUR lists around 50 people still missing, and the acting head of the regional military administration, Mykhailo Semikin, put the figure at 45 on Sunday afternoon, in the Associated Press account filed below. Many bodies recovered have not been identified and DNA analysis continues. HUR said Saturday it had identified some of the Russian service members it says took part in the first strike; Russia’s differing account of its operations around Komyshuvakha stands in the earlier files, and no Russian statement on Sunday’s drone strike was taken in. The accounts of both attacks rest on Ukrainian officials and the Associated Press’s reporting; no party that did not issue them has verified the toll.

Jerusalem at Midnight: Four Conditions Published, the Meetings Set, No Coalition

The mandate’s first day ended where it began: 48 seats in hand, 61 required, 28 days running. Mr. Eisenkot’s four conditions for joining his government stand as he published them: acceptance of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, the values of the Declaration of Independence upheld, universal military, national or civilian service supported, and Hamas recognised as a terrorist organisation. His challenge to Likud and Religious Zionism, to back a government under him if they stand by their calls for unity, drew no answer taken in on Sunday. The two agencies’ magnitudes, 5.7 and 5.5, are separate estimates for the same earthquake.

Subjective
Reuters — oil falls on the open as Trump says fresh Iran attacks are ‘unlikely’

PERTH, Nov 9: oil prices fell at Monday’s open after President Donald Trump said he was highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict progress, even as both countries reported that shipping had been hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz. Brent was down 64 cents, or 0.64 percent, to $97.67 a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate fell 35 cents, or 0.40 percent, to $90.51; Brent briefly fell over $1 a barrel. The president had hinted at renewing major attacks on Iran after last week’s midterm elections, but there has been no sign of a large-scale American military operation. Iran has said it would respond by striking American and Israeli targets.

At Al-Ayyat the dead settled at seven and the chief prosecutor's late count put the injured at 125, with no cause stated. In Kraków the six of the square were named by age and nationality, the square reopened, and the joining of the square to the house remained a spokesman's 'highly likely.' In Hormuz an Iranian Navy statement raised the day's claimed tanker fires to four, a maritime account tentatively named one vessel, and Reuters could confirm none of them; a drone halted Iraq's Khor Mor gas field and took 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts off the Kurdistan grid, with no claim of responsibility. Gadi Eisenkot published four conditions and no coalition exists; the Senate count stayed frozen at Friday's figures, Mississippi at 2,574 votes and Alaska at 637; and oil fell at Monday's open after the president said fresh attacks on Iran were highly unlikely while talks progress.
