Six people killed and sixteen injured after a gunman opened fire from a car in Kraków’s historic centre on Saturday, November 7; police shot and detained the suspect, who authorities say acted alone; an earlier version of the account is corrected to record that a British citizen was among the six killed and five of the wounded were foreign nationals, including a Portuguese woman; the number injured was initially given as fifteen and later reported as sixteen, with some reporting counting the wounded suspect among those hurt; reports give the suspect’s age as 24 in police accounts and 25 in later international reports; and Kraków’s mayor declared city mourning from Sunday, November 8 through Wednesday, November 11, with the president announcing national mourning for November 8 and 9.

Subjective
Reuters, via SRN News — a judge orders Paraguay’s ex-president Peña held before trial

Asunción, November 7: a judge ordered former President Santiago Peña held in pretrial detention at a military facility while prosecutors investigate his ties to Ueno, Judge Humberto Otazú saying detention was necessary to ensure he remained in the country; former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo was ordered to pretrial detention in a holding center; Mr. Peña’s attorney said he is pleading not guilty and predicted the investigation will end in dismissal; prosecutors allege he influenced agencies and state entities to keep public money at Ueno despite his financial ties, having been a shareholder in its holding company until March 2025; the two charges could carry up to ten years each; and the central bank said $160 million had been paid to nearly 1.2 million savers under the deposit guarantee.

Subjective
Reuters, via Duke FM — prosecutors charge ex-President Peña, seek pretrial detention

Asunción, November 7: prosecutors charged former President Santiago Peña with breach of trust and administration for personal gain and asked a court to jail him pending trial, a day after his impeachment over the collapse of Ueno; former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo was charged with breach of trust, producing false public documents, and administration for personal gain, with his detention also sought; prosecutors allege Peña used his position to keep large amounts of public money deposited at Ueno despite his financial ties; he has denied wrongdoing and called the bank’s problems a regulatory matter; and the central bank said $160 million had been paid to nearly 1.2 million savers.

Subjective
AnewZ — Paraguay’s ex-President Peña charged over the Ueno Bank collapse

November 7: prosecutors charged former President Peña and former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo Spalding and asked a court to hold both in pretrial detention; both men declined to say anything at the hearing; prosecutors also asked for their assets to be frozen and for six months to formulate the final case; Mr. Peña’s lawyer rejected pretrial detention as unjustified; a judge in a separate case has ordered six former Ueno directors held in pretrial detention; prosecutors have charged twenty-seven people in total; and authorities have seized assets linked to Ueno’s controlling shareholder.

Subjective
Valcore News — Peña removed and detained as Alliana becomes president

Former President Peña arrived at the Public Prosecutor’s Office at about 11:15 a.m. Saturday to be questioned over the collapse of Ueno Bank, a day after the Senate removed him; prosecutors charged him with breach of trust, as an instigator, and administration for personal benefit, charged Carvallo as well, and asked a court to hold both men and freeze their assets, the judge not yet having ruled at that account’s filing; Peña spent Friday night at the Presidential Escort Regiment after crowds gathered at his home; the Senate voted 44 to nil, with one member absent, to remove him; Vice President Pedro Alliana has been sworn in; and the charges are stated as charges, not findings, with Peña rejecting the accusations.

Subjective
Reuters, via SRN News — explosions heard in areas in southern Iran

Cairo, November 7: explosions were heard on Saturday evening in several areas in southern Iran, including on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, state television reported; state TV suggested the explosions might be linked to Iranian military activities in the waterway; officials have not confirmed any missile strikes, and Tasnim cited a source as saying the Qeshm explosions were not related to missile strikes; the Revolutionary Guards Navy said early on Sunday that two oil tankers were on fire after hitting mines as they attempted to pass through an unauthorized route in the strait; and Tasnim had said earlier on Saturday that two missiles struck Qeshm Island, with no official information on possible damage.

Subjective
Associated Press, via Military.com — the military says it fired on a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman

Published November 7 at 9:20 p.m. EST: Central Command said late Saturday it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship after it ignored multiple warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port; the disclosure follows at least two instances in which the command did not announce strikes it had taken in the region; state media also reported explosions on Qeshm Island and several explosions in the port of Jask on Saturday evening, the cause not immediately clear; the Iranian military said late Saturday that two tankers had hit mines in the Hormuz area and caught fire, without identifying their flags or destinations; and the president said Friday the military had carried out new limited strikes against an Iranian air defense system, which he described as minor.

Subjective
Israel.com — blasts across Iran’s Hormuz coast, casualties reported at Jask, the American role unconfirmed

November 7, updated 11:08 p.m. Israel time: state television widened the list of places where blasts were heard to Qeshm, Jask, Sirik, and Bandar Abbas, all close to the Strait of Hormuz; a correspondent reported people in Iran speaking of casualties resulting from strikes on the port of Jask, without a number, and a senior Iranian official threatening retaliation at the same time; the wire account describes the cause as unclear while the other refers to strikes at Jask; neither report includes a statement from the American military or government about Jask or Qeshm; and the claim of an American strike on an anti-ship missile launcher rests on unofficial channels as relayed by outlets.

Subjective
Virginia Times Now — Iran missile range restriction lifted, the Guards say

Tehran: the Revolutionary Guards said Saturday the restriction on the range of the country’s missiles has been lifted, spokesman Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi saying Iran would demonstrate its ability to respond to threats on the battlefield; the announcement was made at a press conference marking Aerospace Week; the earlier policy was a deliberate limit of 2,000 kilometres; the remarks followed the supreme leader’s warning that threats should receive an immediate response without geographical limits and an order to update target lists covering American and Israeli assets; the spokesman cautioned the statement was not itself proof of a new capability; and the coverage contained no evidence Iran has tested or fielded a missile beyond the former limit.

Subjective
Signal Post News — Iran lifts its missile range limit, and says it will prove the new reach in practice

Tehran, November 7: the Guards confirmed the self-imposed 2,000-kilometre ceiling on ballistic missile ranges is ended, retiring a nine-year-old reassurance; the spokesman answered that the restriction “has been lifted for us” and added that the new reach has to be demonstrated in practice, not merely announced; the remarks followed the supreme leader’s order of a response to any threat without geographical limits and a review of target lists covering American and Israeli assets; there is no evidence Iran possesses or has demonstrated an operational missile exceeding the former limit, its longest declared systems led by the Khorramshahr-4; and the announcement came a day after American strikes on an Iranian air-defence system amid stalled diplomacy.

Subjective
Jamaica Inquirer — the United States launches a task force to disrupt Iran’s land-based supply routes

Central Command announced on Saturday it had established a task force to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials, expanding its naval blockade of Iranian ports; Task Force Iron Gate will reinforce the blockade’s success, Admiral Brad Cooper said; based in Tampa, Florida, the task force will coordinate with other agencies on preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea; and a former deputy assistant defence secretary described its role as finding where weapons systems are coming in, how they could be cut off, and how Iran is transporting its energy.

Subjective
JBiz News — Erdoğan says he called Trump, reaffirmed Turkish support for American-Iranian diplomacy

Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan told President Trump by phone that Ankara would continue its peace efforts and that tensions between Iran and the United States should be resolved through diplomacy, Erdoğan’s office said on Saturday; Erdoğan also told Trump Turkey would continue to contribute to efforts to end the war in Ukraine and that contacts with both Kyiv and Moscow should be intensified, according to the readout from his office; and the item is filed as a developing story, with no agreement announced in it.

Subjective
Bosphorus News — Eastern Mediterranean strategic brief, November 7

Erdoğan and Trump spoke by telephone on November 7; Erdoğan urged a diplomatic settlement of the American-Iranian confrontation and said Ankara was prepared to support peace efforts, and the call also covered bilateral relations, the Russia-Ukraine war, and contacts with Kyiv and Moscow; the Turkish readout did not identify the American strike near Qeshm Island as a separate agenda item or announce a new mediation role for Türkiye; the Guards’ spokesman said Iran had lifted its missile-range restriction, naming no new ceiling and supplying no test results or deployment details; Qatar’s media office rejected reports that its prime minister had declared the negotiations a failure, saying the two sides were still seeking an agreement; and no date or accepted terms for talks had been announced by the cutoff.

Subjective
Nation Path India — Russia strikes Kyiv ahead of American-mediated Abu Dhabi peace talks

Russia launched ballistic missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and surrounding regions on November 7, damaging residential buildings, energy facilities, and a major bridge, days before negotiations in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 involving Russia, Ukraine, and the United States; Kyiv’s mayor said missile debris struck a five-storey apartment building and another residential building was damaged; Russia’s delegation will be led by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky; Ukraine’s team will be led by Rustem Umerov, with Presidential Office chief Kyrylo Budanov also participating; the United States is expected to be represented by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner; and no comprehensive peace agreement has been reached.

Subjective
DevDiscourse, carrying Reuters — Russia pounds power facilities around Kyiv, damages a major bridge

Russian forces hammered energy infrastructure around Kyiv with missiles and drones overnight, straining power supply and heating as temperatures headed towards zero, officials said Saturday, three days before Russia and Ukraine take part in American-brokered talks; explosions rocked Kyiv as waves of ballistic missiles hit and damaged the Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River, the mayor said; Russia’s delegation for the first trilateral talks since February will include senior military officials and diplomats including Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov, the Kremlin spokesman told Interfax; the delegation, headed by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, will also include Yuri Zhigarlovsky, Mikhail Galuzin, and military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov.

Subjective
EuropeSays — Russia strikes Kyiv’s energy infrastructure and the Northern Bridge ahead of the Abu Dhabi talks

Kyiv faced widespread damage on November 7 after Russia launched 172 attack drones and 36 ballistic missiles at the capital and other regions, striking energy infrastructure, residential housing, and a major bridge over the Dnipro; Russia’s defence ministry confirmed the strike, claiming the bridge was used to transport weapons and military equipment; Ukraine’s president said Russia had launched the 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in a Telegram post with photographs of the damage; Russia’s defence ministry also claimed its air defences shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight, a figure not independently verified; Russia’s delegation will include Medinsky, Ryabkov, Galuzin, Kostyukov, and Zhigarlovsky; and Ukraine’s delegation will be led by Rustem Umerov and include Budanov, Arakhamia, Lytvyn, and Kyslytsia.

Subjective
USA Today — Mississippi and Alaska Senate races still undecided as legal fights loom

Nearly every major race of the midterms has been called, but not Mississippi and Alaska, where the ballots that will decide two Senate seats are still being sorted, scrutinized, and increasingly litigated; neither will change who controls the chamber, Democrats having claimed the Senate on election night with 54 seats to Republicans’ 44 in the called races; in Mississippi, Scott Colom leads Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by some 2,500 votes according to the Associated Press, which has not called the race, with thousands of affidavit ballots in play and Republicans estimating roughly 20,000 ballots outstanding and voters able to resolve problems through November 10; in Alaska, Mary Peltola leads Senator Dan Sullivan by 637 votes with roughly three-quarters of ballots counted, the Justice Department’s suit was dismissed before the voting, the Peltola campaign opened its own legal front on November 6, and absentee ballots can arrive through November 18, the day of the ranked-choice tabulation.

Subjective
Election Central — Alaska and Mississippi Senate race update: they are still counting votes

Four days after Election Day, two Senate races remain unresolved and both are remarkably close, and neither can change which party runs the chamber, Democrats having secured at least 54 seats; in Mississippi, Scott Colom holds a lead of roughly 2,500 votes, at about 49.1 percent to 48.8 percent, with all Election Day precincts reported but thousands of absentee and affidavit ballots still being processed, the wire estimating Friday afternoon that roughly 30,000 ballots could still be outstanding, mail ballots arriving through November 10, and counties certifying by November 13; in Alaska, Mary Peltola leads Dan Sullivan by only 637 votes, at 48.2 percent to 47.9 percent, with roughly 74 percent of the expected vote reported, the remaining vote including absentee, remote, and overseas ballots, and a ranked-choice tabulation targeted for November 18 if no candidate reaches a majority.

Subjective
Al Jazeera — what is delaying the Senate election results in Mississippi and Alaska

An explainer of the two undecided races: in Mississippi, mail and affidavit ballots are still being processed under a ten-day window, counties certify by November 13, and the secretary of state counted roughly 3,600 mail ballots outstanding in his Wednesday statement beside an unknown number of affidavit ballots; in Alaska, ranked-choice tabulation is not published until November 18, fifteen days after the election, and nearly a quarter of the vote remains uncounted; as it stands, the Democrats will usher in the 120th Congress on January 3 with a majority of at least 54 seats.

Subjective
Focal News — the Boebert campaign cries foul as Laubacher’s lead narrows in Colorado’s 4th

Representative Lauren Boebert trails the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, by 3,172 votes as of 6 p.m. Friday, a margin of 0.83 percentage points, with more than 97 percent of the vote counted and the race still too close to call; her campaign lawyer said the campaign is investigating unusual voting patterns and expects a recount, though Colorado law requires an automatic recount only at a margin of 0.5 percent or less of the leading candidate’s total—about 923 votes at Friday’s figures, less than one-third of the current gap; a campaign fundraising email misstated the recount law; Ms. Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, led by more than 7,000 votes earlier in the count; and her campaign has not responded publicly to the allegations.

Subjective
Fadd — Berkshire Hathaway nearly doubles buybacks to $9.6 billion as earnings fall

Berkshire Hathaway released its third-quarter results on Saturday, November 7: it spent about $9.6 billion buying its own shares, more than twice the second quarter’s $4.5 billion, bringing 2026 repurchases to about $14.4 billion, and bought roughly another $2 billion in the first four weeks of the fourth quarter; operating earnings came to $12.705 billion, down 5.8 percent from $13.485 billion a year earlier; overall earnings fell 28 percent to $22.112 billion; insurance underwriting profit fell 43 percent to $1.352 billion and insurance investment income fell 14 percent; and cash and equivalents rose 3 percent to $377.435 billion from $365.514 billion at the end of the second quarter.

Subjective
Shanti — Diwali, the Indian festival of lights and its traditions

Diwali, from the Sanskrit for row of lights, is the biggest festival of the Hindu calendar; its date follows the lunar calendar and falls on the new moon of the month of Kartik, the darkest night of the year; in 2026 the main day falls on Sunday, November 8, and the festival lasts five days, from Friday, November 6 to Tuesday, November 10 in that account’s span; the high point is Lakshmi Puja after dark on the main day, honouring Lakshmi and Ganesha, with dozens of lamps lit, incense, sweets shared, and gifts exchanged; and the account offers the festival to a European reader as a November evening of light against the early dark.
items.summary: The midnight file for Sunday, November 8, 2026: police found three more bodies at the Kraków suspect's home, a judge in Asunción ordered former President Santiago Peña and former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo held before trial, explosions were heard across Iran's Hormuz coast and two tankers were reported on fire after hitting mines while American forces disabled a vessel that tried to breach the blockade, and no Senate race was called for a fourth day. Collected at 0000.

items.title: Six Dead in Kraków, Charges in Asunción, and Kyiv Struck Three Days Before the Talks
items.content_html:
The Evening File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Six Dead in Kraków, Charges in Asunción, and Kyiv Struck Three Days Before the Talks

The day’s developments whole at 1800: a gunman fired from a car into Kraków’s Main Market Square and killed six people before police shot and arrested him; prosecutors in Asunción charged the removed president and the former central bank chief and asked a court to jail both pending trial, while $160 million went out to nearly 1.2 million savers; Iran’s Guards lifted the self-imposed limit on missile ranges while Washington and Doha both said the talks had made progress; Russian missiles struck Kyiv three days before the Abu Dhabi talks, and Moscow named its delegation; the first considered responses to the Miller appointment set the terms of the next two years in Washington; and no Senate race was called for a fourth day.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Saturday, November 7, 2026. This edition completes the day continued in Edition No. 14, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400, and Edition No. 15, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the evening figures differ from the midday figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Evening in Brief

Saturday produced one atrocity, one indictment, and three statements of position, and closed nothing the week left open. In Kraków, at about 3 p.m. local time, a man drove into the Main Market Square and fired at random from his car, killing six people—four women and two men—and wounding at least fifteen, two of them police officers, before officers shot and arrested him three minutes after the first report, in the interior minister’s account; the minister said in his evening briefing that everything points to the shooter having been influenced by far-right ideology, a matter he said will be investigated, and the president will declare national mourning for November 8 and 9. In Asunción, prosecutors charged former President Santiago Peña with breach of trust and administration for personal gain and former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo with those charges and producing false public documents, asked a court to hold both men in pretrial detention and freeze their assets, and the central bank reported $160 million paid out to nearly 1.2 million Ueno savers under the deposit guarantee. In Tehran, the Revolutionary Guards’ spokesman said the self-imposed limit of 2,000 kilometres on ballistic missile ranges “has been lifted for us,” following the supreme leader’s order that threats be answered without geographical limits; no file on the shelf shows an Iranian missile demonstrated beyond the old limit. In Washington, the responses to Friday’s appointment of Stephen Miller as chief of staff, effective Monday, divided on the record: allies called the pick perfect and critics, including one Republican congressman, called it a misreading of the voters’ verdict, while in Houston the mayor’s order limiting police cooperation with federal immigration officers took effect as the week’s first local answer to the election. On Iran, the president’s Friday words stand as the latest American position—“We’ve made a lot of progress with Iran”—beside Qatar’s statement that significant progress has been made; no agreement, no text, and no larger strike decision had been announced by 1800. Kyiv was struck by Russian missiles in the night, three days before the Abu Dhabi talks open, and Moscow named its delegation on Saturday. The count did not move: Mississippi and Alaska stand uncalled for a fourth day, and the markets, closed Saturday, stand where Friday left them. The desk files the day in that order.

Kraków: Six Dead in the Main Market Square

The attack began at about 3 p.m. local time and the suspect was in custody minutes later. Reuters’ Kraków file, filed below, reports that police began receiving calls at about 3 p.m. that an assailant had opened fire from a car at people in the Main Market Square, the historic centre of Poland’s second-largest city; that the dead are four women and two men; that the alleged gunman is a 24-year-old Polish citizen who wore military-style clothes and used military weapons, with many weapons and ammunition found in his vehicle; and that police shot and arrested him. A police spokesperson told a broadcaster the weapon was an AR-15 rifle and that the man held a firearms licence. The account of the official statements records that the toll was first given as five dead and was later confirmed at six dead and fifteen injured by the regional government office; that two police officers are among the injured, one of them shot three times and in very critical condition, with surgery under way; and that police denied reports that an officer had died or that a second perpetrator was being sought—“The only known perpetrator of the incident is in police custody.” The suspect has not been named publicly by the police. The defence minister denied reports that he was a member of the armed forces, in the accounts filed below.

The evening added the government’s first reading of the motive, and it is filed as a reading, not a finding. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński, in his evening briefing as carried in the Reuters file, said: “Everything points to the fact that the shooter was influenced by far-right ideology, a matter that will also be subject to investigation.” He said five foreigners were among the sixteen wounded taken to hospital—one more than the fifteen in the afternoon’s official count—and that four of the dead had been identified, one of them a foreigner; Portugal’s foreign ministry said a Portuguese woman was among the injured. A later account filed below reports the national police chief saying a British citizen is among the dead, and Prime Minister Donald Tusk, speaking in Kraków after meeting the security services, calling the attack terrorism and saying Poland has not had such a drastic case before. Mr. Tusk’s afternoon statement asked politicians of all stripes not to exploit the tragedy and said all the circumstances will be established. President Karol Nawrocki’s spokesperson said he will declare national mourning on November 8 and 9; the city has declared mourning through November 11. Condolences arrived from President Zelenskyy of Ukraine and from the European Union’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, in the same file. No charge against the suspect had been announced by 1800 ET, and no motive has been established by any court or investigator on the record.

Asunción at Evening: Charges Filed, Detention Asked, Savers Paid

The case the midday edition left at the prosecutor’s door was filed in the afternoon. Reuters’ Asunción file, updated after the appearance, reports that prosecutors on Saturday charged former President Santiago Peña with breach of trust and administration for personal gain and asked a court to jail him pending trial; that former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo was charged with breach of trust, producing false public documents, and administration for personal gain, with his pretrial detention also sought; that prosecutors allege Peña used his position to influence agencies and state entities to keep large amounts of public money deposited at Ueno despite his financial ties to the lender; and that the two charges against Peña could carry up to ten years in prison each, in the prosecutor’s statement. A second account adds that both men declined to say anything at the hearing, that prosecutors asked for both men’s assets to be frozen and for six months to formulate the final case, that twenty-seven people have been charged in total, and that a judge has ordered six former Ueno directors held in pretrial detention. Peña’s lawyer, Ricardo Preda, rejected pretrial detention before the charges were filed, saying nothing justified it. Peña has denied wrongdoing and said the bank’s problems were a regulatory matter. The charges are charges; the detention request is a request; a judge has not ruled on it, and no court has ruled on any allegation in the case.

The other half of the day in Asunción is money moving back to savers, and a new government forming under protest. The central bank said on Saturday that the equivalent of $160 million had been paid out to nearly 1.2 million savers under the deposit guarantee scheme, in the Reuters file—the first payment figure of the crisis, against a bank that served about three million customers and held as much as $850 million in public money. The fuller account of the week filed below records that President Pedro Alliana’s first decree appointed Ariel Martínez as minister of the interior, a post he held in 2018, with Juan Carlos Baruja arriving at Public Works; that the prosecutorial hypothesis examines deposits by public bodies and social security entities between 2023 and 2026 and allegedly irregular credits to companies linked to Grupo Vázquez; and that protests over the Ueno case continue, with protesters and opposition sectors questioning Alliana and some calling for early elections. The guarantee’s structure stands as the central bank published it: a first group paid in full up to ten million guaraníes, an advance of up to forty minimum wages, and a coverage limit of seventy-five minimum wages per depositor—three different figures, not three payments to be added. What Alliana promised in words, that those affected will recover their funds, and what the guarantee pays in stages, remain two different statements, and the desk keeps them separate.

Washington at Evening: The Miller Appointment Read From Every Side

Friday’s appointment produced its considered readings on Saturday, and they divide cleanly. The facts stand as filed Friday: Susie Wiles submitted her resignation on Thursday evening; the president announced Stephen Miller, his deputy chief of staff and the architect of the administration’s immigration enforcement programme, as her successor, effective Monday; Mrs. Wiles will move to the president’s political operation; and the president told CBS News he intends further changes, saying of his Cabinet, “I love my Cabinet. I think they’re good. But I’ll be doing maybe a few changes.” Saturday’s analysis, filed below, reads the appointment as the president doubling down after first suggesting openness to working with Democrats: allies who urged the change argued Mr. Miller had proven he could carry out the president’s programme without a learning period and could repair the party’s standing with its own movement; Steve Bannon called him “a perfect pick.” The other reading is on the same record: Representative Marlin Stutzman of Indiana, a Republican, said in a local radio appearance, “We lost Latinos because of the deportation look,” singling out Mr. Miller, and added that the party must wake up to being in the minority. Representative Robert Garcia, the incoming Oversight leadership’s ranking member, said, “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.” Representative Chellie Pingree of Maine called the choice a move “from very bad to worse than you could possibly imagine.” An immigration-reform advocate quoted in the analysis said calls to work with the president on reform are not realistic while Mr. Miller is in the White House. The president’s own words on the pick were: “Stephen’s been with me from the beginning. He gets it. Very good politically. And he’s a very good man.” Mr. Miller posted that serving as chief of staff is “the privilege of my lifetime” and that “the mission now is more clear than ever.” Both readings agree on one fact: the appointment takes effect Monday, and the two years of divided government begin with it.

The election’s first local consequence in Texas took effect the same weekend. Reuters’ Houston file reports that Mayor John Whitmire on Friday ordered the city’s police to curtail cooperation with federal immigration officers: officers on routine stops are barred from alerting Immigration and Customs Enforcement solely on the basis of a civil immigration warrant, and may notify the agency only when the person is also being arrested on a jailable offence. The mayor said he acted after consulting the state’s newly elected governor, lieutenant governor, and comptroller, to “reduce fear and anxiety” across the city and because “elections matter.” Police Chief J. Noe Diaz said he supported the change and the department had begun implementing it. The order reverses a policy the mayor adopted in April under pressure from Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid on Tuesday; department figures carried in the accounts filed below show officers contacted the agency nearly 200 times from April through September and handed people directly to it at least 36 times. The order does not bar federal agents from operating in Houston on their own authority. It is the first such order of the post-election week on the shelf, and it was made by a mayor of the president’s opponents’ party in the largest city of a state his party swept on Tuesday—filed as the local record, under the same roof as the appointment above it, because the evening file is the day whole.

Iran at Evening: The Range Limit Lifted, Progress Claimed on Both Sides, No Decision Announced

Tehran’s announcement of the day is a policy ending, stated by the Guards in one sentence. Tasnim’s file reports that Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, spokesman for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, announced at a press conference for the force’s Aerospace Week that restrictions on the range of Iran’s missiles have been lifted, saying the country must demonstrate its expanded capabilities in practice rather than merely make statements. The fuller account adds that the remarks followed Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei’s order of an immediate and effective response to any threat without geographical limits, and a review of the military’s target database to include American and Israeli assets. The wire’s account puts the change plainly: the self-imposed limit of 2,000 kilometres, in place since 2017 under the former supreme leader, is ended, suggesting Iran may seek weapons able to reach more distant targets. Every account on the shelf carries the same caution, and the desk repeats it as part of the fact: no file shows Iran possessing or demonstrating an operational missile beyond the old limit, and General Mohebbi himself said the capability must be shown in practice before it is claimed. A restraint is lifted; a weapon is not thereby in hand.

Against that announcement, the diplomatic file gained words from both principals and no paper. The president, speaking to reporters in West Palm Beach on Friday in the account filed below, confirmed the limited strikes on Iranian air defences near Qeshm Island—“We do minor strikes”; “we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five”—and said repeatedly that his administration is speaking with Tehran’s representatives: “We’re dealing with them now. They want to make a deal. We’ve made a lot of progress with Iran.” He gave no details of the progress. Qatar’s prime minister said the same day, in the midday file, that significant progress had been made and the aim is a good agreement rather than a perfect one, and Qatar’s media office denied reports that the talks had failed. The Qatari proposal, as reported in the accounts filed below, would have Washington lift its blockade and release some frozen Iranian funds, Iran admit international inspectors to damaged sites, and the Strait of Hormuz reopen on the arrangement’s second day, without Iran surrendering its nuclear stockpiles; Tehran’s deputy security chief said Iran is not satisfied with paper commitments and must see practical steps, and Tehran’s own seven conditions stand unmet and unwithdrawn. The explosions reported from Qeshm in the night remain unconfirmed as to origin and damage, and the United States has not announced any new attack. The larger decision promised on Thursday—whether to resume the war in full—had not been announced at 1800 on Saturday. Progress is claimed in Washington and in Doha; it is described in neither capital; and the missile announcement in Tehran is the day’s only new fact with a text behind it.

Kyiv and Abu Dhabi: Missiles in the Night, a Delegation Named, Three Days Out

Kyiv was struck in the night between Friday and Saturday, and the counts of the injured do not agree. The Associated Press file reports missile explosions in Kyiv early Saturday leaving at least five people injured, damaging homes and commercial properties, closing traffic on a bridge over the Dnipro River, and triggering new power and water outages. A second account puts the injured at two and records Mayor Vitali Klitschko reporting explosions in the suburbs as missiles targeted infrastructure, after President Zelenskyy’s Friday warning that Russia was preparing strikes on energy facilities, bridges, and civilian infrastructure. Mr. Zelenskyy’s Saturday statement, in the accounts filed below, gives the barrage at 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones over Kyiv and twelve other regions, four missiles intercepted, and nine people wounded including a child; Russia’s defence ministry confirmed it targeted the Northern Bridge, saying it facilitated the transport of weaponry and military equipment. The desk prints the three injury figures as three figures—two, five, and nine—from three hours and three sources, and does not choose among them. No deaths in Kyiv had been confirmed in the accounts taken in by 1800.

The talks the missiles precede acquired their cast on Saturday. The Kremlin spokesman told Interfax, in the Saturday accounts filed below, that Russia’s delegation to Abu Dhabi will be led by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky and will include Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov, and a General Staff officer, Yuri Zhigarlovsky. The American president’s Thursday position stands: after meeting the Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev privately, he predicted a big agreement involving more than Ukraine, possibly all of Europe, and gave no details and said he had not met the Ukrainian delegation. Ukraine’s president, in the interview account filed below, said he does not know many details of the framework being floated, warned that a deal between Russia and Europe would not be simple and could be dangerous, and held that ending the war comes first and guarantees second—the same position as his Thursday demand that guarantees be clear on paper. The talks open Tuesday, November 10, the first trilateral meeting since February. In his Saturday evening address, Mr. Zelenskyy also spoke to a second file: the corruption investigation, Operation Carthage, in which anti-corruption authorities have charged senior security and law-enforcement officials with shielding a criminal ring. Reuters’ Kyiv file reports him calling the alleged crimes “frankly shameful, absolutely unacceptable,” saying dismissals at the security service have already occurred and more personnel decisions will follow, and proposing legislation requiring all security-service employees to publicly declare their assets. A court on Friday ordered a former general of the service arrested pending bail. The allegations are allegations; the dismissals and the bill are acts.

The Count at Evening: A Fourth Day Without a Call

Neither Senate race was called on Saturday, and the day’s contribution to the file is an explanation of the wait. The explainer filed below sets out the machinery: in Mississippi, mail and affidavit ballots are still being processed under a ten-day window, counties certify by November 13, and the secretary of state counted roughly 3,600 mail ballots outstanding in his Wednesday statement beside an unknown number of affidavit ballots; in Alaska, ranked-choice tabulation is not published until November 18, fifteen days after the election, and nearly a quarter of the vote remains uncounted. The Saturday account of the two races carries the standing figures: Scott Colom ahead of Cindy Hyde-Smith by some 2,500 votes in Mississippi in the wire’s tally, with Republicans estimating roughly 20,000 ballots outstanding—an estimate ten thousand below the figure in circulation at midday—and voters able to resolve ballot problems through November 10; and Mary Peltola ahead of Dan Sullivan by 637 votes in Alaska, with the legal fronts in that race opened by both sides, the Justice Department’s suit before the voting and the Peltola campaign’s records suit on Friday. Democrats will hold at least 54 Senate seats in the 120th Congress whatever the two races decide; what remains open is the size of the majority, for a fourth day. Colorado’s 4th District stands where Friday left it, Eileen Laubacher ahead of Lauren Boebert by 3,278 votes, uncalled. Tuesday, November 10 now carries the next Alaska update, Mississippi’s ballot deadline, both congressional parties’ leadership elections, consumer prices, and the opening of the Abu Dhabi talks.

Europe’s Hoaxes and the Week’s Settled Markets

Friday’s third wave of hoax bomb threats is the evening’s European file, and its totals also disagree. The fullest account, filed below, counts at least 18 flights disrupted on Friday to or from nine countries, while the European transport commissioner put Friday’s total at 11; nine of the flights used Prague’s airport, Hungary scrambled fighter jets to escort three threatened aircraft, and four aircraft over France landed at Paris Orly for inspection. Every threatened aircraft landed safely and no explosives were found on any plane or at any site. The threats spread on Friday to newsrooms: Ireland’s broadcaster evacuated its Dublin headquarters and ran pre-recorded programming for hours, other Irish outlets emptied their offices, and a British broadcaster confirmed it had received a threat. Friday’s emails were signed with a name claiming leadership of the group behind the week’s hoaxes; a different signature on Thursday’s threats named a movement whose founder denied involvement and said the group has not existed since 2021. Investigators have found no evidence that a hostile state or a terror group is directing the hoaxes. Spain’s foreign minister said the identical methods across so many countries could not be coincidence and called the most reasonable assumption “an attempt at hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare”; Ireland’s prime minister said the episode showed how relatively simple it can be to disrupt the normal operation of society. Both statements are on the record; the authorship of the threats is not. The markets add nothing to the day: the exchanges are closed, and the week stands settled as filed at midday—the S&P 500 down 2.7 percent, Brent crude at $98.32, down 13.3 percent, and Berkshire Hathaway’s third quarter, operating earnings down 5.8 percent and cash at a record $377.4 billion, as the day’s one scheduled report. Monday’s open waits on the Iran file, as it waited on Friday.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On Kraków’s wounded, the afternoon’s official count is fifteen and the interior minister’s evening figure is sixteen taken to hospital; the desk prints both and notes the hour of each. On Kyiv’s injured, the figures are two, five, and nine, from a city account, the wire, and the president, and no confirmed death stands in any of them. On the hoax flights, the counts are eleven and eighteen for the same Friday. On Mississippi’s outstanding ballots, the estimates in circulation on Saturday run from roughly 20,000 to roughly 30,000. Against the triangle, the evening’s load-bearing facts are single-valued: six people are dead in Kraków and the only known perpetrator is in police custody; Peña and Carvallo stand charged, detention and an asset freeze are asked and not yet granted, and $160 million has been paid to nearly 1.2 million savers; the missile-range limit has been lifted in words, with no missile shown beyond it; progress on Iran is claimed in Washington and Doha and described in neither; Russia has named its Abu Dhabi delegation and the talks open Tuesday; Stephen Miller takes the chief of staff’s office on Monday; Houston’s order is in effect; no race was called; and the Shenzhen meeting of three presidents, eleven days out, received no new word. Saturday’s file therefore closes as it opened in the brief: one atrocity, answered by an arrest and an investigation; one presidency, answered by a charge sheet and a payment ledger; two wars, answered by announcements and preparations; and an election, answered so far by an appointment, a mayor’s order, and a count that will not move until Tuesday. The log proceeds to midnight.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-seven items.

Subjective
Reuters, via 98.5 The River — Poland in shock as six dead after mass shooting in Krakow

Krakow, November 7: a gunman shooting randomly from a car killed six people and wounded at least fifteen in the city’s main square on Saturday before police shot and arrested him; the interior minister said in his evening briefing that everything points to the shooter having been influenced by far-right ideology, a matter to be investigated, that five foreigners were among the sixteen wounded taken to hospital, and that four of the dead had been identified, one a foreigner; Portugal’s foreign ministry said a Portuguese woman was among the injured; the shooter wore military-style clothes, used military weapons, and had many weapons and ammunition in his vehicle, a police spokesperson said; and the president will declare national mourning on November 8 and 9.

Subjective
People — at least 6 dead, 15 injured after a man drove into the market square and opened fire

November 7: a man drove into Krakow’s Main Market Square at about 3 p.m. local time and began firing at random people from his car, killing at least six and injuring fifteen, including two police officers, one of whom was shot three times and is in very critical condition; the toll was first reported as five dead and was later confirmed at six by police and the regional government office; the dead are four women and two men, not yet publicly identified; police denied reports that an officer had died or that another perpetrator was being sought, stating that the only known perpetrator is in police custody; the gunman, a Polish citizen, was shot by officers, detained, and taken to hospital; and Prime Minister Donald Tusk offered condolences and appealed to politicians of all stripes not to exploit the tragedy.

Subjective
Gazette & Herald — six killed and at least 15 injured in Krakow shooting

November 7: a gunman opened fire in Krakow’s Main Square, a major tourist destination, aiming at random people as he drove by, leaving six people dead and at least fifteen injured, with police officers among the wounded; four women and two men were killed; a police spokesperson told TVN24 the perpetrator wore military-style fatigues and used a military-type long gun; the interior minister wrote that two officers were wounded, one seriously; a tram driver reported his vehicle shot at from a moving car near the square at about 3 p.m.; and Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on X that police are investigating the attack and its circumstances.

Subjective
New York Post — footage shows the moment police shot the Krakow gunman

November 7: footage shows a police officer firing six shots at the gunman who opened fire in Krakow’s Main Market Square on Saturday, killing six people and wounding at least fifteen; the masked attacker, a 24-year-old Polish citizen not yet named by police, began firing randomly from a dark vehicle as he drove through the square on Saturday afternoon; police began receiving calls at about 3 p.m.; after the shootout the suspect was taken into custody and is in hospital, police said; unverified footage shared on social media showed people fleeing as shots rang out; police said the suspect wore military-style attire and used an AR-15 rifle; and the dead are four women and two men.

Subjective
Reuters, via Duke FM — Paraguay prosecutors charge ex-President Peña, seek pretrial detention

Asunción, November 7: prosecutors charged former President Santiago Peña with breach of trust and administration for personal gain and asked a court to jail him pending trial, a day after his impeachment over the collapse of digital lender Ueno; former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo was charged with breach of trust, producing false public documents, and administration for personal gain, with his pretrial detention also sought; prosecutors allege Peña used his position to influence agencies and state entities to keep large amounts of public money deposited at Ueno despite his financial ties to the lender, having been a shareholder in its holding company until March 2025; Peña has denied wrongdoing and said the bank’s problems were a regulatory matter; the two charges against him could carry up to ten years in prison each, the prosecutor said; and the central bank said the equivalent of $160 million had been paid out to nearly 1.2 million savers under the deposit guarantee scheme.

Subjective
AnewZ — Paraguay’s ex-President Peña charged over the Ueno Bank collapse

November 7: prosecutors charged former President Santiago Peña and former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo Spalding over the collapse of Ueno Bank and asked a court to hold both in pretrial detention; Peña is charged with breach of trust and administration for personal gain and Carvallo with the same charges plus producing false public documents; both men declined to say anything at the hearing; prosecutors also asked for both men’s assets to be frozen and for six months to formulate their final case, the detention decision resting with a criminal court judge; Peña’s lawyer rejected pretrial detention, saying nothing justified it; in a separate case a judge has ordered six former Ueno directors held in pretrial detention, prosecutors have charged twenty-seven people in total, and authorities have seized assets linked to Ueno’s controlling shareholder; and breach of trust carries up to five years in prison, or up to ten in serious cases.

Subjective
Demócrata — prison is sought for Santiago Peña after the fall of Ueno Bank

November 7: the Public Prosecutor’s Office attributes to the former president alleged acts of breach of trust and administration for his own benefit and has requested pretrial detention for Carlos Carvallo as well, the request amounting neither to a judicial ruling nor to a conviction; the investigation examines deposits by public bodies and social security entities between 2023 and 2026 and allegedly irregular credits to companies linked to Grupo Vázquez; both men refrained from declaring at their appearances, in ABC Color’s reporting; President Pedro Alliana’s first decree appointed Ariel Martínez as minister of the interior, with Juan Carlos Baruja arriving at Public Works; the central bank’s guarantee structure is set out in stages—a first group paid in full up to ten million guaraníes, an advance of up to forty minimum wages, and a coverage limit of seventy-five minimum wages per depositor; and protests over the Ueno case continue, with some sectors questioning Alliana and calling for early elections.

Subjective
Sociedad Media — Peña detained at home, due before prosecutors Saturday

Asunción, November 7: Santiago Peña spent Friday night in custody after the Senate removed him as president over the collapse of Ueno Bank, the Senate voting unanimously among the 44 senators present with one absent; the Public Ministry said its agents detained Peña and former central bank president Carlos Carvallo Spalding for the alleged commission of breach of trust and other offenses; Prosecutor Silvia González confirmed Peña would appear Saturday at 11 a.m. before the Economic Crimes and Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office, after which prosecutors must file formal charges and request precautionary measures; and the probe covers alleged irregularities in the supervision of Ueno, possible conflicts of interest tied to Peña’s links to Grupo Vázquez, and the placement of public funds in the bank, including pension and health fund money.

Subjective
CNN — how one of the president’s most controversial advisers rose to chief of staff, and what it means

November 7: the president first suggested openness to collaborating with Democrats after the midterm losses, then, growing agitated, replaced Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller amid encouragement from allies to ramp up the fight; the analysis reads the elevation as doubling down and a signal of greater use of executive authority; some Republicans expressed dismay, Representative Marlin Stutzman saying the party lost Latinos because of the deportation look and must wake up to minority status; Steve Bannon called the pick perfect; Representative Robert Garcia said Stephen Miller should lawyer up, and Representative Chellie Pingree called the choice a move from very bad to worse than imaginable; the appointment, effective Monday, is assessed as likely to end early hopes of comprehensive immigration legislation; and the president said of Miller that he has been with him from the beginning, gets it, and is very good politically.

Subjective
CNN — Stephen Miller replacing Susie Wiles as chief of staff, sources say

November 6: Susie Wiles is departing as White House chief of staff days after the Republican midterm losses, in the first major personnel move since the elections, and will be replaced by Stephen Miller, a longtime aide who orchestrated the administration’s immigration agenda; the president voiced fury at the strategy that led to the losses, people familiar with the matter said, and signalled to CBS News that more changes will follow; Mrs. Wiles submitted her resignation on Thursday evening, the move takes effect Monday, and she will move to the president’s political operation, the president saying she has done an outstanding job; Mr. Miller posted that it is the privilege of his lifetime to serve as chief of staff and that the mission now is more clear than ever.

Subjective
USA Today — in elevating Stephen Miller, the president taps an immigration champion

November 6: days after voters rejected the administration’s agenda in the midterm elections, the president elevated Stephen Miller to chief of staff; Miller is best known as an immigration hawk, his influence as deputy chief of staff for policy extending far beyond immigration to all levels of policymaking and to foreign affairs; the outgoing chief of staff, Susie Wiles, is a longtime aide with a lower-key profile; the president praised Miller on departing the White House on November 6, noting he has been with him from the beginning, as a policy adviser and speechwriter on the 2016 campaign and in the first administration; and the selection came after Democrats won both the House and the Senate.

Subjective
Reuters — before his promotion, Stephen Miller designed the immigration crackdown

November 6: facts on the president’s next chief of staff: Stephen Miller, 41, raised in Santa Monica, California, developed a reputation as a combative conservative as a columnist at Duke University’s student newspaper; in the second term he has been deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser and is best known as the architect of the administration’s toughest immigration policies; and with the budget director he worked for months ahead of the midterms on executive actions the president can take without approval from Congress.

Subjective
Reuters, via 98.5 The River — Houston mayor curtails police cooperation with ICE, saying ‘elections matter’

November 6: days after elections swept Democrats to statewide leadership in Texas, Houston’s mayor ordered the city’s police department on Friday to curtail cooperation with federal immigration officers, contrary to Republican-backed state law; Mayor John Whitmire said he acted after consulting the state’s newly elected governor, lieutenant governor, and comptroller, to reduce fear and anxiety across the most populous city in Texas and because elections matter; under the new policy, officers on routine traffic stops or detaining someone for another reason are barred from alerting Immigration and Customs Enforcement solely on the basis of a civil immigration warrant, and may notify the agency only if the person is also being arrested on a jailable offence; Police Chief J. Noe Diaz said he supported the change and the department had begun implementing it; and the mayor said the order enforces the state’s Senate Bill 4, which he opposed as a state senator.

Subjective
Tasnim — restrictions on the range of Iranian missiles lifted, Guards spokesman

Tehran, November 7: the spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps announced that restrictions on the range of Iran’s missiles have been lifted, saying the country must demonstrate its expanded capabilities in practice rather than merely make statements; the announcement was made at a press conference marking the Guards’ Aerospace Week; and the spokesman said the Islamic Republic will demonstrate its capabilities to respond to threats on the battlefield.

Subjective
The Insight International — Iran says it has lifted its self-imposed limit on ballistic missile ranges

Tehran, November 7: the Revolutionary Guards said they have lifted a self-imposed limit of about 2,000 kilometres on the range of their ballistic missiles, suggesting Tehran may seek weapons that can reach more distant targets; Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi told a news conference marking Aerospace Week that the restriction has been lifted for us, in the reporting of Tasnim and Mehr; the remarks followed the supreme leader’s order of an immediate and effective response to any threat without geographical limits, and a reported review and update of the military’s target database covering American and Israeli assets; and the claims could not be independently verified.

Subjective
The Daily Guard, carrying the Associated Press — Iran says it has lifted its self-imposed limit on missile ranges

November 7: Iran’s Revolutionary Guard says it has lifted a self-imposed limit of 2,000 kilometres (1,200 miles) on the range of its ballistic missiles, suggesting the country may seek to develop missiles capable of reaching more distant targets as fears of renewed all-out war rise; the item is published under the wire’s copyright notice for 2026.

Subjective
Reuters, via 98.5 The River — Qatar says its mediation efforts between the US and Iran continue

November 7: Qatar’s prime minister said the country’s mediation efforts between the United States and Iran were continuing to prevent the situation from spiralling out of control; the American administration remained willing to find a solution even after the midterm elections; significant progress had been made and he expressed confidence a settlement could be reached, saying the aim is a good agreement rather than waiting for a perfect one; Iran has been proposing its own seven-day plan since September, so far rejected by the president; Tasnim said initial reports indicated two missiles had struck Qeshm Island, with no official information on possible damage; and the United States has not yet announced any attack on targets inside Iran.

Subjective
Madhyamam — the president confirms strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island

November 7: the president confirmed that American forces carried out strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, describing them as limited attacks on Iranian air-defence systems; he also said Washington had made a lot of progress in negotiations with Tehran, giving no details; ‘We do minor strikes,’ he told reporters in West Palm Beach, Florida, saying an anti-aircraft device the Iranians built was knocked out in about fifteen minutes, maybe five; he said repeatedly on Friday that his administration is speaking with Tehran’s representatives—‘We’re dealing with them now. They want to make a deal’—and Qatar, mediating between the sides, dismissed reports that the negotiations had collapsed, its foreign ministry spokesperson saying such claims benefited only those seeking to prolong the war.

Subjective
Associated Press, via KCAU — missiles target Kyiv and injure 5 as Ukraine prepares for talks

Kyiv, November 7: missile explosions struck Kyiv and left at least five people injured early on Saturday as Ukraine prepared for new talks next week with Russia and the United States; negotiators from the three countries are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi for talks aimed at ending the war, the fourth round brokered by the present administration after the most recent round in Geneva in February; and the missiles damaged homes and commercial properties, closed traffic on a Kyiv bridge over the Dnipro River, and triggered new power and water outages, national and city authorities said.

Subjective
AnewZ — Russian missiles hit Kyiv ahead of Abu Dhabi peace talks

November 7: Russian forces launched a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv early on Saturday, injuring two people and damaging residential buildings, three days before American-led peace talks with Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi; Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported explosions in the capital’s suburbs as missiles targeted infrastructure; the attack followed a warning from President Zelenskyy that Russia was preparing further strikes on energy facilities, bridges, and civilian infrastructure, a warning he gave in his nightly address on Friday after intelligence identified preparations for another wave; and Ukrainian officials had not confirmed whether Saturday’s attack was the one described in the warning.

Subjective
CNN — the president teases a big, beautiful European security deal after meeting the Russian envoy

November 6: the president promised a new security deal for Ukraine that might involve all of Europe after meeting a top Russian envoy on Thursday, but the proposal offers few details and has left European capitals puzzled; ‘It’s going to be a big agreement… it might involve all of Europe. It’s going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone’s going to be thrilled,’ he told reporters, without details; Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said he did not know many details of the potential framework, warned a deal between Russia and Europe would not be simple and could be dangerous, and held that ending the war must come first and security guarantees second; the Russian envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, attended a White House event hosted by the first lady marking a ceasefire in the occupied city of Oleshky, and the president said he did not meet the Ukrainian delegation; and NATO confirmed talks among NATO, American, Ukrainian, and European counterparts in Brussels on Thursday ahead of the Abu Dhabi meeting.

Subjective
AnewZ — the president meets the Russian envoy, says a Ukraine deal is within reach

November 6: the president predicted a breakthrough in efforts to end the war in Ukraine after meeting President Putin’s envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, ahead of American-mediated talks between Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11; he met Dmitriev privately on Thursday after the envoy attended a White House event alongside Ukrainian representatives organised by the first lady; he declined to reveal what they discussed and expressed optimism that an agreement could be reached soon, suggesting it could extend beyond Ukraine to wider European security; the president confirmed he had not met the Ukrainian delegation on Thursday; and his envoy Jared Kushner said American officials held productive and substantive discussions with Ukraine, NATO, and European partners in Brussels on Thursday.

Subjective
Reuters, via WYSL — Zelenskiy criticises Ukraine’s security service over the corruption scandal

Kyiv, November 7: President Volodymyr Zelenskiy promised more personnel decisions at the domestic security service on Saturday following a corruption scandal that has fuelled public anger over official impunity; anti-corruption authorities unveiled charges this week against several senior security and law-enforcement officials over their alleged role in shielding a vast criminal ring; investigators said the group ran scam centres, traded drugs, and produced fake currency and cigarettes with the help of top employees of the security service, the National Police, and the Prosecutor General’s office; in his evening address the president called the alleged crimes frankly shameful and absolutely unacceptable, said dismissals have already occurred and others will follow, and said he expects a full investigation; a court on Friday ordered the arrest pending bail of a former general of the service; and he proposed legislation requiring all employees of the service to publicly declare their assets.

Subjective
Al Jazeera — what is delaying the Senate election results in Mississippi and Alaska

November 7: two Senate races remain undecided; Democrats will enter the 120th Congress on January 3 with a majority of at least 54 seats; in Mississippi the race between the incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith, and Scott Colom is too close to call with both candidates at about 49 percent and 96 percent of ballots counted, Colom leading by 1,138 votes in the count as of Wednesday night, with provisional and mail-in absentee ballots left to count and ten days allowed to process them; the secretary of state counted roughly 3,600 mail-in ballots still to be tallied on Wednesday, with an unknown number of affidavit ballots, and counties have until November 13 to submit certified results; and in Alaska, Mary Peltola leads the incumbent, Dan Sullivan, by 637 votes in the wire’s tally as of Wednesday night, nearly a quarter of the votes remain uncounted, ranked-choice results will not be published until November 18, and the race has become one of the most closely watched in the country.

Subjective
USA Today — Mississippi and Alaska Senate races still undecided as legal fights loom

November 7: two Senate races remain undecided days after the election, with legal battles looming in both, and neither will change control of the chamber—Democrats hold 54 seats to the Republicans’ 44, and what remains is the size of the majority; in Mississippi, Scott Colom leads the incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith, by some 2,500 votes, less than a percentage point, in the wire’s tally, which has not called the race; thousands of affidavit ballots are outstanding, Republicans estimate roughly 20,000 ballots remain, and voters have until November 10 to resolve problems with theirs; Colom has overperformed among affidavit votes, even in counties the incumbent carried easily, in a Mississippi Free Press analysis of the counties that have finished counting them; in Alaska, Mary Peltola leads the incumbent, Dan Sullivan, by 637 votes with roughly three-quarters of ballots counted; the legal skirmishing there began before the voting, and on November 6 the Peltola campaign opened a legal front of its own; and Alaska’s answer is more than a week away, with absentee ballots accepted through November 18, the day of the ranked-choice tabulation.

Subjective
SOFX — third wave of hoax threats hits European flights and newsrooms

November 7: a third wave of hoax bomb threats in four days disrupted at least 18 more European flights on Friday and spread to newsrooms, forcing Ireland’s broadcaster to evacuate its Dublin headquarters and run pre-recorded programming for hours; every threatened aircraft landed safely and searches found no explosives on any plane or at any media site; the Guardian counted at least 18 affected flights to or from nine countries while the European transport commissioner put Friday’s total at 11; nine of Friday’s flights used Prague’s airport, Hungary’s defence minister said fighter jets escorted three threatened passenger planes, and four aircraft over France landed safely at Paris Orly; Friday’s emails were signed by a claimant who warned this is only the beginning; a different signature on Thursday’s threats named a movement whose founder denied involvement; investigators have found no evidence a hostile state or terror group is directing the hoaxes; Spain’s foreign minister called the most reasonable assumption an attempt at hybrid aggression and psychological warfare; and Ireland’s prime minister said the episode showed how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and undermine the normal operation of society.

Subjective
Zot News — bomb threats widen to media outlets as a third wave hits European flights

November 6–7: a third wave of bomb threats struck European airlines on Friday, with fighter jets scrambled in Hungary to escort three passenger planes, while some Irish media outlets evacuated their buildings after receiving similar warnings; the Irish government described a likely coordinated campaign of disruption, and an Irish official said the media threats were almost certainly linked to Dublin’s hosting of a high-level European summit next week; flights to and from Lisbon, Rome, Prague, and Sofia were targeted, France reported four threats against aircraft over its territory, all landing safely at Paris Orly, and Prague airport said nine flights were threatened; no bombs were found at the media sites; since Tuesday, more than 30 flights and several airports have been affected by threats arriving by phone and email, all false alarms, each triggering emergency landings, evacuations, and searches; a group named in some threats to Italian airports denied involvement; and officials described the week’s disruption relative to the nearly 26,300 flights across the European network on Thursday.
items.summary: The evening file for Saturday, November 7, 2026: a gunman fired from a car into Kraków's Main Market Square, killing six people and wounding at least fifteen before police shot and arrested him; prosecutors in Asunción charged former President Santiago Peña and former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo and asked a court to jail both pending trial, while the central bank paid out $160 million to nearly 1.2 million Ueno savers; Iran's Revolutionary Guards lifted the self-imposed 2,000-kilometre limit on missile ranges while Washington and Doha both said the talks had made progress and no larger American decision was announced; Russian missiles struck Kyiv three days before the Abu Dhabi talks; and no Senate race was called for a fourth day, Mississippi and Alaska standing where they stood. Collected at 1800.

items.title: The Word and the Record: What the File Shows About the Status of American Fascism
items.content_html:
Special Report

The Fascism File — The Definitions and the Institutions

Objective

The Word and the Record: What the File Shows About the Status of American Fascism

The word has a scholarly literature, and the literature disagrees with itself, in print, about the same man. The country has a record: courts ruled and were answered, an election was held on schedule and the opposition won it, and the government’s own death list for its detention system reached its highest year. The desk files the definitions as their authors state and apply them, and the record beside them, and stops where the record stops. Every claim is attributed.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1230 ET; revised at 1254 ET, Saturday, November 7, 2026.

The File in Brief

There is no single scholarly definition of fascism, and no agreed instrument that measures it. What exists is a documented field and a documented record, and the desk files both. The field, in its own texts: Robert O. Paxton defines fascism as political behavior and, after January 6, 2021, applied his own definition to Donald Trump, in print, twice. Roger Griffin defines it as a revolutionary ideology of national rebirth and has declined to apply it. Umberto Eco listed fourteen features and wrote, in the same essay, that any one suffices for fascism to coagulate around it. Jason Stanley defines fascist politics as ten tactics and applies all ten. Stanley G. Payne does not apply the label. The constitutional record is shorter: the United States is a republic in form and a democracy in the source of its authority—the standard description is the compound of the two. The compliance record is documented in both directions: across the fifty years before 2025 the desk found no instance of a president openly refusing a final Supreme Court order, and in 2025–2026 it found written judicial findings that the executive violated lower-court orders—a judge’s catalog of 96 orders violated by ICE across 74 cases; a criminal-contempt finding reversed on appeal; the flagship individual case complied with after 83 days—alongside compliance with the Supreme Court’s two largest merits rulings against the administration in 2026. The deaths record is the government’s own: on ICE’s published detainee-death list, fiscal 2026 stands at 36 listed deaths with two more announced in the agency’s own releases, the highest fiscal year since the agency began operating, against 26 deaths across the preceding administration’s four years; deaths during enforcement operations have no official list and no agreed total, and this report prints the categories separately and sums nothing silently. The revised record prints causes and manners where the official record states them: most stated custody deaths in fiscal 2025–2026 are medical, one fiscal 2026 death carries a medical examiner’s homicide ruling, and 16 of the 38 fiscal 2026 deaths have no public cause; the historical baseline is printed with the record—the measured series opens in fiscal 2004 at its worst rate, and before 2004, the Second World War excepted, the detention record holds cases, not counts. The institutional record as of this week: the midterm elections of November 3, 2026 were held on schedule, and on Associated Press calls the opposition party won both chambers of Congress; no opposition party has been banned, no news organization shuttered by the government, and the courts are ruling against the executive in hundreds of cases and being, in the main and eventually, obeyed, with the exceptions concentrated in immigration enforcement. The expert indices moved: V-Dem reclassified the United States from a liberal democracy to an electoral democracy; Freedom House scored it 81 of 100 and still Free; both measure democracy, not fascism, and say so. Christian nationalism measures at about one American in ten as full adherents, stable since 2022. The fifty-year frame is also documented: the Church Committee’s 1976 report on the FBI’s covert campaign, the post-2001 surveillance settlement built by presidents of both parties, and deportation totals by administration from the department’s own yearbook, in which the current removal pace sits inside the historical range while the detention population and death counts stand at records. The report files these records. It selects no framework and announces no measurement; the frameworks are printed as their authors’ positions, on the shelf below, at full strength.

The Definitions: What the Scholars’ Own Texts Say

Paxton defines fascism by what fascists do. Robert O. Paxton, in The Anatomy of Fascism (2004), argues the doctrine is comparatively incoherent and the behavior is the definition. His closing sentence: “Fascism may be defined as a form of political behavior marked by obsessive preoccupation with community decline, humiliation, or victimhood and by compensatory cults of unity, energy, and purity, in which a mass-based party of committed nationalist militants, working in uneasy but effective collaboration with traditional elites, abandons democratic liberties and pursues with redemptive violence and without ethical or legal restraints goals of internal cleansing and external expansion.” His five stages run from the creation of movements through rooting, seizure, and exercise of power to radicalization or entropy; only Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany passed through all five, and each later stage requires the earlier without the earlier guaranteeing the later. Paxton’s own application is a published record in three steps. In 2016–2017 he resisted the label—“We should hesitate before applying this most toxic of labels”—while noting Trump adopted fascist themes. On January 11, 2021, in Newsweek, he wrote that the January 6 attack “removes my objection to the fascist label” and that “the label now seems not just acceptable but necessary,” emphasizing that the circumstances were profoundly different from interwar Europe. In October 2024 he confirmed the diagnosis—“It’s the real thing. It really is”—while saying the word “generates more heat than light.”

Griffin defines fascism by its mythic core, and sets the bar at revolution. Roger Griffin, in The Nature of Fascism (1991), gives the one-sentence minimum: fascism is “a genus of political ideology whose mythic core in its various permutations is a palingenetic form of populist ultra-nationalism”—palingenesis being rebirth, the myth of a decadent nation regenerated into a new order, and ultranationalism being nationalism that subordinates individual rights and pluralism to the organic nation. His test is ideological: without the revolutionary rebirth myth aimed at a new order and a new man, a movement is in his framework authoritarian or populist, not fascist. Griffin’s own application is a non-application: he has described Trump as an “ochlocrat,” a leader who enables mob rule, practicing illiberal populism, and reads “Make America Great Again” as rebirth rhetoric without the coherent revolutionary ideology, party apparatus, or project of systemic overthrow his definition requires. The desk notes the sourcing plainly: Griffin’s position is documented in scholarly surveys of his published commentary; the desk pulled no single Griffin text devoted solely to Trump, and the same caveat attaches to Payne below.

Eco listed fourteen features and disclaimed the list as a system in the same essay. Umberto Eco, who grew up under Mussolini, published “Ur-Fascism” in The New York Review of Books on June 22, 1995. The features: the cult of tradition; the rejection of modernism; the cult of action for action’s sake; disagreement as treason; fear of difference; appeal to a frustrated middle class; obsession with a plot; the enemy as both too strong and too weak; pacifism as trafficking with the enemy; contempt for the weak; the cult of heroism linked to death; machismo and weaponry; selective populism, the People as a monolithic voice embodied by the leader; and Newspeak, an impoverished vocabulary to limit critical reasoning. Eco’s own caveat is in his text and is load-bearing for any use of the list: the features “cannot be organized into a system; many of them contradict each other, and are also typical of other kinds of despotism or fanaticism. But it is enough that one of them be present to allow fascism to coagulate around it.” By its author’s design, the checklist can register a positive on a single feature. Eco died in 2016 and made no application to Trump.

Stanley defines fascist politics as tactics, and applies his definition in full. Jason Stanley, a philosopher of propaganda, in How Fascism Works (2018), is explicit that a nation need not be a fascist state to exhibit fascist politics. His ten pillars: the mythic past; propaganda, including anti-corruption language used corruptly; anti-intellectualism; unreality, the flooding of the public sphere until shared truth collapses into loyalty; hierarchy; victimhood, the dominant group portrayed as the true victim; law and order, the in-group as naturally lawful and the out-group as inherently criminal; sexual anxiety; “Sodom and Gomorrah,” the heartland against the decadent city; and Arbeit macht frei, the out-group as lazy and public goods reserved for the in-group. Stanley’s own application is the most direct of the set: he has called Trump a fascist leader and MAGA a fascist movement in power, in his books and interviews from 2018 forward. That is his stated position, recorded here as his.

The field does not agree, and the disagreement is part of the record. Stanley G.
