Payne, whose A History of Fascism, 1914–1945 (1995) distinguishes fascism from other authoritarianisms by anti-liberalism, anti-conservatism, and selective anti-capitalism, a party militia, and the goal of a totalitarian new man, has not applied the label to Trump or MAGA, describing the movement as authoritarian populism lacking fascism’s ideological coherence, and warning that overuse of the term undermines precision. Ruth Ben-Ghiat and Timothy Snyder apply authoritarian and fascist frameworks affirmatively, their category of choice in much of their work being “authoritarian” or “strongman,” with fascism used for specific lineages and tactics. Two assessments by former subordinates are the most quoted non-scholar entries in the file. John Kelly, the president’s longest-serving chief of staff, told the New York Times in recorded interviews published October 22, 2024, after reading aloud a general dictionary-style definition: “Certainly the former president is in the far-right area, he’s certainly an authoritarian, admires people who are dictators—he has said that. So he certainly falls into the general definition of fascist, for sure.” The definition was the general one he read aloud, not a scholarly framework. Gen. Mark Milley is quoted in Bob Woodward’s War (2024) calling Trump “fascist to the core”—a secondhand quotation. Both statements came in a campaign’s final weeks; the Trump campaign called Kelly’s accounts fabricated.

Republic, Democracy, or Both: The Constitutional Record

The Constitution uses one of the two words, and the founding texts define it as the other word’s mechanism. The word “democracy” does not appear in the United States Constitution. The word “republican” does, at Article IV, §4: “The United States shall guarantee to every State in this Union a Republican Form of Government.” Madison, in Federalist No. 10, distinguishes a “pure democracy,” citizens administering government in person, from a republic, “a government in which the scheme of representation takes place”; in No. 39 he defines a republic as “a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people.” The structure the text creates: representatives chosen by popular election; senators originally state-chosen, directly elected since the Seventeenth Amendment; a president chosen through the Electoral College; judges tenured during good behavior; and a Bill of Rights removing specified subjects from majority vote. The descriptive consensus of the reference authorities—the National Constitution Center, the Annenberg Classroom, and the standard civics references—is that the United States is both: a republic in form, representative government under a constitution with no monarch, and a democracy in the source of its authority, the people acting through elections. The two terms answer different questions—who holds ultimate authority, and how it is exercised—and the public contest is over the emphasis, not over any text. The undemocratic features of the system are themselves constitutional: the Electoral College, under which a president can lose the popular vote, as has happened five times, most recently in 2000 and 2016; equal Senate representation regardless of population; life-tenured judges; and the Article V amendment supermajorities. These are features of the 1787–1791 design, not departures from it.

Presidents and the Courts: The Compliance Record

The structural fact governs everything below: the Supreme Court has no enforcement arm. Compliance rests on the executive’s Article II duty to take care that the laws be faithfully executed, and on political cost. The Federal Judicial Center’s own history states the norm plainly: substantial compliance, with defiance on rare occasions. Outright presidential refusal to obey a direct Supreme Court order is, in the documented record, close to nonexistent; the historical pattern is resistance, delay, and narrow reading, followed in the landmark cases by compliance. The two pre-window exceptions: in Worcester v. Georgia (1832), Georgia defied the Court’s ruling and President Jackson took no action to enforce it against the state—the famous line attributed to him is apocryphal—and Cherokee removal proceeded; and in Ex parte Merryman (1861), Chief Justice Taney, sitting as circuit judge, held Lincoln’s suspension of habeas corpus unconstitutional, and Lincoln disregarded the order in the Civil War’s opening weeks. That is the clearest case of a president ignoring an order directed at his own conduct—by a single justice on circuit, in wartime, 165 years ago. Against those stand the compliances: Truman, held in Youngstown (1952) to have seized the steel mills unlawfully, complied immediately; Nixon, ordered unanimously in 1974 to produce the tapes, complied and resigned sixteen days later; and at Little Rock in 1957 the executive sent the 101st Airborne to enforce the Court’s orders against a defiant governor.

Across the fifty-year window before 2025, the desk found no documented instance of a president openly refusing a final Supreme Court order directed at him. From Carter through Biden, administrations lost major cases and complied: the George W. Bush administration complied with Hamdan v. Rumsfeld (2006) and then sought and obtained new legislation; the Obama administration complied with the health-care ruling as decided; the Biden administration complied with the ruling striking its student-loan program and then pursued narrower alternatives through rulemaking. That sequence—comply with the order, contest the policy space around it—is the standard modern pattern, the first Trump administration’s travel-ban litigation its standard example. The desk found no court-documented case in this window of a judicial finding that a president defied an order. That is the baseline.

The second Trump administration’s record runs in both directions, and the volume is itself documented. Litigation trackers counted roughly 700 to 800 active or filed challenges to administration actions by 2026; one tracker’s mid-2026 snapshot records plaintiffs winning 262 rulings to the government’s 126, and other trackers give different splits—the desk prints the figure as one named tracker’s dated snapshot, because no rate in this file is method-free. A CNN analysis identified at least 77 federal court orders containing sharp judicial criticism of the administration, from 69 judges, including 11 Trump appointees. The Supreme Court also ruled for the administration repeatedly on its emergency docket in 2025—the White House counted 21 victories by September 2025—and then ruled against it on the merits in the two largest cases of 2026. In Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, on February 20, 2026, the Court held 6–3 that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize the president to impose tariffs; the administration complied with the judgment while substituting a replacement tariff under a different statute, which the Court of International Trade then struck on May 7, 2026. In Trump v. Barbara, on June 30, 2026, the Court held that children born in the United States to unlawfully or temporarily present parents are citizens at birth under the Fourteenth Amendment, invalidating the core of the administration’s executive order. The desk records the holdings and dates as reported; it did not pull the slip opinions themselves, and says so rather than smoothing it over. In the large majority of the individual cases, the documented pattern is the standard one: appeal, seek a stay, and, when stays are denied, implement the order while appealing.

The documented exceptions are written down by judges, and they are concentrated in immigration enforcement. In March 2025 the administration deported more than 200 alleged Tren de Aragua members to El Salvador under the Alien Enemies Act while Judge James Boasberg’s order barring removal was being issued; on April 16, 2025, Boasberg found probable cause of criminal contempt through “willful disobedience of judicial orders”; on April 14, 2026, an appeals panel blocked the contempt proceedings, holding the underlying order was not clear and specific enough to support criminal contempt. Both halves are the record. In January 2026, Judge Patrick Schiltz, a George W. Bush appointee, documented in an order 96 court orders that ICE had violated across 74 cases—the most concrete judicial count in the record, because it is a judge counting his own court’s orders. By January 2026, reporting counted at least 35 show-cause orders since August 2025 requiring the administration to explain why it should not be held in contempt; the figure is press-derived and approximate. The most litigated single case is Kilmar Abrego Garcia’s. Removed to El Salvador on March 15, 2025, under a 2019 withholding order barring that removal, he was conceded by the government, in its own March 31 filing, to have been removed “because of an administrative error.” The District of Maryland ordered the government on April 4 to facilitate and effectuate his return; the Supreme Court on April 10 left the facilitation requirement in place without noted dissent; the district court found on April 11 that the government had made no meaningful effort to comply. The administration’s position through April and May was that “facilitate” did not obligate it to secure a release from a sovereign El Salvador; President Trump said on April 11, “If the Supreme Court said bring somebody back I would do that. I respect the Supreme Court.” On June 6, 2025—83 days after the removal, 57 days after the Supreme Court’s order—the government returned him to the United States, simultaneously indicting him in Tennessee on human-smuggling charges; that prosecution was later dismissed on vindictive-prosecution grounds, a district court finding the closed investigation had been reopened a week after the Supreme Court’s order, and the Justice Department appealed the dismissal in August 2026. No government body counts defied orders, and no official defiance rate exists; a Washington Post analysis relayed by secondary trackers, putting defiance at roughly one-third of cases decided against the administration, is a method-dependent press construction whose dataset the desk did not read. The comparison the sourced record supports is this: in the 1976–2024 window, judicial findings that the executive violated orders are rare to the point that the desk found none at presidential level; in 2025–2026 such findings exist in writing from multiple federal judges, alongside an appellate reversal of the major contempt proceeding, ultimate compliance in the most prominent individual case, and compliance with the Supreme Court’s two largest merits rulings; and no president in the window, including this one on the record assembled here, has openly refused a final Supreme Court merits order and simply continued the struck policy unchanged. What is new is the volume of adverse findings about compliance with lower-court orders, concentrated in immigration enforcement. That sentence is as far as the sourced record goes.

Deaths in Connection With ICE: The Government’s Own Numbers

“People killed in connection with ICE” is not one number, and this report does not print it as one. The record contains three distinct categories that public argument routinely sums. Category A is deaths in ICE custody—in a facility, in transit, or in a hospital while custody remained active—the only category with an official, statutory, name-by-name public list. Category B is deaths during enforcement operations, fatal encounters with ICE and Border Patrol agents outside detention; no official list exists, and counts are press and tracker constructions that disagree. Category C is deaths shortly after release or transfer, excluded from ICE’s count by definition; cases are documented individually and no official total exists.

Category A rests on the agency’s own list, kept under a statutory reporting requirement. Since the Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act of 2018, ICE is required to publish reports of in-custody deaths, and its Detainee Death Reporting page lists each death by fiscal year. A study in JAMA, published April 16, 2026, assembled the full series from ICE’s own sources: 272 deaths in custody from fiscal 2004 through partial fiscal 2026. Fellow detainees told reporters that guards held him in a chokehold and that he said he could not breathe. The suicide count depends on the instrument, and the gap is a finding. A name-by-name reading of ICE’s own announcements yields five suicides in fiscal 2026 and three in fiscal 2025, including cases ICE called presumed suicide. The Associated Press, working from autopsy reports, coroners’ rulings, and police records, counted at least ten suicides from January 2025 through May 2026, seven in fiscal 2026 alone. The counts differ because ICE releases frequently state no manner and some deaths announced without a cause were later classified as suicides by coroners. This report prints both instruments and does not average them.

No comparable cause table exists for the preceding administration. ICE publishes the earlier counts, but no source located published a cause-by-cause tally at fiscal-year granularity for those years. The only peer-reviewed classification is JAMA’s pooled 2021–2026 band—65 deaths spanning both administrations and therefore not divisible between them: other or undetermined, 49.2 percent; cardiovascular, 18.5 percent; infectious, 13.8 percent; suicide, 10.8 percent; neurologic, 7.7 percent. JAMA’s prespecified classification contains no homicide category anywhere in its series; a death by force in its sources would fall inside other or undetermined. The absence of a prior-administration cause ledger is a limit of the public record, not a gap this report fills by inference.

The negative space is part of the record. Malnutrition, dehydration as a stated cause, abandonment as a stated cause, sleep deprivation, waterboarding, torture, and beating do not appear in any official stated cause located for fiscal 2025 or fiscal 2026. One adjacent record must travel with that sentence: ICE’s report on Genry Ruiz Guillen listed hypernatremia and hyperosmolality—conditions associated with severe water deficit—with rhabdomyolysis and a catatonic disorder. ICE did not state dehydration or neglect, and the desk does not rename its words.

The care record is separate from the cause record, and it is adverse in the findings located. In June 2024, independent physicians retained by the ACLU, American Oversight, and Physicians for Human Rights reviewed ICE’s own death reviews for 2017–2021 and judged 95 percent of the deaths preventable or possibly preventable with adequate care—an attributed expert judgment about care over a period spanning two administrations, not a set of cause-of-death rulings. The Associated Press’s May 2026 examination of its ten identified suicides reported repeated violations of ICE’s suicide-prevention standards, including intake screening, risk monitoring, and mental-health care; DHS responded that suicide remained rare and that staff followed strict safety protocols. A death attributed to untreated illness in a facility obligated to treat it therefore presents a documented care question. It is not, on any official cause located for these two years, a torture or beating death. Both halves stand.

The Historical Baseline: The Record Before the Series

The measured series begins in fiscal 2004, and its worst rate is its first year. The JAMA series opens with fiscal 2004: 28 deaths, at 127.7 per 100,000 detainee-years—the highest rate in the series, above fiscal 2020’s 75.6 and above partial fiscal 2026’s 88.9. Fiscal 2026 is the largest count the agency’s list has carried. Fiscal 2004 remains the worst rate. The desk prints both halves: a rising count over a detained population that has more than doubled since the series began, and a rate whose maximum sits at the series’ opening.

The count itself had to be forced into existence. ICE kept no central list of detainees who died in its custody and had no duty to report them to any authority. The first public number was assembled by journalists: in June 2007, investigations by The New York Times and The Washington Post counted 62 deaths in ICE detention since 2004. The cases that forced the issue had simply not been surfaced—Boubacar Bah, who died in 2007 after a fall and thirteen hours in isolation at Elizabeth, New Jersey; Hiu Lui Ng, who died in August 2008 with an undiagnosed fractured spine and terminal cancer; Felix Franklin Rodriguez-Torres, who died of testicular cancer at Eloy, Arizona, in January 2007 and appeared on no ICE list until FOIA records forced him onto it in July 2009. Under FOIA litigation and congressional pressure, ICE produced its first list in the spring of 2009, and on August 17, 2009 added ten previously unreported deaths and one new one, bringing its roster to 104—conceding that more than one in ten deaths had been omitted from the list it had just given Congress. The agency spreadsheet published in January 2010 lists 107 deaths from October 2003 through December 2009, 15 of them suicides.

For the INS era, there is no count to print. No mortality count or rate for immigration detention in 1970–2003 exists in the sources searched—not in GAO’s detention reports of the period, not in INS statistical annuals, not in the advocacy record. The absence has a structural explanation. In 1970 detention was entirely discretionary under the McCarran-Walter framework, and it had been rare in practice for a generation: the INS had operated a near-nondetention policy since 1954, when Ellis Island closed. The compiled average-daily-population series opens in fiscal 1979 at 2,347 detainees. Mandatory detention arrives in 1988, when the Anti-Drug Abuse Act required custody of aggravated felons, and in the 1996 statutes written into INA §236(c), effective 1998. There is no 1970 detention death rate because there was scarcely a detained population to have one.

One era kept a real ledger, and it is the era of actual mass ethnic detention. In the Second World War the government confined roughly 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry; its books count the dead: 128 died in the Army’s assembly centers and 1,862 in the ten War Relocation Authority camps. Causes, where the record gives them: cancer, heart disease, and tuberculosis accounted for the majority; tuberculosis alone caused roughly one death in ten. The killings are also counted, and they are seven: the Densho archive confirms seven homicides by sentry or guard gunfire across the systems—Kanesaburo Oshima at Fort Sill; Toshiro Kobata and Hirota Isomura on the night march to Lordsburg; James Ito and Jim Kanegawa, shot when military police fired into a crowd at Manzanar; James Hatsuaki Wakasa at Topaz; and Shoichi James Okamoto at Tule Lake. Each was adjudicated at the time and each ended in acquittal or exoneration; Okamoto’s sentry was acquitted of homicide and fined one dollar for the unauthorized use of government property—the bullet. At Crystal City, Texas, the Justice Department’s family internment camp, the commander’s official history counts 29 deaths by its closure in February 1948.

The inspection era left one institutional total and, beside it, case files. The National Park Service counts over 3,500 people who died on Ellis Island between 1900 and 1954, about 1,400 of them children—the dead of the island’s hospital, which functioned as detention in medical form; most arrived already ill, and the figure is not a count of people who died because they were detained. At Angel Island, which processed Chinese and other arrivals from 1910 to 1940, no ledger exists at all: the case files document individual deaths, a child of seven months among them, and the station’s historical-society fact-checking reports no documentary evidence for the suicide stories former detainees carried. Before 2004, with the Second World War exception, the American detention record contains cases, not counts.

The Care Owed on Paper

The written standard is distinct from delivery. ICE’s Performance-Based National Detention Standards, Standard 4.3, require covered facilities to provide a continuum of care including screening, prevention, diagnosis, and treatment; medical, dental, and mental-health intake screening no later than 12 hours after arrival; a comprehensive health assessment within 14 days; 24-hour emergency medical and mental-health services; prescribed medication and medically necessary treatment without interruption; and referral or transfer when a detainee’s needs exceed facility resources. The standards operate through ICE policy, contracts, and inspections and are not, standing alone, independently enforceable by a detainee in court.

Because immigration detention is civil, claims arise under the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause rather than the Eighth Amendment’s punishment clause. The Supreme Court’s cases require nonpunitive conditions and describe civil detainees as entitled to more considerate treatment than convicted criminals; Youngberg v. Romeo supplies the professional-judgment standard. The circuits are split in application: several apply deliberate indifference, borrowed from Eighth Amendment doctrine; the Fourth Circuit has applied professional judgment in a civil-detention case; and objective-indifference variants have spread since Kingsley v. Hendrickson. That is the floor and the governing dispute as written. The death reports and reviews above are the separate record of performance.

Category B has no spine, and the spread among its constructions is itself the finding. A compiled list of shootings by United States immigration agents since January 20, 2025 counts at least 43 shooting incidents resulting in 11 deaths, as of late October 2026. The two names the whole country knows are in this category, not the custody category: Renée Nicole Good, 37, a United States citizen shot by an ICE officer in Minneapolis on January 7, 2026, and Alex Jeffrey Pretti, 37, a United States citizen and intensive-care nurse shot by Border Patrol personnel in Minneapolis on January 24, 2026; the department stated Pretti was armed, and video analyses reported he was holding a phone, and the desk records both, unresolved. Other trackers give different totals: Reuters documented seven fatal shootings through July 17, 2026; The Trace counted nine fatalities by October 29, 2026; broader constructions, taking in vehicle pursuits and other encounters, reach 22 to 24. Figures above roughly 70 for January 2025 through October 2026 that circulate in public argument are sums of the custody list, the operations constructions, and tracker-identified unlisted cases across both agencies: a construction, not a count, and printed here only as one.

The Institutions: Opposition, Press, Elections, Courts

The frameworks in the first section of this report were written against regimes that abolished the institutions in this one. The commission asks what the record shows about their current operation, and each item below is observable. The 2026 midterm elections were held on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. On Associated Press race calls as of November 4–7, 2026—uncertified, with counting continuing—the Democratic Party, the opposition, won control of both the House and the Senate. In the Senate, Democrats flipped seven Republican-held seats and held every contested Democratic seat, standing at at least 54 Democratic and aligned seats to at least 44 Republican, with Alaska and Mississippi uncalled. In the House, at least 222 seats were called for the Democrats against the 218 needed. Democrats also flipped five governorships. The new Congress convenes in January 2027, producing divided government for the term’s second half; Democrats did not win the two-thirds supermajorities required to override vetoes or convict on impeachment alone. No major legal challenge to the results had been reported by November 5–7. Election-administration litigation is part of the record: at least 34 federal district-court decisions had halted or blocked administration efforts touching election administration, among them the March 2025 executive order imposing documentary proof of citizenship on the federal registration form—8 of the decisions by judges appointed by Trump himself, on the Brennan Center’s catalog. The administration complied with the injunctions while appealing.

The opposition party operated openly throughout, and the press was not shuttered. Through 2025 and 2026 the Democratic Party held seats, campaigned, raised funds, won special elections, and litigated against the administration. No opposition party has been banned, deregistered, or barred from ballots in any state in the record assembled. No United States news organization has been shuttered by the government in the record, and critical coverage is continuous; it is the source of much of this file. The documented pressure episodes, each attributed: the administration barred the Associated Press from pooled events in February 2025 over its refusal to adopt “Gulf of America” in its stylebook; Judge Trevor McFadden, a Trump appointee, ruled the exclusion violated the First Amendment, and the government dropped its appeals in March 2026. A Reuters review found 75 cases in 2025–2026 in which judges found First Amendment infringements by the administration, spanning universities, law firms, and media matters. The president and his officials routinely characterize critical outlets as “fake news” and enemies, rhetoric documented in the administration’s own posts.

The expert indices moved sharply in 2025–2026, and what they measure is democracy, not fascism; the file prints them under that label and no other. Freedom House, in Freedom in the World 2026, covering 2025, scores the United States 81 of 100, down 3 points from 84, its lowest since the scale began in 2002, and down 12 since 2005; the United States remains rated Free. The V-Dem Institute, in its Democracy Report 2026, records the Liberal Democracy Index falling from 0.75 to 0.57 in one year, its rank from 20th to 51st of 179, and reclassifies the United States from a liberal democracy to an electoral democracy for the first time in over fifty years, describing the speed as unprecedented; its analysts also note the electoral mechanics remain fundamentally intact—citizens vote, and elections are clean—with the decline located in liberal checks, rights, and executive constraint. The Economist Intelligence Unit’s Democracy Index 2025 scores the United States 7.65 of 10, a flawed democracy, its classification since 2016 and its lowest United States score since the index began. These are expert-coded assessments with published methodologies and known critics, and their 2025 moves are contested, including by commentators who argue the coders’ priors drive the results. The file prints the scores, the instruments’ nature, and the contestation. None of the three claims to measure fascism, and the desk does not use them as if they did.

Christian Nationalism: The Scholars’ Measure

The field’s standard sociological treatment defines the term as a demand on the state, not as a synonym for being Christian, evangelical, or patriotic. Andrew L. Whitehead and Samuel L. Perry, in Taking America Back for God (2020), define Christian nationalism as “a cultural framework—a collection of myths, traditions, symbols, narratives, and value systems—that idealizes and advocates a fusion of Christianity with American civic life,” contending that America has been and should remain distinctively Christian “from top to bottom.” Their measure is a six-item scale from the Baylor Religion Survey, built on agreement that the federal government should declare the United States a Christian nation, advocate Christian values, allow religious symbols in public spaces, and take steps to preserve the nation’s Christian character, should not enforce strict separation of church and state, and that United States success is part of God’s plan. On 2007 and 2017 data they sorted Americans into Rejecters, about 21.5 percent, Resisters, Accommodators, and Ambassadors, about 19.8 percent at the top; roughly half the country scored as Accommodators or Ambassadors—a figure that depends heavily on where the scale’s middle is cut, which the authors themselves discuss.

The independent series that tracks the question now measures a stable minority. The Public Religion Research Institute built a separate five-item battery—that the government should declare America a Christian nation, that United States laws should be based on Christian values, that if the United States moves away from its Christian foundations “we will not have a country anymore,” that being Christian is important to being truly American, and that God intends Christians to exercise dominion. Its 2025 American Values Atlas, more than 22,000 interviews conducted February to December 2025 and reported February 17, 2026, finds Adherents at 11 percent and Sympathizers at 21 percent, together about 32 percent of Americans, against Skeptics at 37 percent and Rejecters at 27 percent. The shares have been stable since measurement began in late 2022; its chief executive stated there is no evidence of widespread national growth in the ideology over the series. By party and religion, supporters are a majority of Republicans, at 56 percent, 67 percent of white evangelical Protestants, and 54 percent of Hispanic Protestants, while 82 percent of Democrats and 87 percent of the religiously unaffiliated are Skeptics or Rejecters. The institute also records that 38 percent of Adherents and 28 percent of Sympathizers agreed that “because things have gotten so far off track, true American patriots may have to resort to violence to save the country.” The label is contested from inside: many who score as Adherents reject the term as pejorative, while a smaller, visible set of writers adopts it affirmatively—the 2022 book The Case for Christian Nationalism, by Stephen Wolfe, argues openly for a Christian prince and an explicitly Christian polity; its representativeness is precisely what the survey data measures. Several members of Congress and state officials have used the term of themselves since 2021; the desk built no verified name-by-name catalog in this pass and prints no names it did not individually source.

The enacted footprint is concentrated at state level and in litigation; no federal confessional settlement exists in the record. The documented state items include Ten Commandments display laws, Louisiana’s 2024 classroom-display statute among them, enjoined by federal courts and litigated through 2025–2026, and Bible-infused curriculum materials approved in Texas in 2024—each a real enactment, each contested in court with mixed outcomes. At the federal level, no statute declares the United States a Christian nation; the Establishment Clause stands; and the Supreme Court’s religion jurisprudence has moved toward accommodation in funding and display cases under doctrines grounded in history and coercion tests, not in Christian nationhood. Self-described Christian nationalists hold real offices, and the movement’s organizational footprint is public and active. Its programmatic maximal goals, a confessional state and Christian-law frameworks, are not enacted federal law anywhere in the record assembled. The measurement the record supports is this: a minority ideology with majority weight inside one major party’s coalition—about one American in ten as full adherents, one in three as adherents or sympathizers, stable across the 2022–2025 measurement—with its enacted footprint at state level and in the courts. Whether that constitutes a component of fascism is an application of the first section’s frameworks, left where this report leaves all applications: with the reader.

Capitalism, Corporatism, and the Fascist Economy

The literature’s central term is the one public argument most often gets wrong, and the file corrects it from the standard references. In the scholarly and historical usage, corporatism derives from the Latin corpus, body, and means the organization of society into state-recognized functional bodies—employers’ syndicates, labor syndicates, professional guilds—through which the state manages each sector. It does not mean rule by business corporations; the term for that is corporatocracy, and conflating the two is a documented category error the standard references state explicitly. The widely circulated line that fascism should be called corporatism because it is a merger of state and corporate power, attributed to Mussolini through Gentile’s Enciclopedia Italiana entry, is an attribution the desk could not verify in Gentile’s text; it circulates in polemics from 1944 forward, and this report does not print it as a Mussolini quotation. Mussolini’s own definition is on the record, from his address to the National Council of Corporations on November 14, 1933: “Corporatism is disciplined, and therefore also a controlled economy… Corporatism surpasses socialism and surpasses liberalism, creating a new synthesis.” Fascist corporatism in practice ran through the Charter of Labour of 1927, the twenty-two corporations of 1934, and the replacement in 1939 of the elected Chamber of Deputies by the Chamber of Fasces and Corporations.

The scholarly record on the reference regimes’ economies is that private property survived and independence did not. Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany preserved private property and profit; big business was not expropriated, and in Germany major firms profited enormously. What both regimes abolished was independence: independent trade unions were dissolved, a bright-line fact with no ambiguity in the record; prices, production, and foreign exchange were increasingly state-set; and the Four-Year Plan apparatus in Germany and the IRI holding system in Italy made the state a dominant economic actor. Paxton’s formulation treats fascism as neither capitalism’s agent nor its enemy: a third force that allied with elites and business against the left while pursuing its own goals, at business’s expense when the two conflicted. Payne’s typology counts selective anti-capitalism among the fascist traits. The Marxist tradition defined fascism as, in a 1935 formulation, “the preservation by violence of the private ownership of the means of production”—that tradition’s attributed position. The test the historical record sets up is structural, with three marks: abolition of independent trade unions; compulsory state-sector bodies replacing market and parliamentary allocation; and formal subordination of firms to national plans. The contemporary United States economy exhibits none of the three. Unions remain legal and independent; no corporative chamber exists; and the 2025–2026 federal economic fights—tariffs by executive action, industrial subsidies, government equity stakes in individual firms, the 2025 Intel arrangement among them, labeled state capitalism by critics across the spectrum—occur inside a market system with private ownership intact and are litigated in open court, the tariff program itself struck down in the case recorded above. Scholars who argue the capitalism point against the label, Griffin and Payne among them, make precisely this argument: that the current economic program is recognizably anti-statist in its domestic core—deregulation, tax cuts, hostility to the administrative state—which sits awkwardly with classical fascism’s statist economics. Scholars who apply the label, Stanley among them, argue contemporary fascism can be market-fused. Both positions are in the peer-reviewed record and are printed here as positions.

The question “how fascist is capitalism” inverts in the sources, and the file prints the inversion. No major fascism scholar in the set defines capitalism itself as fascism. The live dispute is three-cornered: whether fascism is capitalism’s emergency instrument, the Marxist tradition’s position; an autonomous movement that used and then subordinated capital, Paxton’s and Griffin’s; or a politics compatible with multiple economic systems, including neoliberalism, Stanley’s. There is no measurement instrument for the question beyond the three positions, and the desk files the three.

The Fifty-Year Frame: The Hegemon at Home

The denominator comes first: the power the United States actually holds. On the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s April 2025 figures, for 2024, United States military expenditure was $997 billion, 37 percent of the world total, 3.2 times the second spender, China, at an estimated $314 billion, and 66 percent of all NATO spending. The United States maintains the world’s only global basing and alliance network; the precise base count is method-dependent and the desk adopts none. Domestically, the federal government fields the largest incarceration system in the democratic world—1,852,900 people incarcerated at year-end 2023, on the Bureau of Justice Statistics’ count, filed in this report, The Word and the Record. The outer question, how the hegemon uses its power abroad, is scoped here and not built: the documented external record of the window is a research project of its own size at this paper’s standard, and this report does not pretend to it. The domestic question is answerable from the government’s own investigated record, and the three baselines follow.

Baseline one is secret: the FBI’s covert campaign, documented by the Senate in the Bureau’s own files. The Church Committee’s final report of April 26, 1976 records that COINTELPRO, run from 1956 to 1971, was designed to “disrupt” groups and “neutralize” individuals deemed threats to domestic security—covert action against Americans engaged in lawful political activity, from the Communist Party and the civil-rights movement to the antiwar movement and elected officials. The documented tactics include infiltration, anonymous letters to spouses to destroy marriages, procuring IRS investigations to deter protest leaders, and falsely labeling members of violent groups as informants to expose them to physical attack. The campaign against Martin Luther King Jr. included wiretaps, hotel-room bugs, and an anonymous letter urging suicide. The Committee found the targets ranged far beyond persons who could properly be characterized as enemies of freedom. The reforms that followed were the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978, permanent intelligence committees, and the executive ban on assassinations. COINTELPRO was secret—exposed by a burglary in 1971, not by oversight—and its exposure produced that settlement. The signature domestic-enforcement technologies of 2025–2026 are conducted openly, announced by the government, and litigated in real time. Whether openness is better or worse is argument; that the mode differs from the 1956–1971 baseline is record.

Baseline two is the post-2001 settlement, bipartisan in construction and continuation. The USA PATRIOT Act’s Section 215 was interpreted to authorize bulk collection of all Americans’ telephone metadata, under a secret court order to Verizon disclosed on June 5, 2013, by Edward Snowden, compelling daily production of records on millions of customers with no suspicion requirement. The FISA Amendments Act of 2008, at Section 702, authorized programs collecting internet communications from nine major United States technology companies, targeting non-United States persons abroad while incidentally collecting Americans’ communications at scale; Section 702 has been repeatedly reauthorized, and the desk located the statute’s sunset timeline running into April 2026 without verifying the 2026 legislative outcome, and prints the gap as a gap. The USA FREEDOM Act of 2015 ended Section 215 bulk collection as such. The same settlement produced warrantless wiretapping under the President’s Surveillance Program, disclosed in 2005; the torture program documented in the Senate Intelligence Committee’s 2014 summary; Guantánamo; and the 2001 military-force authorization’s two-decade career across four presidents. The largest documented domestic-surveillance expansion of the last fifty years was built before, and inherited by, the current administration; it is the standing baseline of standard operating procedure for state power at home.

Baseline three is the deportation record itself, from the department’s own yearbook, and the current regime’s distinguishing features are not its removal totals. On the department’s Yearbook Table 39—a removal being a compulsory movement under a removal order, a return a confirmed departure without one, an expulsion the Title 42 category of 2020 to 2023, and all broad totals counts of events, not of unique people—the Obama administration’s fiscal 2009–2016 totals are 3,062,466 removals and 2,186,427 returns, a combined 5,248,893; the label applied to that record was coined by an advocate, Janet Murguía of the National Council of La Raza, on March 4, 2014: “this president has been the deporter-in-chief.” The first Trump administration’s removals and returns sum to about 1,795,000, about 2,002,000 with fiscal 2020’s Title 42 expulsions. The Biden administration’s fiscal 2021–2024 totals are 2,032,300 removals and returns plus 2,754,120 expulsions, about 4,786,000 on the broadest count; the Migration Policy Institute’s characterization is “nearly 4.4 million repatriations” through February 2024. For the current term, the Institute estimated about 980,000 deportations from January 20, 2025 through July 31, 2026—a pace below the Obama-era removal peak on the order-based measure, with the detention population and the death counts at records. The distinguishing features of the current regime in the documented record are the abolition of the enforcement-priority tiers that had structured ICE since 2014, by Executive Order 14159 of January 20, 2025—with the nuance that ICE’s fiscal 2026 budget justification reintroduced priority language nearly identical to the rescinded 2021 memo, on the Heritage Foundation’s analysis—; the scale of third-country removals, 27,943 from January 20, 2025 to August 5, 2026 on ICE data obtained under the Freedom of Information Act, as filed in The Interview and the Edit, the special report of November 7; interior enforcement at a visibility not seen in the earlier regimes; and the detention-death series filed above. Behind the window stand the deep-history anchors, also filed in The Interview and the Edit: the Palmer Raids of 1919–1920, which deported 556 people after mass arrests; the Mexican Repatriation of the 1930s, which removed hundreds of thousands, up to 60 percent of them United States citizens on the standard scholarly estimate; and Operation Wetback, whose official figure above one million is contradicted by the scholarly consensus of about 300,000. Mass expulsion with weak process is a recurring American practice across a century, under presidents of both parties and none. That is the baseline fact any departure claim must clear.

Filed together, the three baselines run under administrations of both parties, and the file states the continuity without drawing from it. The covert-action baseline is a bureau program of 1956–1971, exposed in 1976. The surveillance baseline was built after 2001 and continued by presidents of both parties, its founding emergency declaration renewed annually by Obama, Biden, and Trump alike. The deportation baseline’s largest combined total in the window belongs to a Democratic administration, its second-largest broad count to another, and the Republican administrations in the series sit below both on the order-based measure—while the current administration’s detention population and custody deaths stand at records on the same government’s figures. A reader running the first section’s frameworks against this record has both parties’ administrations on the page, in the government’s own numbers. The desk files the continuity and draws no conclusion from it.

January 6: The Same Instrument, Applied to the Other Famous Count

The January 6 death ledger is complete only when it carries every side and separates the day from its aftermath. The District of Columbia medical examiner supplied the causes for the deaths of the day. Attendee, officer, and defendant in the table are positions in the event and its prosecution, not findings about any death.

NameSideDateOfficial causeMannerTiming
Ashli BabbittAttendeeJan. 6, 2021Gunshot wound, left shoulderHomicideOf the day
Kevin GreesonAttendeeJan. 6, 2021Hypertensive atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseaseNaturalOf the day
Benjamin PhillipsAttendeeJan. 6, 2021Hypertensive atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseaseNaturalOf the day
Rosanne BoylandAttendeeJan. 6, 2021Acute amphetamine intoxicationAccidentOf the day
Brian SicknickOfficerJan. 7, 2021Acute brainstem and cerebellar infarcts due to acute basilar artery thrombosisNaturalNext day
Howard LiebengoodOfficerJan. 9, 2021SuicideSuicideAfter
Jeffrey SmithOfficerJan. 15, 2021SuicideSuicideAfter
Kyle DeFreytagOfficerJuly 10, 2021SuicideSuicideAfter
Gunther HashidaOfficerJuly 29, 2021SuicideSuicideAfter
Christopher StantonDefendantJan. 9, 2021SuicideSuicideAfter
Matthew PernaDefendantFeb. 25, 2022SuicideSuicideAfter
Nejourde MeachamDefendantAug. 28, 2021Suicide, reportedSuicide, reportedAfter
Mark AungstDefendantJuly 2022Suicide, reportedSuicide, reportedAfter
David HomolDefendantApr. 17, 2024Suicide, reportedSuicide, reportedAfter

The only homicide on January 6 was Babbitt’s, and the official reviews cleared the officer who fired. Capitol Police Lt. Michael Byrd shot Babbitt as she climbed through the broken window of the Speaker’s Lobby door. The Justice Department declined charges after finding no evidence that Byrd did not reasonably believe deadly force necessary in self-defense or defense of Congress; the Capitol Police found the shooting lawful and within department policy. Boyland’s examiner ruling also has a printed dispute beside it: a pathologist retained by her family concluded compressional asphyxia, while District police internal affairs cleared an officer whose baton strikes near Boyland became part of the family’s use-of-force claim. No court has adjudicated Boyland’s cause.

Sicknick’s record contains two statements by the same examiner, and both are required. Chief Medical Examiner Francisco Diaz ruled the manner natural and told the Washington Post that the autopsy found no evidence of an allergic reaction to chemical irritants and no evidence of internal or external injuries. Diaz also said Sicknick had engaged the rioters and that “all that transpired played a role in his condition.” No one was charged with killing him; two men were charged with assaulting him with chemical spray. The District’s Police and Firefighters’ Retirement and Relief Board separately found Jeffrey Smith’s January 6 injuries the sole and direct cause of his later suicide—the one formal causal adjudication attached to an aftermath death in the ledger.

The phrasing in public argument and the examiner’s record are different objects. Attorney General Merrick Garland’s January 2025 formulation referred to “the five officers who lost their lives in the line of duty”—Sicknick and the four later suicides. The examiner recorded no officer homicide and no officer death on January 6 itself. Line-of-duty recognition by the Capitol Police, the Justice Department, and benefit boards is an institutional determination printed in the research record; it is not a medical-examiner finding that rioters killed five officers. Any total drawn from the table must say whether it is counting deaths of the day, the next day, or the aftermath.

No corresponding national ledger exists for civil unrest as a whole. No federal body publishes deaths and injuries from riots by side or in total; the FBI’s LEOKA series counts officers feloniously killed in all circumstances—73 in 2021 and 64 in 2024, for example—without a riot subset for killings. Protester-side totals exist only as constructions: Forbes and Associated Press reporting counted about 19 deaths in the opening weeks of the 2020 unrest; the Guardian and ACLED counted at least 25 across 2020; an academic dataset counted 31 associated homicides; and an open-compiled multi-year list reaches 42, each under a different inclusion standard. The absence of a common instrument is part of the fifty-year record.

The Frameworks Applied: Where the Authors Land

This section does the only application work an objective file may do: it records where the frameworks’ own authors and other named scholars land, and the documented facts each side cites. It renders no measurement of its own. Under Paxton’s framework, per Paxton, the label applies, on the ground he names: open encouragement of civic violence to overturn an election. The facts his side cites: January 6, 2021; the 2020 election-overturn effort, documented in the January 6 committee record and the Georgia indictment record; the mass pardons and commutations of January 20, 2025, about 1,500 January 6 defendants, including men convicted of assaulting police; and the president’s “poisoning the blood” rhetoric of late 2023 and after, in his own words. The facts the other side cites within the same framework: Paxton’s stage model requires elite collaboration abandoning democratic liberties and redemptive violence without legal restraint as governing practice; the 2026 midterms proceeded and removed the president’s party from Congress; and the courts operate against him, as filed above. Under Griffin’s framework, per Griffin, the label does not apply: no coherent revolutionary ideology, no new-man project, no party militia, no project to replace the constitutional order. The facts his side cites: the movement’s program is restorative—“again”—rather than futural-revolutionary; its economic core is deregulatory; its organization is a personalist electoral coalition inside an existing party. The facts the other side cites: Griffin himself calls the MAGA slogan palingenetic in form, and critics inside fascism studies argue the rebirth myth need not be coherent to function, since Griffin’s framework runs on mythic core. Under Stanley’s pillars, Stanley applies all ten to the current United States in his own writing; his framework expressly contemplates fascist politics inside a still-functioning democracy, so the institutional record filed above does not, within his framework, refute the application. His critics, Griffin and Payne among them, argue the pillars describe illiberal populism generally and thereby dilute the category.

The comparative floor under the whole argument is a matter of record, and both sides of the argument stand on it. The reference regimes’ documented record includes, for Nazi Germany, the industrialized murder of approximately six million Jews and millions of others, a world war killing tens of millions, and the abolition of elections, parties, unions, and courts as independent bodies within months of taking power; and for Fascist Italy, the abolition of parliament, the murder of Giacomo Matteotti, the racial laws, and wars of conquest. No sourced element of the 2025–2026 United States record assembled in this file is of that category or scale, and the abolition list stands unexecuted in the institutional record filed above. That floor underlies two different uses, and the file prints both and takes neither: the argument that the label, applied to the present, fails by orders of magnitude; and the position of the scholars recorded above that the label, applied now, describes a politics and a trajectory—in Paxton’s terms, the territory of his first three stages—not a completed regime, which none of the four framework authors in this file claims.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. The first side is the definition itself: the field’s frameworks disagree about the threshold, and their authors, applying their own instruments to the same man, reach opposite conclusions—Paxton and Stanley apply the label, Griffin and Payne withhold it, and Eco’s list, by its author’s design, cannot settle the question it is most often used to settle. No agreed metric exists, and the democracy indices that moved sharply this year measure a different quantity than the one in this report’s headline. The second side is the compliance record: the fifty-year baseline contains no judicial finding of presidential defiance, and the 2025–2026 record contains such findings in writing from multiple judges, an appellate reversal of the largest contempt proceeding, compliance in the flagship case after 83 days, and compliance with the Supreme Court’s two largest merits rulings—and no official scorekeeper exists by whom that record could be summed into a rate. The third side is the deaths record: the custody list is the government’s own and its current fiscal year is its highest, and the operations category beside it has no official list at all, so the one total the public argument most wants does not exist in any source and is not manufactured here. Around those three open points, the bearings that are single-valued are these: the midterms were held on schedule four days ago and the opposition won both chambers on the Associated Press’s calls, uncertified as this report files; no opposition party is banned and no news organization has been shuttered by the government in the record; the detained population and the custody death count stand at records on the government’s own figures while removal totals sit inside the historical range on the same government’s yearbook; and Christian nationalism measures at one American in ten. The log proceeds.

The Companion Essay

The argument this file does not make is published by this paper’s publisher on his own program, The Chris Abraham Show, in his own voice, as “The Worst Hitler Ever.” The essay takes the position the record above is most often argued from: that the president is the worst fascist ever—that he cannot do the thing the label names, that the villainy is performed rather than executed, and not jackbooting enough to register on the frameworks’ own scales. This paper prints no part of it and adopts none of it; the link stands so the reader can follow the argument the desk declined to carry, from the record above to the case the record supports in another man’s telling.

The File, Clipped

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective, a source with a position, printed because it is useful, and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Twenty-two items.

Subjective
Robert O. Paxton — The Anatomy of Fascism, Knopf, 2004

The field’s standard behavioral definition, quoted in the report above from page 218, with the five stages of fascism from movement to radicalization or entropy, and the finding that only Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany passed through all five. The framework against which its author later measured an American president.

Subjective
Robert O. Paxton — “I’ve Hesitated to Call Donald Trump a Fascist. Until Now,” Newsweek, January 11, 2021; and The New York Times Magazine, October 23, 2024

Paxton’s own application of his framework: the January 6 attack removes his objection, the label “now seems not just acceptable but necessary,” the historical circumstances remain profoundly different from interwar Europe; in 2024 he confirms the diagnosis and says in the same interview that the word generates more heat than light.

Subjective
Roger Griffin — The Nature of Fascism, 1991

The “fascist minimum”: a palingenetic form of populist ultranationalism. Griffin’s published commentary on the present case, as carried in scholarly surveys of it, withholds the label—an “ochlocrat” practicing illiberal populism, rebirth rhetoric without the revolutionary ideology his definition requires.

Subjective
Umberto Eco — “Ur-Fascism,” The New York Review of Books, June 22, 1995

The fourteen features, from the cult of tradition to Newspeak, with the author’s own caveat printed in the same essay: the features cannot be organized into a system, many contradict each other, and one suffices for fascism to coagulate around it. The desk files the list and the caveat together.

Subjective
Jason Stanley — How Fascism Works: The Politics of Us and Them, 2018

The ten pillars of fascist politics, defined by their author as tactics a still-democratic polity can exhibit, and applied by him in full to the current United States in his books and interviews from 2018 forward. His framework expressly does not require a fascist state.

Subjective
Stanley G. Payne — A History of Fascism, 1914–1945, 1995

The typology that distinguishes fascism from other authoritarianisms by anti-liberalism, anti-conservatism, and selective anti-capitalism, a party militia, and the totalitarian new man. Payne’s position in scholarly discussion, as carried in surveys of it: authoritarian populism, not fascism, and a warning that overuse of the term undermines precision.

Subjective
The New York Times — John Kelly’s recorded interviews, October 22, 2024

The president’s longest-serving chief of staff reads a general definition aloud and answers it: the former president “certainly falls into the general definition of fascist, for sure,” “certainly prefers the dictator approach to government.” The definition is the general one Kelly read, not a scholarly framework; the Trump campaign at the time called his accounts fabricated.

Subjective
Bob Woodward — War, 2024

Gen. Mark Milley, former chairman of the Joint Chiefs, as quoted in Woodward’s reporting: Trump is “fascist to the core” and “the most dangerous person to this country.” A secondhand quotation in a journalist’s book, filed as attributed.

Subjective
Federal Judicial Center — the history of executive enforcement of judicial orders

The judiciary’s own institutional history: substantial compliance as the historical norm, defiance on rare occasions, the Worcester non-enforcement, Merryman, and the Jackson enforcement line marked as apocryphal. The baseline document for the report’s compliance section.

Subjective
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement — Detainee Death Reporting

The agency’s statutory public list of deaths in its custody, by fiscal year, kept under the Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act of 2018. The spine of this report’s deaths section: fiscal 2026 stands at 36 listed deaths on the page, with two more announced in the agency’s own releases.

Subjective
Basu et al. — “Mortality in US Immigration and Customs Enforcement Detention,” JAMA, April 16, 2026

The full series assembled from ICE’s own sources: 272 deaths in custody from fiscal 2004 through partial fiscal 2026, and the rate series—13.0 per 100,000 person-years in fiscal 2023, 47.5 in fiscal 2025, 88.9 in partial fiscal 2026, the highest since fiscal 2004.

Subjective
Human Rights Watch — the detention mortality measurement, June 25, 2026

The organization’s measurement of the custody death rate against the detained population: the rate up about 138 to 140 percent year over year on a 77 percent rise in the population—deaths rising faster than the number detained, on its figures.

Subjective
Senate Select Committee — Final Report, the Church Committee, April 26, 1976

The government’s own investigation of its intelligence agencies, 2,702 pages: COINTELPRO’s disruption and neutralization campaigns against lawful political activity, the informant-labeling and spouse-letter tactics, the campaign against Dr. King, and the finding that the targets ranged far beyond enemies of freedom.

Subjective
Department of Homeland Security, Office of Homeland Security Statistics — Yearbook of Immigration Statistics, Table 39

The department’s own removal, return, and expulsion series by fiscal year, from which the report’s administration-by-administration totals are summed: Obama 5,248,893 removals and returns combined; the broadest full-term Biden count about 4.79 million with expulsions; the first Trump administration about 2.0 million on the same construction. Event counts, not unique people.

Subjective
Freedom House — Freedom in the World 2026

The index’s United States score: 81 of 100, down 3 points, its lowest on the current scale, down 12 since 2005—and the rating unchanged: Free. An expert-coded assessment of democracy, printed in this report under that label.

Subjective
V-Dem Institute — Democracy Report 2026

The index’s United States movement: Liberal Democracy Index 0.75 to 0.57 in one year, rank 20th to 51st of 179, and reclassification from liberal democracy to electoral democracy for the first time in over fifty years—with its analysts’ own note that the electoral mechanics remain fundamentally intact.

Subjective
Economist Intelligence Unit — Democracy Index 2025; Pew Research Center, 2026

The EIU’s United States score, 7.65 of 10, a flawed democracy as classified since 2016 and the lowest United States score in the index’s history; and Pew’s side-by-side republication of the Freedom House, V-Dem, and EIU series from 2005 to 2025, the cleanest single exhibit of the trend lines.

Subjective
Public Religion Research Institute — American Values Atlas, 2025 (reported February 17, 2026)

The Christian nationalism battery on more than 22,000 interviews: Adherents 11 percent, Sympathizers 21 percent, Skeptics 37 percent, Rejecters 27 percent; supporters a majority of Republicans at 56 percent; the shares stable since measurement began in late 2022.

Subjective
Andrew L. Whitehead and Samuel L. Perry — Taking America Back for God, Oxford University Press, 2020

The field’s standard sociological treatment: the definition quoted in the report, the six-item Baylor Religion Survey scale, and the four-way sort from Rejecters to Ambassadors, with the authors’ own discussion of how the middle categories are cut.

Subjective
Stockholm International Peace Research Institute — “Trends in World Military Expenditure, 2024,” April 2025

The denominator of the hegemon question: United States military expenditure $997 billion, 37 percent of the world total, 3.2 times the second spender, 66 percent of NATO spending.

Subjective
Just Security — Litigation Tracker; CNN — the judicial-criticism analysis, 2026

The trackers behind the report’s litigation volume: roughly 700 to 800 challenges filed or active, one mid-2026 snapshot at 262 rulings for plaintiffs to 126 for the government; and CNN’s count of at least 77 orders containing sharp judicial criticism, from 69 judges, 11 of them Trump appointees. Method-dependent figures, filed as their makers’ counts.

Subjective
Brennan Center — the election-administration decisions catalog, 2026; Associated Press — midterm race calls, November 3–7, 2026

The catalog of at least 34 district-court decisions halting administration election-administration efforts, 8 of them by Trump appointees; and the AP calls on which this report’s midterm record rests—both chambers to the opposition, seven Senate flips, five governorships—uncertified as filed.
items.summary: The scholarly definitions of fascism as their authors state and apply them, the constitutional record, the courts and the compliance record, ICE's own death reporting, the institutions after the midterms, and the fifty-year frame. The whole record, attributed.

items.title: Explosions Again on Qeshm, a President Removed in Asunción, and the Count Still Waits
items.content_html:
The Midday File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Peña Before the Prosecutors, the Count Unmoved, and Oil Down Thirteen Percent on the Week

The news at midday on a closed-market Saturday: the week’s one completed presidency ended the morning in a prosecutor’s office in Asunción, the mediator in Doha said the talks live and progress has been made, the count in Mississippi and Alaska did not move and its published figures do not agree with each other, and the markets’ week stood settled—stocks down for a fourth week, oil down thirteen percent—under the one report of the day, Berkshire Hathaway’s softer quarter and record cash.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Saturday, November 7, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 14, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today. Where the midday figures differ from the morning’s, the difference is stated here, in the open. The overnight edition stands unrevised, as a log stands.

The Midday in Brief

Saturday at noon is a short file, and the desk files it short. The morning produced one completed act, in Asunción, where former President Santiago Peña arrived at the Attorney General’s Office to appear before prosecutors, a day after the Senate removed him over the collapse of Ueno Bank and authorities placed him under house arrest. It produced one official statement of consequence, in Doha, where Qatar’s prime minister said the mediation continues, progress has been made, and the aim is a good agreement rather than a perfect one. The count produced nothing: no new totals were reported from Mississippi or Alaska by noon, and the figures in circulation disagree with each other by several hundred votes in Mississippi, which the desk states plainly below. The markets produced a reading rather than a session: the exchanges are closed, the week stands settled at the S&P 500 down 2.7 percent and Brent crude at $98.32, down 13.3 percent on the week, and the one scheduled report of the day, Berkshire Hathaway’s third quarter, arrived at 0800 with operating earnings down 5.8 percent and a cash position at a record. The desk files the day in that order.

Asunción at Midday: The Former President Before the Prosecutors

The removal is complete, and the case has begun. Reuters’ Asunción file, filed below, reports that former President Santiago Peña arrived at the Attorney General’s Office on Saturday to appear before prosecutors, a day after he was impeached and placed under house arrest in the crisis triggered by the collapse of the digital lender Ueno. Prosecutors said on Friday that the charges against Peña were still being determined but could include influence peddling. A second account puts the appointment at 11 a.m. before the Economic Crimes and Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office, with Prosecutor Silvia González confirming that Peña spent Friday night detained at his Asunción residence; after his statement is received, or his refusal to give one is recorded, prosecutors must file formal charges and request precautionary measures from the duty court. The accusations in the impeachment itself are on the record from Friday: conflicts of interest, manipulation of regulatory oversight, diversion of pension funds, and participation in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank. Peña has denied wrongdoing. Those are allegations, stated as allegations; no court has ruled on any of them.

The government that replaced him is at work, and its first subject is the depositors. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in on Friday to complete the term through August 2028. The figures of the collapse stand as filed overnight: Ueno served about three million customers, roughly 60 percent of Paraguay’s adults, and held as much as $850 million in public money; regulators seized it on November 3 after its solvency fell below half the required level; the deposit guarantee covers up to about $38,000 per depositor, and preliminary central bank estimates place 97 percent of account holders fully within that ceiling, with payment required within 15 days under banking law. Alliana told compatriots affected by the collapse that they would be fully compensated, in the account filed below. What the new government has not yet put on the record by noon is the machinery: which office pays, on what schedule, and from what fund. That is the next fact in this file, and it has not arrived.

Qeshm and Doha: No Confirmation From Washington, a Statement From the Mediator

The war’s midday state is the night’s state, with one addition from the mediator. Reuters’ Saturday file on the mediation reports that Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani said the country’s mediation efforts between the United States and Iran were continuing to prevent the situation from spiralling out of control; that the American administration remained willing to find a solution even after the midterm elections; that significant progress had been made; and that he expressed confidence a settlement could be reached. His sentence, as carried, is: “We cannot wait to reach a perfect agreement; we hope to reach a good agreement.” The same file records the other side of the morning: Tasnim said initial reports indicated two missiles had struck Qeshm Island with no official information on possible damage, and the United States has not yet announced any attack on targets inside Iran. The explosions reported from Qeshm in the night remain unconfirmed as to origin and damage; Iran’s claims of American drones destroyed over the island remain unconfirmed by Washington; and the mediation, by the mediator’s own statement, remains open.

Qatar’s International Media Office added the correction the morning required. Circulating reports that the prime minister had said the two sides had failed to reach an agreement are, in the office’s words, “false and misleading,” and his remarks were “deliberately distorted.” The office stated that both sides continue to work towards a deal and that Qatari mediators remain in close coordination with Washington and Tehran. The fuller statement is filed below. A claim of failure circulated, the office running the talks denied it by name, and the prime minister then said progress had been made. No agreement has been announced by any side. The larger American decision the week has waited on since Thursday—whether to resume the war in full—has not been announced by noon either.

The Count at 1200: No New Totals, and the Tallies Disagree

Mississippi has not moved, and the desk corrects its own morning figures to the range the tallies actually support. The overnight edition carried the wire’s Friday-evening margin: Scott Colom, the Democrat, ahead of Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, by 2,574 votes. The accounts the desk took in by noon do not agree on that number. One account puts the separation at nearly 2,500 votes on Friday, with an estimate of about 30,000 ballots outstanding—an estimate revised down from about 44,000 on Friday morning. A second records the Decision Desk HQ tally at 2,734 votes on Friday afternoon. A results page carrying the wire’s data shows 953,314 votes counted with 96.9 percent of the expected vote in and about 31,000 remaining, and calculates that Hyde-Smith would need 53.2 percent of the remaining vote to overtake Colom. The cocked hat on Mississippi at noon is therefore a range, not a point: Colom leads by somewhere between roughly 2,500 and 2,734 votes, with roughly 30,000 ballots estimated outstanding. The settled facts around the range are these: 9,242 affidavit ballots had been processed by Friday, mail ballots postmarked by Election Day may arrive through November 10, voters may resolve identification issues through November 10, counties certify by November 13, and Mississippi has no automatic recount procedure.

Alaska has not moved either, and its next movement is dated. Mary Peltola, the Democrat, leads Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, by 637 first-choice votes, the figure that has stood since Wednesday, with about three-quarters of ballots counted. The Saturday account of the two races files the legal position: in Alaska the skirmishing began before the voting, the Justice Department sued to block certification should the incumbent lose, and on Friday Peltola’s campaign sued the Division of Elections for records identifying rejected absentee ballots and the reasons for each rejection—records the state calls confidential preliminary data, in the suit’s own account filed below. Absentee ballots may arrive through November 18, the day the ranked-choice tabulation is expected, since no candidate has cleared 50 percent; the state is not required to report more votes before November 10. A fourth candidate, a retired teacher also named Dan Sullivan, holds about 3,600 votes, more than five times the margin, and how his voters ranked the two leaders is the open arithmetic of the race. At noon, neither Senate race has been called, for the fourth day.

The Markets’ Reading: A Closed Exchange, a Settled Week, One Report

There is no session to report on a Saturday, so the desk reports the week the session left behind. The closing account stands as filed Friday: the S&P 500 at 7,376.86, up 0.3 percent on the day and down 2.7 percent on the week; the Nasdaq Composite at 24,579.42, up 1.1 percent on the day and down 3.4 percent on the week; the Dow Jones Industrial Average at 51,285.73, down 0.5 percent on the day and 0.9 percent on the week—the worst week for the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq since June, in the week’s recap filed below. Oil’s week is the larger figure. Brent settled at $98.32, down 13.3 percent on the week, its steepest weekly fall since April 2020, and West Texas Intermediate closed at $90.83, down 12.8 percent, in the strait’s daily brief and the market accounts filed below; both benchmarks had peaked on October 30, Brent at $113.43, before hopes of an American-Iranian agreement that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz pulled the premium out. The brief records the strait itself as closed in its own accounting, with two transits recorded on October 25 against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 a day, and 132 vessels holding position away from berth at 1200 UTC. Monday’s open, by every account the desk read, hinges on the weekend’s Iran headlines—which is to say, on the file in the section above this one.

The day’s one scheduled report arrived at 0800 and was softer at the top and larger at the bottom. Berkshire Hathaway’s release reports third-quarter operating earnings of $12.705 billion, down 5.8 percent from $13.485 billion a year earlier, on weaker insurance results; net earnings of $22.112 billion, or $15,502 per Class A share, down from $30.796 billion; investment gains of $9.407 billion against $17.311 billion a year earlier; and share repurchases of about $9.6 billion in the quarter, bringing the nine-month total to about $14.4 billion. The fuller account adds that operating earnings per Class A share, at $8,907, came in above the $8,821.84 average forecast of four analysts surveyed by FactSet; that underwriting profit fell 42.9 percent, with each of the three insurance groups earning less from underwriting than a year earlier; and that the cash position reached $377.4 billion at the end of September, a record. It was the third quarter under Chief Executive Greg Abel. Berkshire’s own instruction in the release is the desk’s: the summary is not adequate for an informed judgment, and the quarterly filing is the document.

Shenzhen Stands: No New Word by Noon

The week’s largest diplomatic fact received no new word on Saturday, and the desk files it standing. Beijing’s confirmation, first made on Wednesday, that China is in communication with Washington and Moscow about a meeting of Presidents Xi, Trump, and Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19 remains the position at noon, in the account filed below. The Kremlin said work is under way to arrange it. The White House has not confirmed it. The three leaders have never held formal talks together. What each capital wants differs on the record: Washington, nuclear weapons; Moscow, Ukraine discussed without Kyiv at the table; Beijing, Ukraine held to be a European conflict and not the meeting’s subject. No final decision has been announced. Eleven days remain.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings, honestly plotted, give a triangle and not a point. On Mississippi, the tallies in circulation at noon put Colom’s lead between roughly 2,500 and 2,734 votes; the desk publishes the range and does not choose inside it. On Qeshm, the reported explosions, the claimed drones, and the confirmed Friday strike are three separate facts that the files do not join, and the desk does not join them. On the mediation, the mediator says progress; no other party has announced an agreement, a date, or a text. On Asunción, the removal and the appearance are complete; the charges are not yet filed and the allegations are not findings. On the markets, the week is settled and Monday is not. The edition closes at noon with the count unmoved, the war undecided, and one presidency ended and answering questions.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 17 items.

Subjective
Reuters, via Duke FM — Paraguay’s ex-president faces prosecutors after impeachment and house arrest

Asunción, November 7: former President Santiago Peña arrived at the Attorney General’s Office on Saturday to appear before prosecutors, a day after he was impeached and placed under house arrest amid a political and financial crisis triggered by the collapse of digital lender Ueno; prosecutors said on Friday that charges against Peña were still being determined but could include influence peddling; his removal brought Vice President Pedro Alliana to power to complete the term through August 2028; and lawmakers who backed the impeachment accused Peña of conflicts of interest, manipulating regulatory oversight and participating in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.

Subjective
Sociedad Media — Peña detained at home, due before prosecutors Saturday

Asunción, November 7: Santiago Peña spent Friday night in custody at his residence after the Senate removed him as president over the collapse of Ueno Bank, the Senate voting unanimously among the 44 senators present with one absent; the Public Ministry said its agents detained Peña and former central bank president Carlos Carvallo Spalding for the alleged commission of breach of trust and other offenses; Prosecutor Silvia González confirmed Peña would appear Saturday, November 7, at 11 a.m. before the Economic Crimes and Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office; after his statement, prosecutors must file formal charges and request precautionary measures; and the probe covers alleged irregularities in the supervision of Ueno, possible conflicts of interest tied to Peña’s links to Grupo Vázquez, and the placement of public funds in the bank, including pension and health fund money.

Subjective
The Daily Caller — Paraguayan president removed from office after bank collapse
